en: The *Nyāyāvatāra*, composed by the great-minded Śrī Siddhasena, the lion among logicians (*tarkapañcānana*),
together with the marginal notes (*ṭippana*) by Śrī Devabhadrasūri and the commentary (*ṭīkā*) by Śrī Siddharṣigaṇi.
Having bowed to Vardhamāna, who taught that the universal and the particular are inseparable,
this *Nyāyāvatāravivṛti* is composed for the purpose of increasing the seeds of mindfulness.
[NAV_0.0] And its opening statement is this:
[NAV_0] "This is commenced for the purpose of elucidating the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

[NAV_0.1] By the words "the means of valid cognition" and so forth, [it is shown that] because sound (*dhvani*) is devoid of any relationship characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*),...

Dharmottara maintains that because validity with respect to an external object is impossible, listeners are encouraged toward listening by means of the doubt regarding the object that arises through the indication of the subject matter (*abhidheya*) and so forth. This is incorrect; for if the word indeed possesses no capacity to illuminate an object, [how could it produce such a doubt?]
How then could this [author] be so proficient even in indicating the subject matter (*abhidheya*) and other such elements?

Furthermore, discerning persons (*prekṣāvantaḥ*) do not entertain doubt regarding the meaning upon hearing this if it were invalid, because that would entail the loss of its status as such, and because there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that activity would never cease even from false cognition (*mithyājñāna*). Arcata, however, says:
“This does not encourage the śrāvakas, because it lacks authoritative status, and because they do not engage with what is not authoritative.”
Otherwise, the status of being a discerning person (*prekṣāvattā*) would be undermined.

Rather, it is for the purpose of pointing out the unestablished nature (*asiddhatā*) of the reason (*hetu*) put forward by an opponent when the occasion arises during the exposition of the meaning of the treatise. For instance, there may indeed be one who speaks thus: "This [treatise] should not be commenced, because it is devoid of a subject matter (*abhidheya*) and so forth."
"Like an examination of a crow’s teeth";

by this statement of his, which illuminates its similarity to that [useless inquiry], the unestablished nature of its reasons is pointed out. That is even more incorrect: for if this [treatise] does not directly define the subject matter and so forth by stating "this is not a means of valid cognition," it would not function [to guide the listener].
Therefore, we see that it is devoid of logic to say that [the treatise] subsequently points out the unestablished nature (*asiddhatā*) of the reasons put forward by the opponent;

for that which is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*) is incapable of effecting anything, otherwise the investigation of means of valid cognition would fall into futility. Consequently, at the beginning of the treatise, it is said that this work, being a means of valid cognition, establishes the subject matter and so forth, thereby inducing the wise to engage with it.
[NAV_0.2] If it is asked, "Since this [scripture] is devoid of any relation, how can it be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to its object?"—then it must be stated:

"In that case, how is it a means of valid cognition even in the case of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)? If it is argued that [perception is valid] by virtue of the relation consisting in the state of the grasped and the grasper (*grāhyagrāhakabhāva*), we reply that here too [scripture is valid] by virtue of the relation consisting in the state of the signified and the signifier (*vācyavācakabhāva*). If it is asked, "How is that [relation] itself [established]?"...

Even in the case of direct perception (*adhyakṣa*), it must be explained how the relationship between the object of cognition and the cognizer (*vedya-vedaka-bhāva*) exists. If you say it is due to "arising from that" (*tadutpatti*) and "having the form of that" (*tadākāratā*), then what is this so-called "arising from that"?
If you say it means "being produced by that," [we reply:]...

We maintain that [the causal efficiency of a thing] is difficult to establish given its momentary perishability. To explain: there are three possible ways in which an object that perishes in a single moment might produce an effect—either in its own moment, or before it, or after it. Among these, the first position cannot be accepted, because there is no operation toward an effect that exists simultaneously with itself.
Otherwise, there would follow the consequence that all momentary objects existing at a single moment stand in a mutual relationship of cause and effect;

and thus, the relationship of grasped and grasper resulting from that would lead to an untenable conclusion. Now, if you think it acts before its own moment—this too is not elegant, because that which is itself non-existent, like a future Śaṅkha-cakravartin, lacks any activity toward an effect existing in a prior time. Or, if you should think that it produces the effect after its own moment—
This too is even more untenable, because that which has perished is incapable of performing an action;
otherwise, there would be the crowing of a dead peacock. Furthermore, as for its having that form, is it due to the transfer of the object's form?

Now, [you argue] that it is because cognition arises as something similar to that [object]? If the first alternative is intended, that is incorrect, because if the object were to impart its own form to the cognition, it would follow that the object itself is formless.

For it would follow that one's own body would be perceived as having a greater magnitude [than it actually is], and there would result the undesirable consequence of the head splitting open or being submerged in water. Or is it the second case?
If so, it follows that the determination of an object occurs by virtue of similarity (*sādṛśya*). Yet, in your philosophical system, similarity does not exist as a real entity (*tāttvika*).

Because it is accepted that the ultimate reality consists of particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) defined as isolated, momentary atoms; and because, while there is a restriction in the apprehension of objects through the power of similarity established by conceptual construction— which arises subsequent to a non-conceptual, isolated perception whose existence is produced by the awakening of latencies (*vāsanā*) accumulated from beginningless time— it would follow without distinction that the blueness residing in all things such as the sky-lotus, which pervades the entire range of time, would be established within a single momentary atom of blue.

And thus, the specific relationship between the grasped object and the grasper would not be established. If it is argued that the conceptualization of "blueness" arises by virtue of the power of perceiving the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the blue object standing before one as pointed out by the tip of a finger, and therefore determines only that very [object], and not what is past, future, or located in a crow’s eye or a water-lily; [we reply:]
In that case, conceptual construction would necessarily be grounded in the particular (svalakṣaṇa),
because it grasps an object capable of causal efficiency as delimited by specific place and time. For instance,
is its determination a conceptualization of that [particular], or is it a perception of that?

That is not yet conceptualization, because according to your own view, conceptualizations do not enter into the intrinsic nature (*svalakṣaṇa*) of things. As it has been said: "Therefore, [cognitions] whose object is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) are said to have the universal (*sāmānya*) as their domain."
And because words and cognitions are impossible with respect to a real entity.

[NAV_0.3] Now, one might say: although conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) do not, in reality, have the universal as their object, nevertheless, because perception and conceptual construction proceed simultaneously, the deluded cognizer determines that the conceptual construction is grounded in the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*).
And so it has been said:
"Because the two minds—the conceptual and the non-conceptual—occur simultaneously, or because of their rapid occurrence, the deluded person determines them to be one. (NAV 0.2)
So, how is this to be believed through oaths—
that one, due to delusion, determines the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) by means of conceptual construction,
and does not, moreover, directly perceive it with a clear manifestation?
And in this way, even perception grasps all individual objects;

yet, due to the delusion of conceptual construction (*vikalpa-moha*), it appears to have only a proximate object—this objection raised by the opponent would be difficult to refute. Alternatively, if the apprehension of that [object] were what constitutes conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), then you would be admitting by your own words that conceptual construction is grounded in the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). And thus, in the pair of conceptual constructions...

Furthermore, the state of having existence culminating in causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsamartha*) approaches even the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). And if one were to assert that the conceptual construction enters the very palace of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*),
then, in that case, it would be impossible to prevent the entry of the word (*dhvani*) into its interior as well.
Because it accompanies that [conceptualization]. As your own teacher has said:

"That alone is the object of words which is the object of conceptualizations. And there is nothing else apart from conceptualization that establishes similarity, because perception is inclined toward grasping the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) which is distinct from everything in the world. Therefore, if its production as something similar to that [object] constitutes its having that form, [then...]
Therefore, according to the reasoning already established, one must admit that conceptual construction has as its object a thing present [to the senses];

and thus, it is proven that the word-sound (*dhvani*) is also its object, which establishes our desired conclusion. Otherwise, there would be no such conformity to its form, since there is no other possible way. Consequently, neither "arising from that" (*tadutpatti*) nor "having that form" (*tadākāratā*) exist as causes for the relationship between the apprehended and the apprehender.
[NAV_0.4] Or let them be so; nevertheless, you must be questioned from the standpoint of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*):
are these the causes of apprehension individually or collectively?
If it is the first position, [then...]
It would follow that the moment of the pot characterized by its final state (kapāla) is the apprehender of [the preceding] moment of the pot,
because it is produced from it;
or else, the moon in the water would be the apprehender of the moon in the sky.

Because it possesses that form. Now, if the second [alternative] were the case, it would follow that the moment immediately following the jar is the grasper of the preceding moment, because it arises from it and possesses its form. Since an object is insentient (*jaḍa*), it cannot be a grasper.
If it is argued that [the definition applies] because cognition possesses both the production of that [object] and its form,
we now understand this:

even this [definition] fails when applied to the nature of the grasper in a cognition produced by a mental attention (*manaskāra*) characterized as a preceding moment of consciousness that grasps an object of the same content.

Because it does not grasp the mental attention (*manaskāra*) existing in the preceding moment that produces [the cognition]. If it is argued that the causal factors for its production and its assuming that form are complete only when accompanied by the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of that [object],
whereas they do not exist in the case of mental attention— then what kind of "accompaniment" is this with something whose object is different?

For indeed, your view is as follows: "Determination (*adhyavasāya*), arising by the power of the awakening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), conceptualizes a universal that lacks objective reality; whereas perception, having acquired its own existence from the external object, directly realizes that very [object] in its form.

Thus, the association with conceptualization does not contribute any specific quality whatsoever to perception. This, then, is the cause for the relationship between the apprehended and the apprehender.
Furthermore, that which you have asserted regarding perception—
that it falls apart the more it is investigated— is not to be relied upon. For instance,

even though perception lacks the characteristics of the relationship between the apprehended object and the apprehending subject as established [by us], there nonetheless exists the state of being an apprehender and the state of being an apprehended object.
Because it is observed to be so,

and because otherwise there would follow the undesirable consequence of the total cessation of all worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), as you yourselves have also admitted; likewise, you must accept that a word possesses the capacity to denote and that an object possesses the capacity to be denoted.
For here too, the loss of what is observed and the destruction of conventional practice are equally applicable. Now, you might argue as follows:

"Just as those who act upon hearing the words of a deceptive person—such as 'A cartload of molasses has been overturned on the riverbank! Run, run, children!'—become victims of deception," [so too would our case be].

"Therefore, there is no confidence in any verbal testimony"—if this is so, then we reply: "In that case, the clear perception which reaches the path of manifestation, touching the shimmering circle of mirage-rays in the desert and appearing as water, is seen to be false; thus, we declare that there is no confidence in any perceptions. The cognition of water in mirage-rays is invalid because it is sublated by a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that presents a contrary object at a later time.
If it is argued that cognitions of other truths, pillars, and so forth do not [constitute valid means of knowledge] because they are subject to sublation,
then why has this same principle been devoured by crows even in the case of sound?

For we do not accept the authority of all words; rather, [we accept it] only of those whose authors are well-ascertained and trustworthy. Thus, we perceive no difference between perception and verbal testimony with respect to their authority. However, this may be the distinction:
because it is produced by a specific causal complex such as the eye and so forth, perception grasps a present and determinate object and possesses a clear manifestation.

Verbal cognition, however, because it lacks such causes, has an indistinct appearance and grasps objects that are either determinate or indeterminate. Nor does this distinction undermine its validity;

otherwise, inference too would be rendered invalid, since it also grasps objects that are indistinct and indeterminate. But in ultimate reality, [perception] has the nature of grasping all objects that pervade the three times.

Furthermore, when the substance of the soul (*jīvadravya*) is obscured by a veil, its transformation into the apprehension of a proximate and distinct object—occurring by virtue of the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) of that veil which depends upon the causal complex of the eyes and other senses—is called "perception" (*pratyakṣa*). However, the transformation into the apprehension of objects that are either determinate or indeterminate, and not vivid, which arises from a subsidence [of the veil] dependent upon sound, is "verbal cognition" (*śābda*). Therefore, [the definition of perception] does not consist in being produced by that [object] or having the form of that [object].

Whether in perception, verbal cognition, or any other form of knowledge, these two exist as real entities. Therefore, it is established that this opening statement sets forth the ultimate subject matter, purpose, and relationship [between them].
In this context, the "subject matter" (abhidheya) is that which is expressed.

And that alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) here, because it is precisely that which is to be established by the context; he defines it by the term "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) as a component [of the definition]. The purpose (*prayojana*) is twofold:
And for both the listener and the author, it is again twofold:
immediate and mediated. Therein, the immediate purpose for the listener is the proficiency regarding the objects of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
for the author, it is the instruction of the student who is being made proficient due to his intelligence. Demonstrating therein his own purpose:

[The word *ārabhyate*] is used [in this sense] because it requires the words "by me" (*mayā*) and "this" (*asya*). However, the author—intending that the purpose of the student will be obtained through the very combination of prefix and root (*upasarga-dhātu-samudāya*) in the expression "for the sake of instruction" (*vyutpattaye*), which already contains that [purpose] within itself—indicates his own activity by means of the causative suffix (*ṇic*):
"for the sake of instructing in the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa-vyutpādanārtham*). The remote purpose is twofold:

[The purpose] is both conventional (*vyāvahārika*) and ultimate (*pāramārthika*). The conventional [purpose] consists of the characteristics of rejection, acceptance, and indifference toward objects that are to be rejected, accepted, or disregarded. The ultimate [purpose] is the attainment of higher prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). Although this [ultimate purpose] is not explicitly stated here, it should be understood as being implied by the mention of the [conventional] purpose itself, because it is the fruit of the immediately following [conventional] purpose. The relationship (*sambandha*), however, is characterized by that of means (*upāya*) and the goal to be attained (*upeya*).
In this context, the means (*upeya*) is the thorough understanding of the subject matter of the treatise (*prakaraṇa*), while the treatise itself is the means (*upāya*).

Therefore, for one who desires that [understanding], this treatise must be undertaken; thus, even without being explicitly stated in words, the connection is understood through the sense of the matter—this is the intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*).
[NAV_0.6] Now the meaning of the words is explained:

In this regard, although the word *pramāṇa* can easily be derived through all the case-factors (*kāraka*) and through the abstract state (*bhāva*), because of the rule "the *kṛtya* and *lyuṭ* suffixes are used diversely" and the statement "it applies elsewhere as well," these [meanings] are respectively denotable by the word *pramāṇa* through derivations based on the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth, as well as the state (*bhāva*).

That is to say, [the means of knowledge] consist of the collection of causes for self, object, cognition, and purposeful action, as well as the activity of the subsidence of karmic obstructions; nevertheless, here only cognition (*jñāna*) is the subject under discussion, because it alone is capable of withstanding critical examination, whereas the examination of the others is preceded by that [examination of cognition] and would otherwise be redundant. To explain:

First of all, there is no purpose in examining the self, because it remains the same whether it is associated with erroneous or non-erroneous cognitions. Nor is there a purpose in examining the object, because that is what is to be attained.

Because [the object] is already understood through the very examination of the cognition that serves as the means; nor because of the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), since once that is apprehended, further examination would be redundant; nor because of the collection of causes, since their own nature is not cognized prior to the arising of the cognition.

Subsequently, because the excellence or deficiency of that [instrument] is understood precisely through the determination of its own nature, [the mention of excellence] would be redundant. Nor is it the excellence of the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*), since its nature is inferred from the arising of the cognition itself. Nor is it the excellence of the mere result (*pramiti*), since that is established as correct only by way of the instrument's own proficiency, being itself accomplished by the instrument. Thus, this is the intended meaning:

Although all verbal referents apply without metaphorical qualification to an object that is overlaid with infinite properties, nevertheless, that alone is what is here considered "cognition"— which, while being identical to the self in its nature as the substratum (*dharmin*), is distinct from it in its nature as a property (*dharma*)— by means of which cognizers determine an object and proceed toward it out of a desire for an object capable of causal efficiency.

That by which something is correctly cognized is called a "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*). Its "explanation" (*vyutpādana*) consists in revealing the nature of its intended definition and so forth, by way of excluding definitions and other characteristics imagined by others. For that purpose: the word *artha* is a synonym for "purpose. It refers to the body of the treatise as it manifests in one's own mind in the form of an object, indicated by the word "this" (*idam*).
For the body of a treatise (*prakaraṇa*) is twofold: word and meaning.

Although it will be manifested externally in the form of words, it is nonetheless directly perceived internally in the form of the true object (*tattvārtha*). It is "begun" (*ārabhyate*), which means it is composed through the arrangement of words, sentences, verses, and so forth.
[NAV_0.7] Furthermore, in this regard, others hold conflicting views concerning the definition, number, object, and result of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). To explain:

first, regarding the definition, the followers of the Sugata (Buddhists) maintain that valid cognition is non-contradictory knowledge (*avisaṃvādi jñāna*). The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that valid cognition is that which apprehends an object not yet apprehended (*anadhigatārthādhigantṛ*). The Naiyāyikas and others maintain that valid cognition is the cause of the perception of an object (*arthopalabdhihetu*).
Likewise, regarding the number:

The Buddhists maintain that there are only two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*). The Mīmāṃsakas hold that perception, inference, verbal testimony (*śabda*), analogy (*upamāna*), presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), and non-existence (*abhāva*) are the means of valid cognition. The Naiyāyikas maintain that perception, inference, verbal testimony, and analogy are the means of valid cognition. The Vaiśeṣikas maintain that perception, inference, and verbal testimony are the means of valid cognition. The Sāṃkhyas accept these same three. The Cārvākas maintain that perception alone is the single means of valid cognition. Likewise, regarding the object-domain (*gocara*):

The Buddhists maintain that the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), which consist of atoms characterized by momentary destruction and mutually distinct, are the domain of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and are ultimately real. The Mīmāṃsakas hold that a real entity consists of both the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*). The Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas maintain that the universal and the particular are mutually distinct. The Sāṃkhyas hold that the universal has the form of the three qualities (*traiguṇya*). [And others hold that] the four elements constitute the ground of valid cognition.
The Cārvākas likewise disagree regarding the result (*phala*):

the Buddhists hold that the apprehension of the object (*arthādhigati*) is the result of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The Mīmāṃsakas and others maintain that each preceding stage is the means of valid cognition, while each subsequent stage is the result.
In this regard, wishing to refute disagreements concerning both the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) and the number (*saṃkhyā*) [of the means of valid cognition], he says:
Valid cognition is knowledge that manifests itself and its object, free from sublation;
it is twofold: direct perception and indirect inference.
Because of the determination of the object. // NA_1 //

In that regard as well, he refutes misconceptions concerning the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) with the first half [of the verse], and misconceptions concerning the number (*saṃkhyā*) with the second half. A definition is an uncommon property (*asādhāraṇadharma*) capable of differentiating [an object] from the forms of others. It is called a "definition" (*lakṣaṇa*) because by means of it the "defined" (*lakṣya*)—that which is to be characterized—is distinguished and delimited as being excluded from those of a different class (*vijātīya*). And here, two things are to be made known regarding that [definition].
Those belonging to other schools (*tīrthāntarīya*) whose internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) are attached to their own views are those who hold contrary opinions (*vipratipanna*);

likewise, there are worldly people of dull intellect (*mugdhabuddhi*) who are unrefined (*avyutpanna*). Therefore, when the definition is first presented for those who hold contrary opinions, the relationship between the definiendum (*lakṣya*) and the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) should be understood as follows:
"That which is well-known (*prasiddha*) to both you and us as 'means of valid cognition' (*pramāṇa')," [is the subject].
That cognition which manifests itself and others should be understood as being devoid of sublation (*bādhavivarjita*);

having restated what is already well-known as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), its previously unestablished qualities—such as manifesting itself and others—are now prescribed. However, when this definition is intended for those of untrained intellect, then, since for every living being some cognition that manifests itself and others and is free from sublation is established, [the definition applies].
Otherwise, there would follow the consequence of the destruction of established conventional usage; thus they are instructed:

"That cognition which is well-known among you as apprehending a certain object in some instance, which illuminates both itself and others, and which is free from sublation—that is valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Let them understand this. Here too, it is a restatement of what is already established.
The application of the established rule is to be employed.
[NAV 1.2] Now, the meaning of the words:
therein, "means of valid cognition" (pramāṇa) is as before. "Sva" means one's own self, that is, one's own nature (svarūpa).

The compound *parārtha* means that whose nature it is to cause another object to appear or to manifest. *Jñāna* is that by which reality (*tattva*) is known or determined. *Bādha* is that by which something is sublated;

this refers to the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that presents a contrary object. The summary of the meaning is: that cognition which is devoid of—that is, free from—such a qualification is *pramāṇa*.

[NAV_1.3] Furthermore, since qualifiers are applied to a definition in view of what is to be excluded (*vyavacchedya*), by the phrase "appearing as itself and others" (*svaparābhāsī*), those specific Buddhists who maintain that cognition appears only as itself (*svābhāsi*) and those such as the Mīmāṃsakas and Naiyāyikas who maintain that it appears only as another (*parābhāsi*) are refuted. For they would assert that, due to the absence of external objects, cognition has an existence restricted solely to its own part (*svāṃśaparyavasitasattāka*);
that is incorrect.

Because it would follow that in the absence of an object to be known, there would be an absence of cognition. Now, if it is argued that even in the absence of an object, various cognitions manifesting forests, temples, and so forth are observed during the state of dreaming, that is not the case for all such instances;

for even that [dream-cognition] depends upon awakening, which is contingent upon the presence of a collection of causes—such as the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the perception of real objects occurring during the waking state.
Otherwise, there would be the appearance of a sixth element distinct from the five elements, which have never been experienced as such. Furthermore, you must be asked:

how can a single cognition be a transformation (*vivarta*) of multiple forms such as white, yellow, and so forth? If you say "due to the impressions (*vāsanā*) of beginningless ignorance," then here too a pair of dilemmas (*vikalpa-yugala*) enters unimpededly:
Then, was that latent impression destroyed by that knowledge or not?
If it was indeed set aside,
then, this being the case, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends it must be stated.

Since there is no cognition [of an object] apart from cognition itself, and since the object would also have to be cognized as distinct [from the cognition] when that [cognition] is cognized, such a [separate object] would be difficult to deny. If it is argued that this [external world], which is the cause of that [cognition], is inferred to be of the very nature of cognition—though distinct from the cognition that is defiled by the forms of the cognized and the cognizer—we say: no.
Because there is no apprehension of a relationship with that [object],
and because it would entail the abandonment of what is perceived and the postulation of what is unperceived. Furthermore,
just as even a single cognition appears in manifold forms due to the power of distinct latent impressions (*vāsanā*), [so too must the object be admitted].

Likewise, even that which is insentient appears as having the nature of consciousness only by virtue of its dependence on that [consciousness]; thus, due to this contradictory consequence, it is the object alone that attains establishment, not the cognition. If, however, it is non-different [from consciousness], then alas, it is simply cognition itself.

Let it be for now that the latent impression (*vāsanā*) does not exist because it is non-different from that [consciousness], just like its own nature. Furthermore, even if one were to claim that it is manifested by another, that too is incoherent;

for if there is an absence of self-luminosity (*svaprakāśa*), manifestation by another (*paraprakāśa*) is impossible. Indeed, a lamp does not exert itself toward the illumination of a jar or other objects without first illuminating its own form. Moreover, if it were to cause an object to be apprehended while remaining unapprehended itself, [it would follow that]...
What has arisen in Devadatta should cause Yajñadatta to grasp it,

since there is no distinction [between them]. Furthermore, in the mere illumination of another, with respect to what do the distinctions of distance, proximity, and so forth appear for objects that are manifesting?
If it is argued that [the self] depends on the body, we say no; for even that [body] possesses the same quality of being manifest.

Therefore, this [cognition] achieves its manifestation when there is the grasping of an external object by means of an inward-turned form, and not otherwise. Now, if it is held that this [self] residing within is grasped through another means of knowledge, such as presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), etc.,...

If it is argued that, in relation to that [other means of knowledge], the distinction between "distant" and "near" will be appropriate, we say no; for even in that case, one does not escape the pair of alternatives. To explain: is that other means of knowledge self-luminous or luminated by another?
If it is self-luminous, what is deficient about the first [consciousness]? If it is luminated by another, [then there would be an infinite regress].

In that case as well, this same logic applies, leading to an infinite regress. Therefore, it is established that cognition itself, while manifesting its own nature, is engaged in the apprehension of the object.

By the term "cognition" (*jñāna*), he refutes the validity of that which has been postulated by the Naiyāyikas and others—namely, that the contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For [it is cognition alone] that is capable of accomplishing purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), such as bathing, drinking, or immersion.
The intended meaning is this: when cognizers act toward an object immediately after having ascertained it, that very cognition is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*);

contact (*saṃnikarṣa*), however, is not [the means], because it is insentient and lacks immediate determination. If it is argued that its status as a means of valid knowledge arises from its being the cause of the apprehension of the object, [we reply:]...

The determination of the extent of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is now shattered, for even the body and so forth would result in being considered a means of valid cognition by virtue of being its cause; let that be for now.

However, by the phrase "free from sublation" (*bādhavivarjita*), [the author] refers to those appearances such as two moons hanging in the sky, which arise for those whose visual rays are obstructed by cataracts and the like.

Furthermore, that cognition which arises in those whose minds are deluded by fallacious reasoning— consisting of the appearance of a world created by momentary destruction, universals, particulars, or a sole Lord (Īśvara), and so forth— due to hearing their respective doctrines—
is set aside because it is overwhelmed by the onset of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establish facts contrary to it. However, by the inclusion of the word "particular" (*viśeṣa*),
the cognition that flashes forth as a yellow hue in a white lotus for those whose visual power is impaired by the thick film of cataracts is [also excluded].

Even if that [cognition] is not sublated by the observer’s own perception at all times due to the non-cessation of its defects, nevertheless, because it is sublated by the perception of another person who perceives the whiteness of that which is produced from water, it is said to be not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
As for the definition of a valid means of knowledge as "that which apprehends an object not previously apprehended," which others have set forth using the complete definition: [NAV 1.6]
He refuted such [definitions] as "a means of valid cognition is that which is non-contradictory" and "a means of valid cognition is the cause for the apprehension of an object. For instance,
what is meant by the phrase "apprehending an object not previously apprehended"?
If it is argued that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which apprehends an object not already apprehended by another cognition,
then is that other cognition one belonging to another person or one belonging to oneself?
If it belongs to another person, [the following applies].
That is incorrect;

for since the knowledge of the Omniscient One has all things as its object, it would follow that the cognitions of all ordinary people lack validity because they apprehend objects already apprehended by him, and because there is the possibility of seeing other persons who grasp those same objects. Alternatively, [if you claim the cognition] is one's own, [then...]

In that regard as well, is the object to be realized a substance (*dravya*) or a mode (*paryāya*), or rather, is it a mode qualified by a substance, or a substance qualified by a mode? Likewise, is it a universal (*sāmānya*) or a particular (*viśeṣa*)?
Or is it a particular qualified by a universal, or a universal qualified by a particular? Thus there are eight positions. Among these, if you accept the first one, that is incorrect.

Because, due to the permanence and unity of the substance (*dravya*), there is no unapprehended portion [to be apprehended]. Now, as for the second [alternative], that too is not tenable; because a modification (*paryāya*) that was destroyed at the time of the arising of the preceding cognition cannot wait until the time of the production of another cognition, the qualification is purposeless. Or, as for the third...

That too is even less tenable, because it does not escape two alternatives. For that mode (paryāya), which is qualified by substance, is either apprehended by a cognition occurring at the same time [as itself] or by one occurring at a different time. It cannot first be apprehended by a cognition occurring at the same time.

Because such a possibility does not exist, the qualification is futile. For it is impossible for a single cognizer to simultaneously possess two cognitive occurrences whose objects consist of a substance and its encompassing modes, since no such experience occurs, and because it would entail the consequence of invalidity due to both cognitions apprehending an object already apprehended by the other. Nor [is it possible] with respect to [cognitions] occurring at different times.

Because that which is being grasped does not persist into another time, since it is connected only to the present moment, severed from the preceding and succeeding moments. By this, the position that substance is qualified by its modes (*paryāya*) is also refuted, as it shares the same logical status. Now, [if it be argued that] it is the universal (*sāmānya*):
That too is incoherent;

for if it were a single entity, its entirety would be grasped by the first cognition, which would entail the lack of validity for subsequent cognitions of the universal (*sāmānya*), since their objects would already have been apprehended. If, on the other hand, it is a particular (*viśeṣa*), it must be stated whether it is eternal or non-eternal. If it is eternal, [then...]

This being the case, since its totality would be grasped by the very first cognition, it follows that subsequent cognitions having that same object as their domain would lack validity, because their objects would already have been apprehended. If it were impermanent, it would be refuted by the critique of the *paryāya* (successive states). Now, if it is a particular qualified by a universal, what constitutes its state of being "qualified"?
Is it identity with that [object], or merely its proximity?
If it were identity, then, like the universal, it too would be apprehended by the first cognition.

Otherwise, because their identity would be lost, it would follow that cognitions other than those having that [particular] as their object would be invalid. However, in the view that [the universal] exists in proximity [to the particular], since both have mutually distinct forms, the refutation raised against both positions follows after like a dog running after its tail. This applies to the position that the universal is qualified by the particular.

This same point should be applied in its reverse order as well. Thus, it is established that the capacity of cognition to apprehend an object not previously apprehended cannot in any way withstand the heavy burden of critical inquiry; therefore, it lacks the defining characteristic [of valid cognition]. Now, non-contradictoriness is being examined:

do you assert the validity of cognition through the attainment of the object indicated by it, or by its indicating an object capable of being attained, or by its having an unshakable object as its domain?
If the first alternative is held, that is incorrect,
because the cognition produced by an object on the verge of perishing, such as a water bubble, arises as invalid.
Because at the time of its attainment, that [object] has already perished. Now, if the second [alternative] is intended, that too is not tenable,
because it would follow that cognitions whose objects are planets, constellations, and so forth— situated in locations inaccessible to attainment— would lack validity.
Because those [objects] are unfit to be attained simply by remaining in an unsuitable location. Now, as for the third position:
even there, how do you ascertain that their objects are unshakable?
If you say it is because there is no negation of those objects by another cognition, [we reply:]...
This very point has been stated by us:
what appears harsh to you?
For, apart from a cognition that illuminates both itself and its object and is free from sublation, there is no other way for it to exclude other objects through another cognition.
Let us examine this. That very [definition] has been accepted by you as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) on the basis of logic.

Furthermore, the definition that "the cause of the apprehension of an object is the means of valid cognition" does not withstand scrutiny, because it would follow that the body and so forth are also means of valid cognition due to their being causes of that [apprehension]. [Objection: A means of valid cognition is a cause of the apprehension of an object that is immediate.
If it is argued that [the means of knowledge] is not the body and so forth,

then in that case, cognition alone— being that which manifests both itself and others and being unimpeded— is the valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa), and not sensory contact (sannikarṣa) and the like.
Because even when that [cognition] exists, there is no determination of the object. Therefore, this alone is the excellent definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Now, he states its number:
"Perception," and so forth.

In that context, with respect to ultimate direct perception (*pāramārthika-pratyakṣa*) as established in the Siddhānta, the word *akṣa* is well known as a synonym for the soul (*jīva*). However, here, because the discussion concerns conventional direct perception (*vyāvahārika-pratyakṣa*), the term *akṣa* is taken to denote the sense organs (*indriya*). Consequently, *pratyakṣa* means "that which has gone toward the *akṣa*. Thus, the cognition that arises in dependence upon a sense organ and directly perceives an object is *pratyakṣa*.

This is the meaning. And this is the etymological ground (*vyutpatti-nimitta*) for the word *pratyakṣa*, but not its basis for application (*pravṛtti-nimitta*). For when derived in this way, it characterizes a specific type of cognition that directly grasps both the object and the subject, because it is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in that very sense.

Just as the word "cow" (go), although derived from the act of going, refers to a specific individual possessing a hump and other such features— whether that individual is moving or not— because it is well-established in that very sense,
and not even to a person or the like who possesses the act of going.

"By way of the opposite. And thus, it is stated that the self-awareness (*svarūpasaṃvedana*) of all cognitions is also perception (*pratyakṣa*), because even in that case there exists the direct realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa*) of the object of apprehension (*grāhya*), which is its own nature. That which exists beyond the sense organs (*akṣa*) is "indirect" (*parokṣa*). It is that cognition which, independent of the operation of the sense organs, determines an object indirectly through the operation of the mind.
That is the sense of "indirect" (*parokṣa*).

The two words "and" (*ca*) indicate that perception (*pratyakṣa*) and indirect cognition are of equal status. By this, the claim made by others—that "perception is the eldest among all means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*)—and so forth, is refuted.
Because there is no distinction between the two regarding their validity,

and because the difference between clear and unclear manifestation, though it exists, is not a factor in determining seniority. If it is argued that perception is senior because it precedes inference,
this is not an absolute rule.

Because, in all cases, the presence or absence of the signs of life—such as inhalation and exhalation—is determined by the impossibility of [life] otherwise; for we observe the cognition of "living" or "dead" even when the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) that witnesses the living soul has ceased.

Otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the absence of worldly convention (*lokavyavahāra*). Since inference (*parokṣa*) proceeds on the strength of a relationship grasped by direct perception in some instances, one might conceive of direct perception as being superior; yet [this is not the case], as in the instance of acting upon the force of words such as, "Look, the deer is running! [where inference occurs despite the lack of immediate sensory contact].
The domain of animals is accessed by way of twisting the neck;

likewise, through recollection or the grasping of conventions, or through curiosity to see ever-new objects and so forth, one perceives what was previously beyond the senses—such as the forest deities and the like—as being directly perceived. Thus, the priority of the indirect (parokṣa) would be established.
Regarding the phrase "of two kinds": according to the maxim that "every sentence functions with a restriction," [it follows that it excludes others].

Otherwise, since it would fail to demonstrate a determinate object, the utterance of such [a statement] would result in futility; furthermore, because it would lack the skill to exclude contrary forms, a purposeful activity free from doubt could not be established. Thus, by the restrictive phrase "only in two ways," it sets aside other contrary numbers imagined by others, as those are contradicted by reason.

For instance: the claim that perception alone is the sole means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is incorrect, because in the absence of the imperceptible (*parokṣa*), its status as a valid means of cognition would be untenable. For one observes that certain individual instances of perception are non-deviant (*avyabhicārin*) insofar as they lead to the attainment of objects capable of causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*), while other instances are deviant (*vyabhicārin*) due to being the opposite of those.
Then, at another time, one might again explain the validity or invalidity of such and other perceptual manifestations.
However, perception— which is devoid of reflection on the preceding and succeeding [moments] and whose existence is restricted solely to the apprehension of the object present before it—
is not capable of discerning the similarity among perceptual manifestations occurring in prior and subsequent times as the basis for its own validity.
It is conceded. Furthermore, he is not capable of establishing the validity of even those individual instances of perception that fall within the scope of his own cognition for the sake of another.

Therefore, there must necessarily be another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*), distinct from perception, which—by way of the similarity between the individual instances of perception as they were observed and present instances of perception—communicates their validity and establishes it for others; this [means] is included among the imperceptible (*parokṣa*) and takes the form of inference (*anumāna*).

This must be accepted. Furthermore, by asserting that perception alone is the single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and that there is no other for the purpose of understanding others, one reveals one's own madness;

for through perception, the mental states of others cannot be directly perceived, and it is only by observing specific activities, speech, and gestures that a particular state of consciousness is inferred.

By the principle that "the validity of [a means of knowledge] regarding that which is beyond the senses follows by necessity," one cannot negate heaven, the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), deities, and so forth through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because its domain is restricted solely to what is present before it. Yet, he does not become a mere "donkey-Cārvāka" by failing to negate these;
moreover, he does not accept another means of knowledge for the purpose of negating them. Thus, our minds are filled with wonder as to how he could act in such a contradictory manner. Furthermore:
It must be explained how even perception (pratyakṣa) attains the status of a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa):

because it conforms to the presence and absence (anvaya-vyatireka) of the objects being apprehended. For instance, it emerges by the power of the objects possessing their complete causal complex (sāmagrī).
If you argue that [the cognition] does not arise for a cognizer even when the pair of eyes is wide open due to the absence of that [external object],
then this is exactly the same in the case of the imperceptible (parokṣa) as well;
for that too arises solely from the causal efficacy of the external object.
Because that [cognition] arises by means of a word which is a mark (liṅga) connected with that [object],

otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of it being a semblance of indirect cognition (parokṣābhāsa); and because if that [word] were false, it would be impossible for the ultimate validity of indirect cognition to be undermined.
Otherwise, even perception—which is capable of observing a pair of moons suspended in the sky—would be seen as false;

consequently, all clear observations, though considered true, would fall into falsity. Therefore, like perception, indirect cognition (*parokṣa*) that has become a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) can never arise without the existence of the object being apprehended.
It is established that [the number of means of valid cognition] necessarily ascends to the limit of two.

Likewise, regarding those other enumerations of means of valid cognition asserted by others that exceed the pair [of perception and inference], even among them, whatever— upon critical examination— is found to appropriate the status of a means of valid cognition, like analogy (upamāna) or presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), [is included within these two].

Therefore, that [means of knowledge] must be included within these two alone: perception and non-perception. Furthermore, as for that which, when investigated, does not even qualify as a valid means of knowledge—like the "non-existence" (abhāva) postulated by the Mīmāṃsakas—we have no concern with it, whether it be external or internal, because it is a non-entity; thus, it should be disregarded.
[NAV 1.12] Now, you may ask: how is analogy (upamāna) a valid means of knowledge?

This is explained as follows: First, for a person who has clearly perceived the specific features of a cow and whose mind has been refined by hearing the statement "as is a cow, so is a gavaya," while wandering in the forest, there arises—preceded by a distinct perception of the specific features of the gavaya’s body—the cognition: "this is similar to that," which is produced by the combined operation of the perceptions directed toward both the previously seen cow and the currently seen gavaya.

Or, "the similarity between these two"—thus, that cognition which arises having as its object either an individual (piṇḍa) qualified by similarity, or a similarity qualified by an individual, is *upamāna*. As those who advocate this [view] have said:
"Therefore, that which is perceived must be qualified by similarity."
"The object of comparison (prameya) is either similarity or that which is possessed of it. (NAV 1.12).

Consequently, because the two perceptions of the earlier and later [moments] have their existence restricted to the apprehension of the individual forms of the cow and the gavaya standing before one, because they lack a synthesis of the earlier and later [perceptions], and because they appear with vivid clarity and are devoid of verbal expression, [the cognition arising from them] is more than that [mere perception], being non-erroneous...

Comparison (*upamāna*) is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it establishes similarity—which brings about practical activity—and because it is non-sublated by virtue of illuminating both itself and its object.
If it is argued that no further similarity is perceived apart from the preceding and succeeding individual entities, [we ask]:
what is this "perception" (*upalambha*) by which it is said that similarity is not perceived, if it is indeed perception (*pratyakṣa*)?
If similarity does not appear in perception because it is the object of comparison (upamāna), what fault is there in that?
For it cannot be said that because it does not appear as its object in another cognition, it is therefore devoid of an object altogether.
Otherwise, even in the case of analogy (*upamāna*), the individual (*vyakti*) would not appear as something graspable by perception; thus, perception would be rendered objectless.

For just as perception is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with respect to its own object, so too is analogy. Indeed, when two means of knowledge are equally applicable to a single subject and there is no distinction between them, it is not proper to show partiality toward one. By this, [the same logic applies] to recognition, memory, inference, and so forth.

The validity of those [cognitions] that are non-contradictory and possess imperceptible particulars should be understood as already explained, because they follow the same logical principle. For instance:
the initial perception of an object deposits a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) within the self.
From such a perception, that latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is awakened;

once awakened, it gives rise to the cognition of recognition (*pratyabhijñājñāna*), characterized by the mental formulation: "This is that very same [object]," or "This belongs to that same class," because it establishes two types of universals (*sāmānya*): the vertical (*ūrdhva*) and the horizontal (*tiraścīna*).

Because there is no arising of that [memory] for one who has not previously seen the object that serves as its domain. Likewise, that very same latent impression (*saṃskāra*), awakened by the sight of such an object or by mental application (*ābhoga*) and so forth, produces memory, which is characterized by the non-forgetting of a previously experienced object;

for memory is impossible for a person who has not seen the object. Furthermore, *ūha* (presumption) is inclined toward grasping the connection with a logical mark (*liṅga*) characterized by the fact that the object to be proven—which is not perceived through perception or inference—is otherwise inexplicable.
It will be stated that this is a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*).

As for presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), however, it postulates— on the basis of the otherwise inexplicability of objects such as the "sphoṭa" which have been made the object of perception and other means— a distinct property, such as the power of burning in fire and so forth, which is additional to what was within the scope of previous observation and is non-deviant.
It indeed accepts the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇatā*),

because it possesses the defining characteristics thereof. In the same way, any other cognition whatsoever that brings about an object beyond the scope of perception and functions as a practical activity (*vyavahāra*) due to its being free from further expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatā*) should be established as a valid means of knowledge,
because it illuminates both itself and others and is uncontradicted (*nirbādhatva*).

It is like the cognition of a specific number that arises after one has observed a series of steps arranged from front to back. Furthermore, all these [types of cognition] are included within the category of *parokṣa* (indirect knowledge), because they possess the capacity to cognize the subject at hand by means of perceiving another object that could not otherwise be explained (*anyathānupapanna*). However, if one were to postulate separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for each slight distinction, the fixed number of *pramāṇas* would collapse, as it would lead to an infinite regress.

Because the activity of knowledge is diverse due to the diversity of the destruction and subsidence of obscuration (*āvaraṇa-kṣayopaśama*). But if this is so, how will that twofold division of indirect knowledge (*parokṣa*) which is about to be stated—namely, the distinction between inference (*anumāna*) and verbal testimony (*śābda*)—be justified?

For even in that case, it is not difficult to establish that knowledge arising from the words of a reliable person (*āpta*) is included within inference, since the object [described] cannot otherwise be accounted for (*arthānyathānupapatti*).
Consequently, inference alone remains as the single [means of knowledge];
if it is stated that this very thing is appropriately expressed by the term "parokṣa" (the remote), then it stands as correct.
This lack of regard for the designation used by the learned is true; however, he thinks as follows:

Although it may be possible to include verbal cognition (śābda) within inference through some methodological procedure, others nevertheless disagree with that view; therefore, its validity must be established directly. And it is not possible to state its distinct nature when it is not separate from [inference].

Therefore, it is presented separately. By this, he indicates that even though other types of indirect [cognition] (*parokṣa*) may also be included within inference (*anumāna*), whenever others hold a misconception regarding a particular one, that specific type of indirect cognition should be extracted and its validity established by presenting distinct arguments. And so it is said in another treatise:
It has thus been stated that the definition of *ūha* and the other [subsidiary sciences] provided by the teachers is indeed correct.
How then is it that "non-existence" (*abhāva*), as postulated by the Mīmāṃsakas, is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
We reply: because it lacks an objective domain (*nirgocaratvāt*). To explain:

What need have we for further reflection on this? For it is evident that perception itself—through the method of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—possesses the proficiency to delimit an object, such as "this is indeed the bare ground; there is no jar here. Since there is no object to be grasped beyond that, any attempt to postulate another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) is refuted.
This is because perception, which grasps objects both existent and non-existent, is well-known to every living being. Now, one might perhaps argue:
Because it arises through the door of the sense-faculties, direct perception (adhyakṣa) perceives only the positive aspect (bhāvāṃśa), and its operation concerns that very positive aspect alone.

However, the cognition of non-existence (nāstitājñāna) emerges as a mental [cognition] subsequent to the apprehension of the object, provided there is recollection of the counter-correlate (pratiyogin), and it is independent of the operation of the senses. Thus it has been said:
“First of all, the cognition that ‘this does not exist’ is not produced by means of a sense faculty;
for the sense faculty is indeed capable only of contact with the positive aspect of an entity. (NAV 1.15)
“Having grasped the non-existence of the object and having remembered its counter-positive, a mental cognition of non-existence arises without dependence on the sense organs. (NAV 1.15)
To this it is replied: Is the aspect of non-existence then non-different or different from the aspect of existence?
If it is non-different, how can there be no apprehension of it?
Precisely because it is not distinct from the aspect of the positive entity,

like the nature of that entity itself. If, on the other hand, it were distinct, then since the ground— completely devoid of the absence of a jar and so forth— is apprehended by the first perception, it would follow that the jar and so forth are also apprehended.

Because the non-apprehension of the absence of that [object] is inseparable from the apprehension of its presence. And thus, even if non-existence were to occur later, it would be incapable of displacing those [objects];

otherwise, perception—by apprehending what is unmixed as being mixed—would fall into the error of being mistaken. Furthermore, your intention is that the non-existence of an object is established by the means of knowledge of non-existence (*abhāvapramāṇa*) because of the absence of a [corresponding] means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

“Where the five means of valid cognition do not arise with respect to the nature of an object, there the means of valid cognition known as non-existence (abhāva-pramāṇa) functions for the purpose of awakening one to the existence of that object. (NAV 1.16)
Because of this statement, that is incorrect; for how can the absence of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) be apprehended?

If you argue that this is because there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to apprehend that [absence], then in order to apprehend the absence of that [means of cognition] as well, another means of valid cognition to apprehend it would have to be grasped, resulting in an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Alternatively, if you think that the absence of the object is established through the absence of the means of valid cognition, and the absence of the means of valid cognition is established through the absence of the object;
Thus, this would result in a circularity that is difficult to establish:
as long as the absence of the object is not apprehended, the absence of the means of cognition is not established;

yet the absence of the object will be established through the absence of the means of cognition—such is the rotation. Now, you might argue that even if the absence of the means of cognition is itself unperceived, like the sense organs, it will nonetheless make known the absence of the object.
That is incorrect,
because that [non-existence] is insubstantial (*tuccha*) and characterized by an absence of all causal capacities,
whereas the sense faculty is the opposite of that and is capable of producing cognition. Therefore, perception alone maintains the grasping of specific objects such as the bare ground.

If it apprehends that [object] as distinct from other entities that serve as its counter-correlates (pratiyogi), such as a jar which is its opposite, and not otherwise— because in the absence of the exclusion of heterogeneous things, its own specific determination could not be established,

leading to the undesirable consequence of perceiving it as mixed with everything— then, since there is no further object to be grasped, it follows that the so-called "means of knowledge" (pramāṇa) called non-existence (abhāva), which others have postulated on the grounds that it lacks an objective referent, is invalid. This is the established conclusion.

By stating "in two ways" (*dvidhā*) and thereby demonstrating a fixed twofold division into the perceptible (*pratyakṣa*) and the imperceptible (*parokṣa*), he rejects the twofold division postulated by the Buddhists, namely that there are only perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*).

Because that [verbal cognition] cannot arise from that [intention] due to their lack of connection. For inference alone—arising from the three types of logical marks consisting of effect, essential nature, and non-perception, as characterized by the relations of identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*)—is the valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) beyond direct perception;
it is not verbal testimony, presumption, or the like.

The intended meaning of the phrase "due to the absence of a [logical] connection" (*sambandhavikalatvāt*) is as follows. And this is untenable, because there is no means of apprehending the absence of any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) beyond perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*). First of all, the absence of other means of valid cognition is not understood through perception, because perception has only particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object, and thus it is contradictory for it to grasp non-existence. Nor is it understood through the two types of inference—those based on essential nature (*svabhāva*) and those based on effect (*kārya*).

This is because those two establish a positive entity (*vastu*). Nor can it be established through non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), for even that is contradictory to proving absolute non-existence. For non-apprehension is described as being of four kinds with respect to its fundamental divisions, namely:

apprehension of the contradictory (*viruddhopalabdhi*), apprehension of the effect of the contradictory (*viruddhakāryopalabdhi*), non-apprehension of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*), and non-apprehension of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*). First of all, absolute non-existence cannot be established by the other means of valid cognition known as the apprehension of the contradictory.

Because the absence of one thing is established by the affirmation of its contradictory, which is perceptible, the absence of the counter-positive is proven precisely in that very location where it is present. By this, the perception of a contradictory effect is also explained, since that too establishes absence by means of bringing about the presence of something contradictory to the object to be negated. Likewise, the non-perception of a cause establishes the absence of an effect only in that specific location where its occurrence was suspected, not everywhere.

Because it is not established by itself. Non-apprehension of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), which consists in the apprehension of an object associated within a single cognition, indicates the absence of its opposite only in that very location. Therefore, even another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) could only negate [an object] in some instances, not everywhere. Thus, there exists no sublater of another means of valid cognition.

[NAV 1.19] Furthermore, it must be considered from what source the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*) is established. It cannot be from perception itself, because, being non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), even though it exists, it is like something non-existent. The conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that arises subsequent to it does not plunge into the middle of the ocean of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*);

how then, having not entered therein, could it ascertain its true nature? To claim that the determination of validity comes from such a [conceptual construction] which has become a non-means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*) is merely a manifestation of your profound dullness. [Nor can it come] from inference...
If this is argued, we say no,
because that [exclusion] too floats outside of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). If it is argued that the exclusion of non-validity is established by it, we say no,
because an exclusion is not distinct from that which is excluded.
Otherwise, inference would be like a dance in the dark,
because it would lack an objective referent. Furthermore,
is the inference that determines its own validity a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or an invalid one (*apramāṇa*)?

It is not, first of all, non-valid, because its validity would then be unestablished. Nor is it valid, because there is no means of establishing its validity. For its establishment does not arise from perception;

It has been stated that [conceptual construction] is ineffective because it is empty of conceptual content. However, if one attempts to establish that [non-conceptuality] through inference, the same pair of dilemmas remains;

for even in establishing the validity of that inference, there would be the conceptualization of another inference, leading to an infinite regress. Furthermore, inference proceeds only for one who has already grasped the relationship [between the middle and the major terms].
The relationship must be apprehended as having the three times as its domain; yet perception is not capable of characterizing it,
because its existence is restricted to the apprehension of the present moment alone, while the preceding and succeeding moments are of a fragmented nature.

For even the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising at a subsequent time is admitted—according to the conventional perspective—to have that [perception] as its object. If it is argued that it will be apprehended through inference (*anumāna*), [we reply: surely that too must proceed based on a prior relation (*sambandha*). And if that relation is to be apprehended, the same situation applies; thus, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Therefore, one who desires inference must, since there is no other alternative, admit a non-erroneous deliberation (*vitarka*) whose scope is the three times and which is inclined toward the apprehension of that relation. Likewise:

Furthermore, since the two-fold division under discussion has been refuted, let it be that whatever other non-contradictory cognition exists is a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*); enough with this dry arrogance. However, if [valid knowledge] is produced by a reason that is otherwise impossible given the object to be proven, then the two-fold division into perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*) would indeed be established.
Because all knowledge other than perception can be included within inference as a whole—
since there is no cognition of an imperceptible object that occurs without another factor whose existence is otherwise inexplicable (anyathānupapanna)—
[the author] now states the reason for the aforementioned restriction by means of a portion of the sūtra itself:

The phrases "because of the determination of the object of cognition" (*meyaviniścayāt*) and "only in two ways" (*dvidhaiva*) are to be connected here as well, according to the maxim of the crow’s eye (*kākākṣigolakanyāya*). Consequently, the meaning is this:
because the determination—that is, the ascertainment of the essential nature—of the object of cognition, which is the apprehended object, occurs only through two modes;
therefore, there are exactly two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as previously stated, neither fewer nor more. This is the intended sense here.
With respect to self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), there is indeed no distinction among all cognitions, because they are equally capable of directly manifesting [their own nature] in a single form.

However, with respect to external objects, there exists something whose being is obtained through the power of the causal complex of the eye and so forth; it pervades its own parts, persists across different times, conceals its momentary transformations, and remains present while the spherical dimension of its atoms remains unperceived.
The manifestation (*prakāśa*) shines forth directly perceiving a clear appearance (*viśadanirbhāsa*), which is the universal form (*sāmānyākāra*);

therein, the conventional usage of "perception" (*pratyakṣavyavahāra*) proceeds. On the other hand, that transformation of the self (*ātmanaḥ arthagrahaṇapariṇāmaḥ*) which arises through the medium of a logical mark (*liṅga*), a word (*śabda*), and so forth—beholding both determinate and indeterminate universal forms and being devoid of clarity—is indeed characterized by mediacy (*parokṣatā*).
One accepts this. And we do not observe the operation of cognition in any manner other than these two modes;
nor, not observing it, can we tolerate the postulation of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
nor do we expect one to deny either of the first two modes.

Because there is no distinction [between them]. Therefore, it is established that this very twofold division must be accepted. Now, regarding what we previously explained while providing our commentary—that this definition of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is capable of removing the confusion of those who are either mistaken or unlearned—it is [understood] merely from seeing the aphorism (*sūtra*).

Thus those of pure intellect may understand; however, those of dull intellect will not realize it by that much alone. Therefore, with the desire to benefit them, and wishing to set forth the fruit of stating the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*) clearly, [the author], desiring that they should grasp it along with its prima facie objections (*pūrvapakṣa*) so as to be free from further doubt, first raises the prima facie objection and says:
The means of valid cognition are well-known, as is the worldly practice based upon them;
therefore, no purpose is perceived in stating the definition of the means of valid cognition.
[NAV_2.1] Here, one who utters speech and speaks with deliberation must reflect:

"Does this speech of mine produce a refinement in the listener, or not? Otherwise, his quality of acting after due consideration is lost. If he utters that which produces a refinement in the listener, it is well;

otherwise, the opposite occurs. However, this very sentence defining the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa-vākya*) does not produce a refinement in the listener, because it conveys a meaning already deeply rooted in all people from time immemorial.
As it has been said: "Established and well-rooted; the meaning is that they are not to be proven now. "Means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) refers to perception and the others.

The plural number is used with respect to the distinctions among objects beyond direct perception, in order to show that even a universal may be considered, in some sense, distinct according to the difference in individual instances. For instance:
Therefore, when its individual manifestations (*vyakti*) are not intended to be expressed, that means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) maintains a single form;

however, when it is delimited by the delimitation of individual manifestations, it assumes multiplicity—as in the case of perception, inference, and verbal testimony—because its nature consists of being both distinct from and non-distinct from those manifestations. For instance:

When, from a word or from the eyes and other senses, there arises at a distance the cognition "this is a tree," it is the common property of treeness alone that shines forth, independent of specific particulars such as the *dhava*, *khadira*, or *palāśa* trees; therefore, that [treeness] is distinct from them, because it appears in cognition with a form that is different from them.

Like a jar or other such objects. However, at the time of clearly perceiving specific distinctions such as the *khadira* or *palāśa* trees, that [universal] does not manifest with a form exceeding [the particulars]; thus it is non-different [from them], because it is experienced as non-distinct from them.

It is like its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). If it is argued that the form of the universal (*sāmānya*) is truly real only as non-different from the particular (*viśeṣa*), because only that [particular] is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) such as burning or cooking, whereas the differentiated [form] is unreal because it is constructed by conceptual thought (*kalpanābuddhi*), we say: no.

Because when two things are manifesting, it is impossible to deny one of them. Otherwise, even for those who claim that one form is indeed inherently distinct while the other is merely shown by a conceptualizing mind, there would be no contradiction in their speech. Furthermore, the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) is not difficult to establish even in the case of a distinct form.

Because that [cognition] as well is capable of performing the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) common to knowledge. Furthermore, we shall demonstrate that causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is not the defining characteristic of a real entity (*vastu*); therefore, the use of the plural number is for the purpose of showing that in every case there are both universal (*sāmānya*) and particular (*viśeṣa*), which are distinct and non-distinct. For now, let the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) be set aside. The connection [of the sentence] is: "And conventional usage produced by them is well-known. The word *ca* has the sense of the word *api*. By this, the meaning is as follows:

The opponent, though harboring the intention that the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is useless— since even the worldly activities for which such an examination of the means of valid cognition exists, such as drinking water or seeking protection from the cold, are rooted in beginningless habituation— speaks otherwise out of a desire to avoid harshness:

"In the statement of the definition of the means of valid cognition— which consists in describing the unique properties of a means of valid cognition capable of excluding the nature of other things— we do not perceive, nor do we determine, any purpose or its result."
"Because of the extreme subtlety of your intention," he asks with a sarcastic intonation (*kāku*) and thus mocks him. Furthermore, there are two possible positions:
is the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*) stated as being itself uncertain, or as being certain in its own nature? It cannot be the former.

Because that which is not ascertained cannot function as a defining characteristic, like the incoherent ravings of a madman. Now, if it is ascertained, is that [ascertainment] through a non-valid means of cognition (*apramāṇa*) or through a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*)? It cannot be through a non-valid means of cognition.

Because that which is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*) cannot function as a determiner. If, however, it were asserted that even what is not a valid means of knowledge can be a determiner, then the search for valid means of knowledge would collapse,
as it would result in futility.

Because it is admitted that [the means of knowledge] can be determined even by what is not a means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*). Now, if it is by a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), is that [means of knowledge] without characteristics (*alakṣaṇa*) or endowed with characteristics (*lakṣaṇopeta*)? If a means of knowledge that determines [an object] were without characteristics, then the statement of the characteristics of all means of knowledge would be useless.
Because the ascertainment of an object is established even apart from that [definition],
just like the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that ascertains the definition intended by you. Now, if it is endowed with a definition,
there too the pair of alternatives follows its course unimpeded:

Is that characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) ascertained or unascertained? First of all, an unascertained characteristic does not characterize the characterized (*lakṣya*). Furthermore, ascertainment must arise either from a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or from what is not a valid means of knowledge.
