Since ascertainment cannot be established through what is not a valid means of knowledge, it must be said to arise from a valid means of knowledge. Is that [means of knowledge] itself without a characteristic or with a characteristic? If it is without a characteristic, what deficiency would there be in the apprehension of the object by the former [characteristic]? If it is with a characteristic...

Whether that definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been determined or not, that very point recurs. Therefore, there is no way to state a definition of the means of valid cognition;

consequently, it must be accepted that the means of valid cognition are already well-known (*prasiddha*). Now, the Teacher (Dignāga), intending to convince his opponent by saying "We have grasped your position," pursues that view and, while agreeing with it, says: "Nevertheless, regarding the statement of a definition..."

Demonstrating its success, he says: "The purpose in stating the definitions of the well-known means of valid cognition is that it shall bring about the cessation of delusion regarding them for those whose minds are confused in this matter. (NA 3)
This was stated by you:

that since the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are already well-established, the purpose or result (*phala*) in stating their definitions— that is, in the matter of describing their unique characteristics— is as follows:
The word "what" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence];

thus, this [objection] is incorrect. For, although the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are well-established for every living being—otherwise there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the total destruction of all worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*) conducted by them—
Furthermore, because the annihilation of that [consciousness] would entail the loss of what is perceived and other such fallacies;
nevertheless, some whose internal organs are seized by pervasive delusion do not discern its true nature even while experiencing it.

Therefore, for us—who observe them with minds overwhelmed by compassion toward that state—by means of revealing the characteristics of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) exactly as they are, [we shall explain].
The mind proceeds toward the statement of the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*) with the thought, "We shall dispel their delusion. This is the purpose:
that there may be the cessation of that delusion.

Regarding that definition of the means of valid cognition, the delusion of the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthya*), who hold contrary views and lack the discrimination between what is a means of valid cognition and what is not, consists in their error.
However, for those of worldly, deluded intellect, it consists of a lack of decisive conviction;
its cessation means its removal through the comprehension of the non-erroneous definition—that is the meaning—and that [cessation] would occur.
To whom would it belong? He says:
Those whose internal organ—the mind—is thus deluded, seized by erroneous grasping, and fallen into a state of mental confusion;

"here" means in this world—this is the intended meaning. If no one at all were to be deluded regarding the well-known definitions of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which have been established since beginningless time, then that which you previously asserted—"the formulation of the definitions of the means of valid cognition is useless"—would hold true.

Thus, that [objection] would indeed be correct. But this is not so, because we observe that even those who are deluded [regarding it] exist. By this, the refutation which was offered—namely, "Is the definition of a means of valid cognition stated as being uncertain or as being certain?"—is also addressed.

One should understand that such [objections] as these do not constitute a sublation for us, because they either prove what is already established or are irrelevant to the point at hand. If it is argued that [this objection] applies even to one whose mind is utterly deluded regarding the elucidation of the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), we say no;
for that which is established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is being elucidated by means of words.

Because its function consists solely in the removal of that delusion. For example, even when one perceives a bare ground through direct perception, if someone— due to the delusion of false views— does not realize the absence of a jar or other objects, he might be addressed as follows:
"There is no jar here, because it is not perceived despite the completeness of the conditions for perception";
for in that case, the distinctness [of the locus from the jar] is established by direct perception.
From such a statement, confusion would be dispelled;
likewise, it should be understood by the learned here as well. Its definition has been determined by perception, because its nature is that of a determinate cognition (*vyavasāya*).

It is established, moreover, that a statement functions to refute the imposition of what is contrary [to reality]. Thus, having generally set forth the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and having removed the objections regarding it, the Teacher now wishes to state the definition of perception (*pratyakṣa*).

To this end, he says: Now, desiring to refute the disagreement concerning the number of those very objects [of cognition], there are others who disagree even regarding the definitions of those two individual instances of the means of valid cognition—perception and inference—which were previously introduced under the characteristics of the direct (*pratyakṣa*) and the indirect (*parokṣa*). Therefore, their definitions must also be stated. First, wishing to express the definition of perception, he says:
Such knowledge that apprehends an object through direct perception is *pratyakṣa* (perception);
other [knowledge] is to be known as *parokṣa* (indirect), with respect to its mode of apprehension.

In this context, "perception" (*pratyakṣa*) is the designation of the definiendum; "a cognition that apprehends an object in a non-indirect manner" (*aparokṣatayā*) is the designation of the definition. That which is indirect (*parokṣa*) is beyond the range of the senses (*akṣagocarātīta*); other than that is the non-indirect (*aparokṣa*).

Its state is *tattā* (thatness); by that [state], which means by way of being directly perceived (*sākṣātkṛtatayā*). The word *artha* means that which is sought (*aryate*), the sense being that it is understood; or alternatively, *artha* means that which is desired (*arthyate*) by those seeking purposeful action such as burning or cooking—that is to say, it is longed for. The cognition which is its apprehender is that which directly determines it by virtue of having the nature of a determinative judgment (*vyavasāya*).
The synthesis is that "perception is precisely that which is of such a nature. In this context, by the inclusion of the term "cognition" (jñāna),
he sets aside the Sāṃkhya claim that "perception is the functioning of the auditory organ and the other senses."

Because the ears and other [senses], being modifications of primordial matter (*prakṛti*), are insentient by nature, their activity— characterized as a functional operation— cannot be directly perceived.

If it were argued that they are directly perceived because they are the cause of the determination of objects, then the activity of the collection of insentient causes such as light would also have to be considered directly perceived,
as there is no distinction [between the two cases].

[NAV 4.2] Because the phrase "the apprehender of the object" depends on the upcoming term "in view of its own apprehension," this [statement] refutes those who, even regarding external objects, prattle that all cognition is devoid of any determination of the form of an object.
For just as internal self-awareness is active in the apprehension of its own part, so too is it active externally; otherwise, like external objects, other mental continua would also collapse.

Because, by the analogy of a dream, that inference would result in being nothing more than a mere delusion, since it is simply one's own consciousness manifesting in such and such ways. And thus, the categories of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and objects of knowledge (*prameya*), the established and the establisher, cause and effect, and so forth, would all dissolve;

for apart from the self, there would follow the cessation of the activity of cognition even between its own preceding and succeeding moments. If you argue that you are acting in accordance with the proof of the reality of non-dual consciousness (*advayavijñāna*), [we reply:]...
It might be argued:

"If this were not contrary to you—who, by abolishing all worldly conventions as perceived by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), imagine an unseen non-dual reality based on the latencies of false views—then [we reply]: there is no manifestation of external knowledge that possesses the status of a valid means of cognition in the absence of an object."
"Because it would follow that there is no cause.

Furthermore, "the grasper" (grāhaka) should be understood as the determiner (nirṇāyaka), since in the absence of determination, the apprehension of an object is impossible. Therefore, that which was asserted by the followers of the Tathāgata:
The definition that "perception is free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous" is thereby refuted,
because it is devoid of logical justification. For instance:

They refute the arguments for the non-conceptual nature of perception as follows: "Indeed, this [perception] arises through the power of the object (*arthasāmarthya*), because it grasps an object capable of performing a proximate causal function (*sannihitārthakriyāsamartha*). Furthermore, there are no verbal expressions (*dhvani*) in the object, because [verbal expressions] are produced by other causes that are distinct from the causes of the object."

Consequently, having arisen and bringing forth its own object as a sensory experience, it reproduces its own form. Therefore, it is not logical for there to be a conjunction with a word within the consciousness that apprehends that [object].

Furthermore, if it were not to grasp that [object] even when the object is present and functioning as its producer, then the sensory experience would have to remain waiting for the conjunction with the vocal sound that expresses it—an operation accomplished by memory.
In that case, a final farewell has been offered to the apprehension of meaning. For indeed:
not perceiving that object, one does not recollect the sound that expresses it as having a convention established for it therein, due to the absence of a means.

And if one does not recollect [an object], one cannot apply it to the object present before the eyes, because it is impossible to apply it without the application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāpana*); and if one does not so apply it, according to your own position, one would not see it, and thus through such blindness one would fall into total blindness. Furthermore, if even sensory cognition were held to be defiled by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), [it would lose its status as direct perception].
In that case, even that [perception] would cease upon the emergence of another conceptual construction, just like a conceptual construction such as a kingdom of the mind;
yet this is not so,
because visual perception directed toward a nearby cow-individual does not cease even when a conceptual construction of an object such as a horse arises.

Furthermore, because it is established that even for one whose all conceptual constructions have been withdrawn, there occurs a perception of objects that are clearly present; therefore, sensory cognition does not experience contact with words.

To this, the following reply is given: as for what was first stated—that perception is devoid of sound because it arises from the causal capacity of an object that is itself non-verbal—[this is refuted].
That is incorrect;
for one cannot say that something is "devoid of verbal expression" merely because it arises from an object not conjoined with words.

Otherwise, if it were said to be "arisen from an insentient object," it would itself be insentient. Now, if you argue that it is not insentient because of its association with mental attention (*manaskāra*) which is of the nature of cognition (*bodha*), [we reply:]...

If that were the case, then because of its association with mental attention (*manaskāra*) conjoined with verbal expression, it would also be accompanied by verbal expression. Furthermore, how could atoms, which are distinct [from one another], while producing a cognition whose object is themselves by way of imparting their own form, manifest therein a form that does not exist within them—a form that pervades their own parts and persists through a succession of time? If you say "due to error" (*vibhrama*), we say no.

It is not the case that only that which exists in the object appears [in cognition], because even a coarse form (*sthūrākāra*) that does not exist there appears. The same applies to the word (*śabda*). If that which is non-existent were to appear in the cognition apprehending the object, what would be lost?
And as for what was said: "Even when the object is being engaged, if it were the case that [the word] exists while awaiting its connection with the word produced by memory," and so forth, up until—
It would result in blindness;
that is equally true for your position as well. For instance:
even when there exists non-conceptual sensory cognition whose object is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), there is no determination of the object as "this" or "not this."
As long as the subsequent pair of conceptual constructions does not arise by way of affirmation and negation—
according to the statement that "its status as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) exists only in that very portion where it generates a conceptual construction"— [it remains a valid cognition].

Because even though it exists as non-conceptual, it is, with respect to linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*), as if non-existent. And that conceptualization can only arise for one who remembers the universal of the expression (*abhilāpasāmānya*) that occurred at the time of the linguistic convention;
and from what would the seed for remembering the universal of the expression be awakened?
If you say, "From such a perception," [we reply:]...
But surely that perception, because it is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), does not go beyond the object;

how then could it awaken the seed of a conceptualization whose object is a universal (*sāmānya*)? Furthermore, it is your own dogmatic insistence that an object cannot produce a cognition whose nature is the determination of a universal. Therefore, like the object itself, the perception directed toward it—being devoid of determination—is not the seed for the recollection of a linguistic universal as its domain.
That which is unawakened does not produce recollection;
recollection that has not arisen does not apply a word;
a word that is not applied does not determine the object.
An object that is not ascertained does not enter into practical discourse (*vyavahāra*); that which has not entered into discourse is no different from what is unseen;
and that which is no different [from the unseen] characterizes the blindness of the knower. Therefore, because there is an absence of ascertainment in any way whatsoever, by itself—

Even though non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka-darśana*) is itself unperceived, it gives rise to conceptualization (*vikalpa*) by means of awakening latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), thereby expressing its own activity with respect to certain specific aspects;
likewise, if the object itself were also unperceived because it does not fall within the causal complex of the eye and other sense faculties, [it could not be known].
Because it has such an intrinsic nature,

we do not see anything at all unreasonable in the view that it brings forth a self-referential cognition conjoined with verbal expression, by means of awakening mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) whose object is the universal of verbal expression produced at the time of linguistic convention. Nor is this conceptual cognition comparable to the conceptual constructions of a daydream or the like.

Because [the former] is produced by the causal complex of the eye and so forth, whereas the other arises from the mind alone; therefore, how could the latter cease upon the manifestation of another conceptualization?
For it is only a mental conceptualization that is ceased by another conceptualization.

However, because this [conceptual cognition] proceeds by force through the power of its cause, by this [argument] the claim that "it would not manifest in the state where all conceptual constructions have been withdrawn" is also refuted;

for it is impossible to withdraw this by the will of the cognizer, since its capacity is established only in the withdrawal of mental conceptual constructions. And this demonstrates the extreme inferiority of the position of absolute non-conceptual perception even compared to the position of perception associated with words.
This was grasped by us while demonstrating it.

However, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), verbal expression is not admitted in direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) because of its proficiency in directly apprehending the object through a clear determination (*viśadavyavasāya*). That [perception], moreover, is present and perfectly distinct.

That which perceives an object— such as a pillar— as something that pervades its own constituent parts, persists through different moments of time, conceals its momentary transformations, has the dimensionality of atoms unperceived,
possesses both similar and dissimilar forms in relation to other objects, and constitutes the general form of its own constituent atoms, is called "conceptual" (*savikalpaka*).

This is for the purpose of refuting non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) which is inclined toward grasping the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of atoms characterized as being devoid [of parts] and momentary— as imagined by others—
or else for the purpose of demonstrating that its object is in some way capable of association with verbal expression. And thus, when an object has been made the domain of perception,
all linguistic conventions (*śābdavyavahāra*) concerning it— such as the grasping of the relationship between a name and the named— are non-metaphorical (*nirupacarita*).
It is said that they "strive" [to function]. If, however, perception were not a manifestation capable of being associated with words, what would be the fault?
If this is asked, the consequence would be the total abolition of all worldly activity due to the non-arising of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). To explain:

Even a perception that is endowed with extreme clarity is incapable— despite the intensity of the impressions of practice (*abhyāsa-vāsanā*)— of depositing the seed of memory or of awakening such a perception of the object occurring at a later time,
since it is through the arising of conceptual constructions of universals (*sāmānya-vikalpa*) that worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) proceeds.
Even though momentariness and other such properties are accepted as being perceived by non-conceptual direct perception at all times, they are not actually seen [by it].
Therefore, in whatever portion of an object subsequent linguistic activity occurs, a prior cognition must be admitted as the determinative factor.

Otherwise, due to momentariness and similar factors, all conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) would collapse across every aspect [of an object]. Therefore, the quality of being "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*) never enters the range of experience for the cognizer of perception either. It is difficult to believe that something exists when it is not experienced, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); thus, this is not a valid definition.
[NAV 4.6] Even non-erroneousness (*abhrāntatva*) is not tenable, because according to your own view, a cognition that grasps a stable and gross object is of a distorted nature,
while its opposite does not manifest even during the time of a dream. Therefore, if non-erroneousness consists in grasping an object exactly as it exists, [then it cannot apply to your position].
That is simply not possible, because atoms that perish moment by moment in isolation never appear [to cognition],

and because they alone possess ultimate reality. Now, if one intends to speak from a conventional perspective regarding this pot and so forth, which is a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākṣama*), [then it may be so].
In that case, if what is intended by "non-erroneous" is that which does not err, then the term "free from conceptual construction" (kalpanāpoḍha) must be discarded,
because there is now no coexistence with this [term].
Because that which enters into practical activity (*vyavahāra*), such as the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a jar and so forth, is apprehended precisely through determination (*nirṇaya*);

otherwise, no practical activity would occur, and even what is seen would not differ from what is unseen. Therefore, it is established that perception is essentially determinate (*vyavasāyātmaka*); this alone is correct.

By the phrase "by way of being immediate" (*aparokṣatayā*), however, he avoids the confusion of perception with the definition of indirect cognition, because perception consists in the grasping of an object through direct manifestation (*sākṣātkāritva*). By the word "such as this" (*īdṛśam*), moreover, through the previously stated reasoning, he demonstrates—by means of a restrictive qualification—that the cognition is accompanied by a collection of qualifiers; thus, he excludes that which possesses the definitions imagined by others.
This refutes the status of [perception] as direct perception (*pratyakṣatā*). Thus, what they have said— namely,

"Perception is knowledge produced from the contact of a sense faculty with its object, which is non-verbal, non-erroneous, and of a determinate nature"— and likewise, "The arising of cognition in a person when there is a connection with that which exists is perception," and so forth, is shown to be untenable.

Because the manifestation of something previously non-existent (*apūrva-prādurbhāva*) is contradicted by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), for it would entail the absurd consequence that even things absolutely non-existent, such as a hare's horn, could arise. Therefore, this [consciousness], which already exists as the very nature of the self, cannot possibly possess qualifiers such as "arisen" or "born" by way of a transformation consisting in the direct apprehension of an object upon the proximity of a causal complex that produces its specific qualities. If you were to say that this [text] merely indicates such a meaning, [we reply:]...
This being so, there is indeed no disagreement; let that matter rest for now.
Now, he demonstrates the definition of the indirect (parokṣa):
"the other," and so forth. It was stated that perception (*pratyakṣa*) is cognition that apprehends an object through directness (*aparokṣatayā*).

Therefore, it should be known and understood that any other cognition which does not directly apprehend the object is indirect (*parokṣa*). Showing that even this [cognition] is indeed direct with respect to self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), but receives the designation "indirect" with respect to external objects, he says:
"with respect to apprehension."
In this context, "grasping" (grahaṇa) refers to setting [the object] in motion outside [of oneself], following from the subject matter at hand;
otherwise, the qualification would be redundant.
"By that" means by that expectation of observation.
That is to say, by means of an investigation into external activity. Thus, the meaning is this:

although it is itself perception (*pratyakṣa*), nevertheless, because it functions as a non-immediate apprehension when grasping external objects through the medium of signs (*liṅga*), words (*śabda*), and so forth, it is "indirect" (*parokṣa*).

Thus it is said. And this [means of knowledge] possesses the nature of arising by virtue of the cognition of another object that is otherwise inexplicable (*anyathānupapanna*) given the object one desires to know. Because the general definition (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) is present, although it is of a single form, it is divided into two types for the purpose of dispelling misconceptions (*vipratipatti*), namely:

inference (*anumāna*) and verbal testimony (*śābda*). This is because even today others do not recognize that a word itself possesses the quality of being otherwise inexplicable (*arthānyathānupapannatva*).
And it is not possible to describe that which is not separated as being distinct from it;
therefore, it is presented as a distinction.
In this regard, wishing to state the definition of inference (*anumāna*), he says:
Inference is known as that which ascertains the probandum from a mark (liṅga) that is inseparably connected with it;
it is non-erroneous because it is a valid means of cognition, just like direct perception.

[NAV_5.1] Here too, "inference" (*anumāna*) is the designation of the definiendum (*lakṣya*), because it is already well-known and thus merely restated (*anūdya*). "That which ascertains the probandum (*sādhya*) from a mark (*liṅga*) that is inseparably connected with the probandum" is the designation of the definition (*lakṣaṇa*), because it is not yet well-known and thus is what is to be enjoined (*vidheya*). In this case as well, the meaning of the word "inference" is explained according to the sequence of its derivation through grammatical factors (*kāraka*), such as the agent (*kartṛ*).

It should be understood as being like the word *pramāṇa*. Therefore, here too, that cognition by which an object to be inferred (*anumeya*)—such as fire—is measured or determined subsequent to the time of recollecting the connection between the mark (*liṅga*) and its property (*sādhyāvinābhāvitva*), characterized by the apprehension of the mark, is inference (*anumāna*). To the question "Of what nature is it?", he says:

Regarding the phrase "that which ascertains the probandum" (*sādhyaniścāyakam*): it is called "probandum" (*sādhya*) because it deserves to be proven (*sādhanaṃ arhati*), or because it is capable of being proven (*sādhayituṃ śakya*); the meaning is that it is the object of inference (*anumeya*). "That which ascertains it" means, in other words, that which determines its true nature. To the question "Why is that so?", he says:
"From the *liṅga*": that by which an object (*artha*) is indicated or understood is the *liṅga*, meaning the reason (*hetu*). To the question "Of what kind?", he says:
"Inseparable from the probandum" (*sādhyāvinābhūna*). That which exists without [the probandum] is *vinābhu*; that which is other than that is *avinābhu*.
"Inseparable from the probandum" (*sādhyenāvinābhu*) means "inseparable from the probandum" (*sādhyāvinābhu*), which signifies that it does not exist apart from the probandum;

therefore, the knowledge that ascertains the probandum is "inference" (*anumāna*). This is to be connected with the phrase "is intended" (*smṛtam*), meaning it is so accepted by those who know the principles of reasoning (*nītividbhiḥ*).

In this context, by the phrase "that which determines the probandum through the mark" (*liṅgāt sādhyaniścāyakam*), he excludes the possibility that inference is confused with the definitions of perception and verbal testimony. By the phrase "inseparable from the probandum" (*sādhyāvinābhunaḥ*), he explains the rejection of the definitions of the mark (*liṅga*) formulated by others.

Consequently, as for what others have asserted—that there are only three types of marks characterized by the three forms consisting of the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), positive concomitance (*anvaya*), and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—[this is refuted].
Non-apprehension, essential nature, and effect— this has been stated:
"Presence in the object of inference and in what is similar to it, and absence in its absence."
"the three types of reasons are called 'effect,' 'non-perception of the certain,' and 'nature'";
likewise others say: "that which is an effect, a cause, a conjoined, an inherent, or a contradictory is inferential";
and similarly: "the a priori, the a posteriori, and that based on general observation," and so forth—all of this should be understood as being for the most part the prattle of children.
Because it is only the state of being inseparably connected with the probandum (*sādhyāvinābhāvitva*) that constitutes the capacity to prove;
for that which lacks this, even if it possesses the three characteristics, lacks the capacity to prove—
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even such things as "being his son" would possess the capacity to prove.

If it is argued that this undesirable consequence does not apply because a definition consists of the three characteristics (*trailakṣaṇya*) and not just anything whatsoever, like a restrictive rule (*niyama*), we say no.
Because it is precisely the invariable concomitance with the probandum that is illuminated [by the reason];
and if that exists, what is the use of depending on the three characteristics, since that alone is the means of cognition? For instance:
From the moon in the water [one infers] the moon in the sky;
from the rising of the Kṛttikās [the rising of] the cart-shaped constellation;
and from one mango tree in flower [one infers] all mango trees in flower.

We infer the blooming of the night-lotus pond from the rising of the moon, or shade from a tree, and so forth, even in the absence of the mark’s presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*). If you argue that time and the like do indeed exist as the subject (*dharmin*) in those cases, and thus the mark is apprehended as being present in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), [we reply:]
This is to avoid an over-extension;

for if the impermanence of sound were to be proven in this manner, it would follow that even the blackness of a crow and the like would be a means of proof, since one could likewise postulate "the world" and so forth as the locus (*dharmin*) in those cases as well. Likewise, [the argument] "sound is impermanent" is also devoid of positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
The argument that "because of audibility" (*śrāvaṇatvāt*) can be established as a valid reason (*samyag-hetu*) is untenable;

thus, positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is not even a defining characteristic of a logical reason. For, according to your own implication, all existence has already been encompassed by impermanence; how then could the property of being audible—which is a property of existing things—venture to exist in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) apart from impermanence?

Because that which is devoid of it would result in being without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), just as existence is impossible for something that is exempt from impermanence. By this [it is shown that]: "The living body possesses a self (*sātmaka*), because it possesses breath and so forth."
Because [if things were] devoid of self-nature, there would follow the consequence of their deficiency,
just like a jar and so forth— this too has been explained as a prover (*gamaka*),
since the property of "not being otherwise possible given the probandum" (*sādhyārthānyathānupapannatva*) exists here as well.
However, since the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and positive concomitance (*anvaya*) have been demonstrated not to be defining characteristics,

that restriction to the three types of logical marks (*liṅga*)— namely, effect, essential nature, and non-perception— which is asserted on the grounds that the existence of a relationship characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*) occurs only in these cases,
is likewise untenable.

If a Vaiśeṣika should think: "Even though color and so forth lack the two aforementioned types of relation, they are observed to indicate taste and so forth. Let it be that their status as indicators does not arise from identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*);
rather, it will arise from inherence (*samavāya*).
Nevertheless, 'the impossibility of being otherwise' (*anyathānupapannatva*) alone is the definition of a logical reason (*hetu*)."
That [position] must be examined differently. For he should be questioned regarding his conceptualization:
Is inherence non-different from the inherent things, or is it different? If it is non-different, then it is merely the inherent things themselves.
There is no inherence,
because it is not distinct from that [substance],
just like its own essential nature. If it were distinct, [it would follow that it is not inherent].
How would he abide in those [qualities]:
as a whole, or perhaps by way of a single part?
If it were as a whole, [then...]
That is incorrect,

because it would entail the consequence of there being a plurality of inherences, since each inherence would have to be fully present in every substrate of inherence. Or, if [it were argued that it inheres] by way of a single part, [then...]
That too is not tenable, because the loss of partlessness follows from the consequence of having parts;

and even if it were to exist in its own parts, the dilemma of whether it exists in its entirety or in part would still arise. Furthermore, in that case as well, if one adopts the position of totality, there would be multiplicity.

It remains exactly as it was. However, in the case of the "partial" (ekadeśa) view, there would be an infinite regress due to the necessity of further parts. Therefore, one should not place hope for the capacity to indicate [the probandum] based on the power of inherence (samavāya), because that very [inherence] is poorly established in that regard. By this, the indicative capacity of things connected by conjunction (saṃyogin) is also refuted.

Because the same objection applies. Even for a contradictory [reason], its capacity to indicate the absence of the contradictory is nothing other than the fact that it is "otherwise impossible" (*anyathānupapannatva*);
for in the absence of that, its status as an indicator would be untenable.
[NAV 5.4] Thus, whatever other definition of a logical mark (*liṅga*) conceived by others constitutes a factor for its indicatory capacity, it does not deviate from being "otherwise impossible."
Because that which is possible even without the probandum lacks the capacity to indicate it; thus,
it is established that this must be included within the definition of the mark (*liṅga*) as a pervader (*vyāpaka*),
while the opposite must be rejected.
[NAV_5.5] Having thus established the definition of inference, we shall now address that which was asserted by the disciples of the Son of the Śuddhodana,
namely: "Inference is erroneous,
because it manifests a universal (sāmānya)."

Furthermore, because that [conceptual cognition] is excluded by the alternatives of being either different or non-different from the external particular (svalakṣaṇa), it is not [directly] connected to it;

yet, since it determines that [particular] as having that [conceptual] form, and because grasping something as what it is not is the definition of error, the validity of inference nonetheless arises through a mediated process due to its dependence on the power of the external particular. For instance:
Without the object, there is no existence of the logical mark (liṅga) bound by a relationship consisting of identity or causality;
without that [mark], there is no cognition having it as its object;
and without that cognition, there is no recollection of the previously determined relationship.

If that [object] is not remembered, there is no inference; thus, because it does not deviate from the object, even an erroneous cognition is accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). As it has been said:
"The apprehension of something as what it is not is an error, yet it is a valid means of knowledge due to its connection [with the object]. To refute this, he says:
"Non-erroneous," and so forth. That [cognition] is inference;
it is "erroneous" (bhrānta) because it errs—that is, it is mistaken—regarding its own object-domain; other than that is "non-erroneous."

This means, in short, that it grasps the object without error; and this is the thesis (*pratijñā*). It is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because by means of it an object is measured—that is, determined—exactly as it exists;

its state of being such is its reality (*tattva*), and [the proof proceeds] from that. This, however, is the reason (*hetu*). "In the presence of the senses" (*samakṣam*) means they are conjoined with them;

"like that" (*samakṣavat*) is the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Thus, this [argument], which possesses all its constituent members (*avayava*), serves to refute the erroneous nature of inference.

Since the introduction (*upanaya*) and conclusion (*nigamana*) are already implied by the demonstration of the three members [of the syllogism], the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been indicated;
however, the formal application (*prayoga*) should be seen as follows: "Inference is non-erroneous."
Because it is a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*);
for whatever is a valid means of cognition here is non-erroneous, such as direct perception (*samakṣa*),
and inference (*anumāna*) is likewise accepted by you as a valid means of cognition.

Therefore, let it be understood that because it is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it is non-erroneous (*abhrānta*). In this regard, the proponent of the [real] object (*arthavādin*) is unable to demonstrate the deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavikalatā*) in the example characterized by direct perception (*samakṣa-lakṣaṇa*), since he himself accepts that direct perception is non-erroneous. Furthermore, because the proponent of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*) denies everything, he is simply unfit for the conventional usage of means and objects of knowledge (*pramāṇa-prameya-vyavahāra*);
thus, one need not refute his objections regarding the defects of one's own proofs (*svasādhana-doṣa*) with reference to him.
Because there is no possibility for such a doctrine to arise, as its thesis is sublated by one's own words.
To explain: does the statement that establishes the non-existence of everything exist, or does it not exist?
If it exists, then there is a loss of the thesis (*pratijñāhāni*). If, on the other hand, it does not exist, [then the non-existence of everything remains unestablished].
There is the establishment of all entities,
because there is no negator.
Furthermore, the proponent of cognition [maintains that reality is] non-conceptual, devoid of the forms of the cognized and the cognizer, and beyond the scope of all conceptual constructions.

By accepting that cognition— which is to be known through isolated, ultimate self-awareness— is in fact entirely erroneous because it is produced by the power of latencies accumulated since beginningless time and is defiled by the forms of grasped object and grasping subject appearing as external,
one would assert that the example under discussion, which is characterized by direct perception, is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhya*).
Therefore, in order to refute that view, he says:
"Even that which is erroneous is not [invalidated] perception, because its status as a means of valid cognition is certain;
for the statement 'erroneous [perception] is a means of valid cognition' is a contradiction. (NA 6)
[NAV_6.1] That which is revolving in your mind is this: not only is inference erroneous,
but even that direct perception (pratyakṣa) which you have adduced as an example is likewise indeed erroneous.
Because of the statement, "Everything is erroneous with respect to its object," this [objection] is not [valid]. Why? He says:
"Because of the ascertainment of its being a valid means of cognition (pramāṇa)."
The meaning is: "because of the determination of the nature of valid cognition.

Now, one might raise an objection from the perspective of a bystander, suspecting: "If an opponent understands that validity (*pramāṇatā*) is otherwise inexplicable without non-erroneousness (*abhrāntatā*), then, by accepting that [validity], how could he maintain a contrary position regarding erroneousness? Anticipating this, [the author says: NAV_6.2.

By establishing the contradiction between being erroneous and being a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), [the author] excludes [cognition] from being a *pramāṇa* and, showing that it is nonetheless pervaded by the non-erroneousness asserted as its only possible refuge, says:

"Erroneous," and so forth. That speech which consists of the statement, "It is erroneous—that is, inverted—and yet it is a *pramāṇa*, the cause for determining the object to be grasped"—such a sound conveying such a meaning is contradictory, because its core contains mutually inconsistent [prior and posterior] meanings.
[NAV_6.3] But is it not the case that there is no contradiction here?

For indeed, with the intention of explaining the conventional from the perspective of those who have not realized the ultimate truth, we declare the validity of perception and inference, whose existence is produced by the awakening of extremely firm latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), while we are constructing the worldly convention.

This is because, according to that intention, those two are non-contradictory insofar as they lead to the attainment of the object shown [by them]. However, for those whose births are produced by the manifestation of weak latent impressions (*vāsanā*), there is a lack of validity; this is because, even regarding the object shown by that very intention, there is deception.

Furthermore, from the perspective of one who investigates reality (*tattvacintaka*), all appearance—which surges outward and is defiled by the turbidity of the forms of the grasped and the grasper—is erroneous, because its nature is the opposite of ultimate non-dual consciousness.
Because external appearance has a nature that is corrupted by its inability to withstand an investigation into the object it grasps. For instance:

an object must be either of the nature of a whole (*avayavin*) or of the nature of parts (*avayava*), as there is no other possibility. First of all, an object of the nature of a whole cannot withstand investigation.
Because, in the absence of parts, it is impossible for there to be a whole, and because the logical alternatives regarding its subsistence in those [parts] are untenable. To explain:
does this [whole] subsist in them by way of a single part or in its entirety? It cannot first be by way of a single part.

This is because it [the whole] is itself partless. If one postulates further parts as the basis for its existence within those [subordinate] parts, there follows the consequence of having to postulate yet further parts for their existence as well;

thus, there would be an infinite regress. Nor does it exist in its entirety [in each part], because that would entail a multiplicity of wholes, since the form [of the whole] would be fully present in every individual part. This is the fault in the position that [the whole] is distinct [from its parts].
If it is argued that [the whole] does not exist in the case of non-difference, we say no; for even in that case, there would be either merely the parts or merely the whole,
because they are not distinct from one another.
It would possess the nature of each of its parts.

Furthermore, if one accepts a whole (*avayavin*) that pervades all its parts, then when a portion of a cloth or similar object is seen to be dyed or shaken, it would be impossible to avoid seeing the entire cloth as dyed or shaken; for it is illogical for a single entity to be simultaneously affected by contradictory properties such as being dyed and not being dyed. Nor does an object consisting of parts fall within the scope of rational investigation.
Because parts such as the hands, feet, head, and neck, being composite entities in relation to their own constituent parts, are already discarded by that very refutation [of the whole].

If it is argued that the state of being a part is established for atoms due to their partlessness, we say no; for even they would necessarily possess six parts through their connection with the six cardinal directions.

Because there is no existence otherwise [than as a representation], and because it is devoid of an external object, the aspect of the apprehended (*grāhyākāra*) directed toward that [object] is false.

When that is false, the aspect of the apprehender (*grāhakākāra*) also does not establish its own persistence, since an apprehender is impossible in the absence of an apprehended object. Its very nature exists only in dependence upon that [apprehended].
And when the forms of the apprehended object and the apprehending subject dissolve, the form of pure consciousness remains,
because its nature is never non-deviant in any circumstance;
therefore, that alone is the ultimate reality.

To this, the following reply is given: that which was asserted— that consciousness is ultimately non-dual, whereas its manifestation in the forms of the apprehended object and the apprehending subject is unreal—
is untenable.
Because there is a lack of valid evidence. For instance:

consciousness is perceived as manifesting both externally and internally through various forms—such as joy, dejection, and so forth—as well as through transformations consisting in the grasping of objects endowed with manifold properties like stability, grossness, and the like.
However, a cognition devoid of the forms of the object and the subject, such as that which you describe, never at any time enters the range of experience for anyone.

For the appearance of non-duality is not experienced even in the state of dreaming. Furthermore, those who contemplate reality (*tattvacintaka*) do not establish their own intended positions without valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*); otherwise, they would not be persons whose words are worthy of being heeded by the discerning. Otherwise, one who asserts that a single, insentient, and immutable Brahman appears as manifold, sentient, and subject to momentary destruction due to ignorance (*avidyā*) would be beyond refutation. As for the refutation offered by way of the whole (*avayavin*) and its parts (*avayava*), with the intent of negating external objects— [The text continues: ...it is stated that this is merely a futile effort, like striking the sky with one's fist. For the whole is not distinct from its parts; rather, it is simply a collection of parts. And since the parts themselves are likewise [subject to analysis], there is no whole at all. Even if a whole were admitted, it would still be perceived through its parts. Moreover, the parts are not perceived separately from the whole, nor is the whole perceived apart from the parts. Therefore, the whole does not exist as something distinct from the parts. Nor can it be said that the whole is merely the collection of parts, because a collection is a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). Furthermore, if the whole were nothing other than the parts, then when one part is seen, the whole would be perceived in its entirety, just as when a single part is grasped. But this is not the case. Thus, the whole is not established. Consequently, the refutation of external objects based on the analysis of the whole and its parts is a mere waste of effort. For the proponents of external objects do not maintain that the whole is something other than the parts; rather, they hold that the parts themselves, appearing in a certain configuration, are designated as a "whole" by conventional usage. Therefore, the critique of the whole is irrelevant to their position. Thus, the attempt to refute external objects through the analysis of the whole and its parts is as futile as striking the sky with one's fist. It is only the ignorant who, failing to understand the nature of things, engage in such fruitless disputes. Those who seek truth should instead rely upon the means of valid cognition and abandon these vain arguments. Thus ends the section on the refutation of the whole and its parts. Now follows the refutation of atoms (*paramāṇu*). [End of excerpt]
Furthermore, because its body has been shattered by the hammer of appearances recognized by all living beings— both internal and external— as being manifest, it is,
for those who observe it as being spat out from the midst of devotion, little more than the oaths of a procuress intent on deception;
thus, it does not please the minds of wise men.

If one were to deny the manifestation of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), there would be no arising of fallacious conceptual constructions (*kuyuktivikalpa*), because they are rooted in that [perception]. Furthermore, even regarding cognition (*saṃvedana*), the objection concerning its subsistence as a single entity amidst multiple forms such as white and non-white—namely, the dilemmas of difference and non-difference, or of being a whole versus a part—is exactly the same; thus, it is not a valid refutation. Since the manifold transformations (*vivarta*) of forms are unreal, cognition, which is ultimately real, does not [share their defects] with them.

If you argue that this involves considerations of difference and non-difference, then surely an inescapable circularity presents itself. For instance: the establishment of the unreality of those [dualities] depends upon the establishment of non-dual cognition; [and conversely, the latter depends upon the former].

And because of the logical principle that when that [the whole] is established, its unreality follows; furthermore, just as a non-dual consciousness existing in a single moment experiences a connection with preceding and succeeding moments, so too, if partless atoms were to enter into contact with spatial parts or with other atoms, what would be improper? Nor is there any refutation against the positions of absolute difference or non-difference between the whole and its parts.
That [objection] does not undermine our position, because those two—whose forms are mutually inseparable yet whose distinction is intended to be shown—are accepted [by us];

for it is impossible to deny them, since they manifest in exactly that way both externally and internally. By this, the raising of objections regarding contradictions such as passion and dispassion, or trembling and non-trembling, is also refuted.
Because there is no contradiction regarding an object established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
since only that which is sublated by valid cognition is contradictory;
and because false conceptual constructions (*kuyuktivikalpa*) cannot function as sublaters when perception (*pratyakṣa*) is denied, as they would then be rootless.
Because [the object] has been uprooted, there is no arising [of it];

and because all phenomena have distinct grounds for their application (*pravṛtti-nimitta*), any contradiction produced by their opposites is cast far away. Furthermore, cognition itself, with respect to ultimate and conventional discourse, takes forms such as perceptible and imperceptible, conceptual and non-conceptual, erroneous and non-erroneous, and so forth.
For one who accepts external objects, the cognition that negates the superimposition of contradictory properties merely indicates [one's own] stupidity.
It is established that there is no valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that is in any way erroneous, because that would entail the loss of its own essential nature (*svarūpa*).
[NAV_6.5] But surely, the cognition is erroneous because the object it reveals is unreal, not by virtue of its own nature;
and at the time of its arising, there exists no discerning determination by anyone that "this has an unreal object" while "that has a non-unreal object."

Because that which is considered erroneous and that which is considered non-erroneous are manifested as having a single identical nature. Furthermore, when even such things as a pair of moons—which fall within the range of clear perception—are seen to enter into the state of unreality, then there can be no confidence at all, since the suspicion that even those appearances considered to have entirely real objects might possess unreal objects does not cease. Nor should one postulate the attainment of the object and so forth as the cause for dispelling doubt, because even in the state of dreaming, such attainment occurs while the unreality of the object is established. If it is argued that its lack of truth is due to the occurrence of a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*), we say no.

Because that [cognition] is restricted to its own specific object, it lacks the capacity to sublate [the other]; otherwise, Devadatta’s cognition apprehending blue would result in sublating a previously arisen cognition of yellow. Furthermore, the equality [of the two cases] is established by the absence of any sublater for any appearance whatsoever. Therefore, this is merely an error on your part regarding which cognitions are mistaken and which are not.
"Because everything has a false object due to the absence of discernment.
To this, he replies: "Clearly, because it is not established that all appearances are erroneous..."
A means of valid cognition, which ascertains both itself and others, is established when both [parties] have agreed upon it.
[NAV_7.1] He thinks as follows:
even one who asserts that all cognition is erroneous must nevertheless admit that the means of proving it is non-erroneous.
If that [cognition] were erroneous, then because the object it presents would be unreal, it would follow that all cognitions are non-erroneous;
otherwise, its being erroneous would be impossible. And in this way, other cognitions of the same class would also be non-erroneous;
consequently, since the error of every appearance—that is, of all consciousness—would not be established, the state of being inverted could never be accomplished.

The connection [of the words] is as follows: that which is clear (*sphuṭa*), which determines itself and others, and which illuminates both self and other by virtue of being well-ascertained (*suniścitatayā*), is valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And that [valid cognition] is established—that is, it comes into being—only when the pair consisting of its own nature and its object is accomplished;
otherwise, since there would be no object of cognition (*prameya*), there would be no valid cognition. Therefore, the intention is that one who accepts valid cognition must also accept the object.

[NAV_8.0] Having thus established the definition of inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*) and having refuted the misconceptions regarding the erroneous nature of those who possess it, [the author], since there is little more to be said, now states the definition of verbal testimony (*śābda*), which is included within the very definition of inference for others (*parārthānumāna*) already explained:
"From a statement that is observed, desired, and uncontradicted, and which expresses the ultimate reality..."
Knowledge that arises from grasping reality is proclaimed as verbal [knowledge].

In this context as well, "verbal" (*śābda*) is the definiendum (*lakṣya*), because it is that which is being restated (*anūdya*). "Not contradicted by what is seen or what is accepted" (*dṛṣṭeṣṭāvyāhata*) and so forth is the definition (*lakṣaṇa*), because it is that which is being enjoined (*vidheya*). A sentence in which there is an object (*artha*) that is desired—that is, intended to be communicated—and not contradicted—meaning not refuted—by what is "seen," i.e., observed by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is described as such.
That is to say, it is that which is not sublated by an object determined by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*);
therefore, its expressed meaning (*vācya*) is the supreme, non-artificial, purposeful, or practicable goal.
That which has the habit of expressing such [a goal] is "that which expresses the ultimate truth" (*paramārthābhidhāyin*).

The meaning is that it reveals a distinguished object (*viśiṣṭārthadarśaka*). Therefore, the connection is as follows: that means of knowledge (*māna*) which has arisen through the apprehension of reality (*tattva*) and has acquired its own existence by virtue of its habit of grasping the object to be conveyed by the sentence under discussion—that is proclaimed and described by the former teachers as "verbal" (*śābda*). In this context, by the phrase "from what is seen, desired, and uncontradicted," [the author] excludes the words of heretics and the speech of worldly deceivers.

And he rejects its status as verbal [knowledge], because it is sublated by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). By the phrase "from a sentence," however, he shows that since a sentence alone reveals a determinate object, it expresses the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*); thus he states the absence of verbal [knowledge] arising from a word. By the phrase "expressing the ultimate reality," [he refers to] knowledge produced by statements such as the instruction regarding the ornament of the jewel on the hood of the serpent Takṣaka as a fever-remedy.

By the phrase "due to fruitlessness," he rejects its status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). By the phrase "arisen from the apprehension of reality," he excludes the verbal nature (*śābdatva*) of that which has appeared through the listener's own defects—being adept at grasping contrary meanings and so forth—even though it arises from such a statement. By the word "valid" (*māna*), with the sense of the prefix *pra-* implied, he dispels the opponent’s notion of invalidity regarding verbal cognition.
If that [inference] were invalid, it would follow that inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) would perish,
because it consists of verbal expression. If it is argued that its validity is merely figurative (*upacāra*), based on its indicating a three-membered logical reason (*tryavayava-hetu*),
and not real (*tattvataḥ*), then...
This is because that which is not a means of valid cognition (apramāṇa) cannot function as an indicator. Now, if that [inference] were a means of valid cognition in the demonstration of the reason,
then the requirement for another means of valid cognition to support the reason would collapse,
since its nature would already have been determined by that very [first inference].

Furthermore, if [an object] were established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), another means of valid cognition would be redundant. This is not the case, because it would follow that even the perception (*adhyakṣa*) imagined by you would lack validity;

for since it awaits conceptualization (*vikalpa*) regarding the object shown by it, validity would be attributed to that [conceptualization] alone. If you argue that this [conceptualization] merely expresses in words the very object already grasped by that [perception], then another means of valid cognition would be required for the reason expressed by the word.
The principle is the same for "establishing" (*samarthayate*). Verbal cognition (*śābda*) is of two kinds:

worldly (*laukika*) and derived from treatises (*śāstraja*). Among these, this common definition has been set forth for both. Furthermore, "establishment" (*samarthana*) consists in the introduction of sentences concerning the sense faculties (*ihādi*) arising from speech that is non-deceptive.

Thus, while what pertains to the mundane has been prescribed, that which pertains to the learned (śāstraja) must now be prescribed; he demonstrates the nature by which that which arises from the scripture attains the status of a valid means of knowledge:
"It is the original discovery of a trustworthy person, it is not to be transgressed, and it does not contradict what is unseen or what is desired."
The entire scripture, which imparts instruction on reality, is the shatterer of evil paths.
It teaches, instructs, and causes one to grasp the reality of living beings, non-living beings, and so forth;

or, it is called a *śāstra* because by means of it one is taught. To the question "Of what nature is it?", he states its qualifiers: it is *āpta*, meaning one whose entire host of defects such as passion has been extinguished;
that which was first perceived (*upajñam*) by him. By this, he excludes the possibility of it being authorless (*apauruṣeya*).
Because that [scripture] is sublated by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*),
because no speech is perceived in the absence of human activity,
and even when it is perceived, its meaning is not understood.

If one resorts to a person for the sake of ascertaining that meaning, it would result in the fallacy of "an elephant's bath" (where the effort is futile), because such a person, being defiled by passion and other faults, is prone to speaking false things. Furthermore, if the desired goal is achieved even through the practice of those [scriptures] themselves, why not accept a person for the purpose of composing them as well? There is no distinction between the two cases. Therefore, apart from the word of one whose defects have been exhausted, it is not logical for discerning people to engage in matters concerning the next world and other unseen objects based on anything else.
That very same scripture is [the authority], because the meaning of the words is established in its primary sense; let this suffice for now.
For this very reason, it is called *ullaṅghya*: that which is transgressed, understood with superior force, or overcome by others.
Beyond that, nothing else can be transgressed;

that is to say, it surpasses all speech. For this very reason, it is "that which possesses a contradiction with the desired [object]—which is its denotation—as determined by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) through what is perceived" (*dṛṣṭa*); or alternatively, it is that which is "perceived by means of valid cognition."
It is accepted by another statement as being contradictory to those two,
because it expresses a meaning opposed to them.
"Other than that, it is not contradicted by what is unseen or desired;
this means it expresses an uncontradicted object.

By this much, the excellence of the treatise regarding its own purpose has been stated. Now, since the instruction on reality and so forth are for the sake of others, he speaks of the excellence regarding the sake of others:
Reality consists of categories such as the individual soul (*jīva*) and so forth, because they are established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Instruction regarding them (*tattvopadeśa*) is either the revelation of their essential nature or the prescription of their protection and so forth. One who performs that is "the author of the instruction on reality" (*tattvopadeśakṛt*). For this very reason, it is "beneficial for all" (*sārva*), meaning it is conducive to the welfare of everyone.

Because it is beneficial to all people by bestowing the supreme state through the instruction of means for protecting living beings, its quality of accomplishing the welfare of others has been stated by this. Now, he speaks of its very quality of destroying the misfortunes of others: "Kāpathas" are contemptible paths, namely the other sectarian systems.

The meaning is that it is a refutation, a mover [of others], and a deconstructor; it destroys the evil doctrines that cause harm to all people. Verbal valid cognition (*śābdapramāṇa*) arises from such a treatise alone, and not from others.
"Because they are deceptive.
Now, the definition of inference for others (*parārthānumāna*) must be stated;
and observing that it shares the same status as perception (*pratyakṣa*), he states it generally:

The production of certainty in others, just as one has attained certainty oneself, is declared by the wise to be the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the sake of others; the verbal expression is so called only by way of metaphorical designation.

[NAV_10.1] Here, "inference for others" (*parārthamāna*) is the definiendum (*lakṣya*), while "just as one's own certainty," and so forth, is the definition (*lakṣaṇa*). One's own self (*sva*); its certainty (*niścaya*) is the comprehension of the object of knowledge (*prameyādhigama*).
Just like that, the production of certainty in others—those to be instructed—is the manifestation of a cognition that delimits the object of knowledge.
The meaning is that just as there is a determination of one's own object, so too is there the production of a determination for others. By "the wise" (budhaiḥ) is meant the learned;
"for the sake of others" (parārtham) refers to that by which the purpose or goal belongs to another;
and "means of cognition" (mānam) is that by which something is measured.
It has been explained and stated.

Now, one might object: "If the production of certainty is for the sake of others (*parārtha*), then knowledge (*jñāna*) as well—being active toward the communication of [the truth] to others—would likewise result in being for the sake of others. To this, he says:
Speech is for the sake of another,
not cognition,
because its operation follows immediately after that [cognition].

And because it serves solely the purpose of others, whereas the other [the means of knowledge] is remote [from that end], and because it benefits both oneself and others. To the question, "How can speech, which is of the nature of non-cognition, be a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)? he says:

"By way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*): the metaphorical designation of that cognition is the apprehension of something that, though not having that form, is grasped as having that form because it is an auxiliary factor (*aṅga*) to it.
From this, the following is meant:"

The cognition that arises in the person being instructed is called a "means of valid cognition" (pramāṇa) even though it is the speech [of the instructor], because the speech is its immediate cause; this is stated by way of metaphorical designation. In that regard, the fact that inference is for the sake of another is already accepted by others, but they do not accept that the same applies to perception.

It is said that because this [perception] grasps the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) which is empty of the entry of words, it cannot be communicated to others as its own object. Nor can perception, which is capable of grasping the unique particular, be produced in another through words;
for since words produce conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), they would likewise produce conceptual construction in the other. As it has been said:
"Words have their origin in conceptual construction, and conceptual constructions have their origin in words."
Their relationship as cause and effect does not exist; words do not even touch upon the object."
And perception is non-conceptual;
therefore, it is not produced by words. For this reason, taking inference as an example, he says the following in order to establish that perception also has a purpose for others:
"Because it illuminates objects already established through perception and inference..."
Because that [teaching] is the means for others, both [the teaching and the person who teaches it] have the welfare of others as their purpose.

The intention is that both [perception and inference] possess the status of being "for the sake of others" (*parārthatva*)—meaning they serve the purpose of the person to be instructed—because, like inference, perception reveals objects already established [by other means], and because it communicates a cognizable object (*prameya*) already apprehended by oneself;

for the cause [of their being "for the sake of others"] is equal in both cases, and not in inference alone. Furthermore, in this context, the two particles *api* and *iva* should be understood as having been omitted from the text, since they are not heard here and are required to convey that sense. Thus, there is the communication of an object perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
And the intention of one who makes such a claim is this:
"That which another considers to be impossible to demonstrate to others because it is not within their scope—that is incorrect;
for it has already been established that perception exists in the form of a determinate judgment (*vyavasāya*), by way of excluding non-conceptual direct perception."

Because its object, being in some way accessible through conceptualization, is communicable by means of words. For example, just as an object cognized through inference, when communicated to another, assumes the form of speech and is thus "for the sake of others" (*parārtha*),
so too is that which is cognized through perception "perception for the sake of others," since the process of communicating to another is identical in both cases.

This is due solely to the difference in the operation of the speech-act. For instance, when one intends to make known what has been apprehended through inference, one speaks thus: "There is fire here because there is smoke;
wherever there is smoke, there is fire."
As in a kitchen and so forth;
or by way of dissimilarity: where there is an absence of fire, there is no smoke, as in a body of water and so forth.
And likewise: "This is smoke;

therefore, because of this smoke, there is fire here," because it is possible to demonstrate [the conclusion] in that very way to those who have not yet learned or have forgotten the relationship. However, when the relationship is being remembered, it is as follows:
"There is fire here because smoke arises";
by way of dissimilarity: "There is fire here, otherwise smoke would not arise. Furthermore, demonstrating what is already perceived through direct perception, he says this much:

"Look, O King, he is going. Thus, because from both types of speech a cognition arises in the recipient who possesses the complete causal complex—concerning an object that is either inferable or perceptible—it follows that both are for the sake of another. He states this as: "Because they are the means for another," meaning that with respect to the cognition of the recipient, they are the cause for manifesting an object determined by perception or inference residing in the speaker. By this, the reason for the metaphorical designation mentioned in the preceding verse [is explained].
And he observes:
"Furthermore, it has been stated: 'Perception does not arise from a word, because that [word] generates conceptual construction.'"
"Because perception, having the particular (svalakṣaṇa) as its object, is non-conceptual"— this is incorrect;

for there is no contradiction in that [perception], which has as its object an entity consisting of both the universal and the particular and which takes the form of a definitive determination (nirṇaya), being produced by a word through some manner of having a single object.
And since such [a nature] has already been established, if it is argued that [cognition] arises from the causal complex of the eye and so forth,
and not from sound,
then inferential cognition (*anumāna*) likewise arises for a cognizer who has ascertained the reason through perception and the like, and who has not forgotten the [invariable] relation.
It does not follow from the word [itself];

therefore, even that [inference] would lose its status as being for the sake of another (*parārtha*). If it is argued that in that case (inference) the statement is for the sake of another because it expresses a capable reason, we reply that here too [in perception], it is because it demonstrates an object fit for observation. Thus, no distinction is perceived regarding the "being-for-the-sake-of-another" of both perception and inference; let this partiality be abandoned.

[NAV_12.0] Having thus established that both have the purpose of benefiting others, he states their essential nature: "And that speech which conveys an object already apprehended by direct perception is called 'direct perception' (pratyakṣa), because it is the cause for the manifestation [of that object]. NA_12 //

The connection is as follows: that speech which expresses an object apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), being skillful in describing the domain of immediate cognition, is called "direct perception. He shows by means of the word "and" (*ca*)—since it has multiple meanings—that when such speech is expressed in its very form as direct perception, it is "direct perception," but when it is expressed for one who is in disagreement by way of inference (*anumāna*), it is "inference" itself. To the question, "Why is the statement [itself] direct perception? he says:
The meaning is that it is called so metaphorically because the appearance serves as the cause, being the basis for the manifestation of the perception of the person to be instructed.
He states the inference:
"That which expresses a reason inseparably connected with the probandum..."
Inference for the sake of others consists of the statement of the thesis and so forth.
[NAV 13.1] It is called a *hetu* (reason) because it leads (*hinoti*) or causes one to understand the object (*artha*).

That statement which expresses and demonstrates such a reason—which has been previously defined as being inseparable from the probandum (*sādhyāvinābhū*)—is "inference for others" (*parārtham anumāna*), because it is the cause for illuminating inference. What is it like?

To this he says: "The thesis (*pakṣa*)"—whose definition will be stated later—"is the first (*ādi*) among those [members], namely the reason (*hetu*), the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the application (*upanaya*), the conclusion (*nigamana*), and so forth; these are thus [referred to]."

The words of those [proponents] are the sounds that express them; that which has those very [words] as its self—that is, its essential nature—is that which consists of the statements of the thesis and so forth.

[NAV 13.2] Now, one might object: having stated that "inference for the sake of others" (*parārthānumāna*) is the statement expressing the reason, to then say that it "consists of the statements of the thesis and so forth" is a logical inconsistency involving a contradiction between what precedes and what follows.
This is not so;

he thinks as follows: there is not just one mode of inference for the sake of others (parārthānumāna). Rather, one must strive to convince the other person in such a way that their understanding of the object of cognition (prameya) occurs with ease. In that regard, the proof consisting of ten members (daśāvayava) is the means of demonstration. For example:

—the five members beginning with the thesis (pakṣa), as well as their purification. In that regard, when the person to be instructed has already determined the thesis through the very commencement [of the discussion], has not forgotten the example, and possesses the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for grasping the logical connection (*pratibandha*) so that it may be recalled; and because of his cultivated intellect, is capable of inferring the remaining members [of the syllogism];
Alternatively, when one understands the subject at hand merely by that much because the intellect has been refined through extreme habituation, then only the statement of the reason (*hetu*) is made;

for the mention of the remaining members would be useless as it would not produce any refinement in the listener. Thus, the author of the Sūtras stated at the outset that the inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) consists in the presentation of the reason. However, when the person to be instructed has not yet [attained such proficiency]...
Therefore, the presentation of the reason (*hetu*) at such an inappropriate time would be like the sudden fall of an unseen hammer; thus, the thesis (*pakṣa*) is also pointed out.

Likewise, while the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that grasps the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is not being recollected, the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is also described, for otherwise the capacity of the reason would not be understood.

Even when the means of valid cognition has been recollected, the application (*upanaya*) is shown for one who does not know how to apply it to the subject of the example (*dārṣṭāntika*). Nevertheless, the conclusion (*nigamana*) is stated for one who still possesses an expectation [for further clarification].

Otherwise, the intended subject matter would remain unestablished due to confusion. Thus, wherever there is a disagreement regarding the essential nature of the thesis (*pakṣa*) and so forth, its purification must be performed by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); otherwise, those [elements] would fail to establish their own probandum. Furthermore, all of these constitute members of the proof (*sādhanāvayava*), because they serve as the means for the understanding of the person to be convinced.
But surely it has been stated that inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) consists in producing certainty in another just as one has produced certainty for oneself;
yet this sequence is not experienced at the time of inference for oneself,
because for one who knows the relationship, the realization of the probandum is established by the mere perception of the reason (*hetu*).
For the cognizer does not first establish a thesis and then seek out a reason from it,
nor does he construct an example and so forth,
because such a process of cognition does not occur. Furthermore, the capacity of the reason alone is inferred through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
It does not belong to the thesis-statement and the other members [of the syllogism], because the probandum is established even without them;

nevertheless, if one were to conceive of them as being part of the proof, it would result in an infinite regress. And if they possessed that capacity [to prove the probandum], [it would follow that they themselves require further members].

In that case, because the object to be proven (*sādhya*) would be understood from the mere presentation of the thesis (*pakṣopanyāsa*) alone, the reason (*hetu*) and the subsequent members [of the syllogism] would become useless;

for it is only in this way that their efficacy is established, and not otherwise. Therefore, that alone which makes the object to be proven known independently of anything else is the reason (*hetu*), the means of proof (*sādhana*).
"Not the thesis and so forth.
To this it is replied: what was stated—that "inference for the sake of others is said to be the production of certainty in another, just as one has certainty oneself"—is correctly stated.
You do not understand that it is solely for that purpose,
because the statement of equality with the suffix *vat* is made precisely from the perspective of certainty (*niścaya*).
However, it is not intended that there be a complete identity [between the word and its object];
