otherwise, one would understand the probandum in an inference for oneself even without uttering the sound, which would entail the absurd consequence that the production of certainty in another could occur without uttering it. And this is not the case.

Since it is impossible to communicate with another without uttering words, one must accept words for that purpose; and by the same logic, whatever else is indispensable for communicating with another must also be accepted. Furthermore, in the absence of the thesis (*pakṣa*) and other members [of the syllogism], it is not possible to communicate a specific object of proof.

Because it lacks the cognition of the meaning to be proven—such as the reason, the object of operation, and so forth—it remains expectant; and thus, due to the absence of the understanding of the intended object, it would remain uncommunicated.
Therefore, the thesis and other members must be shown for the sake of communicating that [meaning], and they too would be parts of the proof (*sādhana*). As for what was said:
"It is not a proof because it lacks the imitation of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)," [that is refuted].
It is incorrect [to claim] that the probandum is established from the mere reason alone;

for even from the mere words of a person whose non-deceptiveness is certain—such as "there is fire here"—a cognizable object is sometimes established. Consequently, it would follow that even a [formal] reason would lack the status of being a means of proof (*asādhana*). This is because [the object is established] even in the absence of that [reason].
Because the probandum is established. And this is logical, since the authority of the speech of one who does not deceive has already been proven. As for what was said:
"If these [words] were to possess efficacy..."
If it were argued that the reason would be redundant because the probandum is understood from the mere thesis alone,
that is highly improper, as the same [objection] applies to your position as well.

In that case as well, since the object to be proven (sādhya) is understood precisely through the presentation of a capable reason (*samartha-hetu*), otherwise its capacity would be impossible. Furthermore, who could prevent the subsequent confirmation of that very [reason] by means of a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and the restatement of it in the subject of the thesis (*pakṣadharmin*) for one who has already grasped the pervasion (*vyāpti*) everywhere— both of which would result in pointlessness?

If it is argued that "the capacity of the reason is not understood in its absence, therefore it is purposeful," then since a specific person to be informed cannot be informed without the thesis and the other members [of the syllogism], their purposefulness is no less easily established; let this obstinacy be abandoned. Therefore, like the reason...

The members of the syllogism (*pakṣa* and so forth) are also means of proof, because even the reason (*hetu*) sometimes depends upon them for its establishment regarding the object to be proven; thus, its independence is not established. Having taken all this into account, it was said: "That consists of the statements of the *pakṣa* and so forth.
Thus, having introduced the *pakṣa* and other members by way of their meaning, he first states the definition of the *pakṣa*:

The thesis (*pakṣa*) is the acceptance of what is to be proven, unrefuted by perception and other means of valid cognition. Its formulation should be employed here as that which illuminates the objective domain of the reason (*hetu*). (NA 14)
That which is being cooked (*pacyate*) is the *pakṣa* (the subject); that which is being manifested is the *bhāva* (the state). To the question "Of what nature is it?", he says:
it is the acceptance (*abhyupagama*), that is, the acknowledgment (*aṅgīkaraṇa*), of that which is to be proven (*sādhya*), i.e., that which is to be inferred (*anumeya*).
The meaning is the acceptance of a thesis in the presence of the judges and others. Is it merely a matter of formal admission?
No; he says: "not contradicted by perception and so forth. Perception (*pratyakṣa*) is direct, manifest cognition;
by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), inference (*anumāna*), one's own words (*svavacana*), and common worldly consensus (*loka*) are included.
The connection is that the thesis (*pakṣa*) is one that has not been set aside or contradicted by them. For example:
"Everything consists of multiple natures" (*sarvam anekāntātmakam*), and "An omniscient being exists" (*asti sarvajña*).

Or [the text] begins with "ityādi. To address one who might think that this [thesis] need only be intended and should not be expressed by words at the time of inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), he says:

"The application (*prayoga*), that is, the verbal expression (*abhidhāna*) of that thesis, must be performed—that is, it is to be prescribed—here in this context of the discussion on inference for others. Why? He says:"
Regarding the phrase "illuminator of the scope" (*gocaradīpaka*) for the cause previously determined,
it is because of the rule: "In the case of *nimitta*, *kāraṇa*, and *hetu*, all [case endings] are generally seen."
And because the indication has the state [of being] as its primary meaning, the sense is that it serves to demonstrate the object [of the reason]. This is the intended meaning here:
for not in every case is a reason presented by a respondent—after first adorning the beard of one whose position is already determined merely by the context.
Rather, it is only in some cases and in some manner.

Therefore, when the person to be convinced (*pratipādya*) still does not understand the meaning of the thesis (*pakṣārtha*), if the reason (*hetu*) were stated prematurely, there would be a fault characterized by confusion due to delusion regarding the object; thus he says:

Otherwise, for the person to be convinced, the reason would be subject to the suspicion of being contradictory, just as in the case of one who is deluded regarding the intended scope of the proponent's reason.

"Otherwise" (*anyathā*) means resorting to the opposite of what was stated, that is, failing to formulate the application of the thesis (*pakṣaprayoga*). The meaning is as follows: for that respondent (*prativādin*), who is to be convinced, the reason (*hetu*) would be suspected of being contradictory—that is, stained by the suspicion of contradiction—because he is confused or wavering regarding that which is intended and accepted by the proponent (*vādin*) who presents the reason, namely the object-domain of that reason. Consequently, even if it is a correct reason (*samyag-hetu*), [it becomes flawed].
The intention is this: out of delusion, one might state a contradictory refutation, thinking, "This [reason] resides only in the counter-example (vipakṣa)";

however, because the thesis (pakṣa) has been presented, this fault does not apply to that which has its scope determined by the reason. He states this very point with a clear example, beginning with "yathā" (just as). This is for the purpose of presenting that example.
For a person observing the qualities of an archer while he is shooting,
there is no distinction between his excellence and its opposite without the specification of a target.

Just as when an archer shoots an arrow without specifying the target, the merits and defects he perceives appear erroneously to the observer—such that even a merit appears as a defect, or a defect appears as a merit—so too, when a proponent presents a reason without specifying the thesis (*pakṣa*), the merits and defects characterized by the capacity or incapacity to prove the intended probandum appear even in reverse to the judges, the opponent, and others. This is the underlying meaning (*bhāvārtha*). However, one who moves with a bow is an archer; his excellence consists in his skill at hitting the target, and it is regarding this that the spectators have curiosity—therefore, it is he alone who is mentioned.
Otherwise, a fault must also be observed. "Of those looking on" means of the people whose habit is to look on; "of him as he pierces through" means, for instance, as he somehow releases the arrow.

The meaning is this: just as for an archer there can be no determination of the target to be pierced without a specified aim, and just as the qualities and defects—which are respectively the virtues and faults—become mutually contradictory in the absence of that aim, so it is for the proponent. Therefore, it is established that when the opponent does not understand the meaning of the thesis, the proponent-archer must first specify the target of the thesis before discharging the arrow of the reason. Now follows the occasion for defining the reason (*hetu*).
And that [inference for others] should be understood as being no different from inference for oneself;
however, the formal syllogism (prayoga) is not shown there,
because inference for oneself consists of the nature of cognition itself.
But here,
it must be shown, because inference for the sake of others consists in the form of speech;
therefore, he demonstrates it:
The application of the reason may occur either through its actual occurrence or otherwise;
in either of these two ways, the establishment of the probandum would be achieved. (NA 17)

In the context of inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*), it was established that—by way of excluding other definitions formulated by others—the sole characteristic of a logical reason (*hetu*) is its exclusion from all instances where the probandum (*sādhya*) is absent. This same [characteristic] must also be made manifest in inference for others (*parārthānumāna*); however, the arrangement of words proceeds in various ways depending on the occasion. Bearing this intention in mind, he states the two-fold nature of that [inference for others]: [NAV_17.1] For, in the discussion of inference for oneself, it was determined that the single characteristic of a reason is its exclusion from all cases where the probandum is absent, by means of setting aside other definitions devised by others. In inference for others as well, that very same [characteristic] is to be revealed; yet, the formulation of speech proceeds in some manner or another depending on the circumstances. With this in mind, he speaks of its two types:

The connection is that there would be a two-fold application of the reason (*hetu*). To the question "How so?", he says: "In that very way" means that *tathopapatti* is the occurrence or existence precisely when the probandum (*sādhya*) exists; by means of that *tathopapatti*.

"Just as there is fire here, because smoke arises in that very way"—by this phrase "or otherwise," he indicates *anyathānupapatti* (the impossibility of being otherwise) through the metaphorical application of the whole to its part. "Otherwise" means in the absence of the probandum; "impossibility" (*anupapatti*) means non-existence, or rather, by that very impossibility of being otherwise...
The application of the reason would be as follows: "There is fire here, because smoke would otherwise be impossible."

And if one should think that both of these [reasons] must be employed for a single probandum, then, for the sake of instructing such a person, he says: "By either one— whether by an application of 'establishment otherwise' (*tathopapatti*) or by an application of 'impossibility otherwise' (*anyathānupapatti*)— there is the accomplishment (*siddhi*), that is, the completion, of the probandum, which is the object intended to be communicated, upon the cognition of the person being instructed."
Since there would be a repetition, therefore neither of the two should be employed.
Since the formulation of the statement differs in both syllogisms,
yet the meaning does not; and since the fruit of a syllogism is the establishment of the probandum by the probans, and that is accomplished by either one alone.
The second application would merely indicate the speaker's lack of skill;
the intention is that [the argument] is "due to its pointlessness" (*nairarthakyāt*).
Now follows the occasion for the definition of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), and that is twofold:

[It is established] by way of similarity and by way of dissimilarity. Regarding that, he speaks with reference to the example of similarity: "That is considered an example by way of similarity where the pervasion between the probandum and the probans is most firmly ascertained; it is held [to be so] because it causes the recollection of the relationship. (NA 18)

The *dṛṣṭānta* (example) is that in which, through the power of two observed instances (*avalokita*), the internal final determination of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) occurs—either by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—serving as the basis for establishing the relationship between the probandum and the probans.

That which possesses a common property (*sadharma*) is "possessing a common property" (*sadharmā*); the state of being such is "similarity" (*sādharmya*). To the question, "Of what kind is it? he says:
The *sādhya* consists of the object one desires to know; the *sādhana* is the logical reason (*hetu*) that makes that [object] known;
and the *vyāpti* is the pervasion between those two, the *sādhya* and the *sādhana*.
An example based on similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is that wherein it is determined with certainty—that is, decisively ascertained—in the form: "This does not exist without that. For example:
"There is fire here, because smoke is present in exactly that manner."
"Like the kitchen and so forth. He states that this [reason] should not be employed against an opponent who has not forgotten the necessary connection:
"Because of the recollection of the relation," where the ablative case is used with the elision of the suffix *lyap*.
This is intended by the experts in logic (*nītivid*) with reference to the recollection of a relationship that was previously grasped but subsequently forgotten,
and not at other times. For when the person to be instructed has not yet understood the relationship characterized by the inseparable connection (*avinābhāvitva*) with the probandum (*sādhya*),
then the relationship must be made known through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

It is not established by a mere example alone; for it is not the case that simply because something is observed together with another, it follows everywhere that "this does not exist without that," as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Once the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) has been grasped and is being remembered, the reason (*hetu*) need only be presented.
Since the object desired to be known is established by that much alone, an example need not be stated,
as it would be redundant. However, when the relationship, though grasped, has been somehow forgotten,
the example is then stated for the purpose of recollecting it.
[NAV_18.2] But how, one might ask, can there be an understanding of a relationship that pervades all times and places?

First of all, even perceptual cognition (*pratyakṣa*), though determinate in nature, is not capable of observing the relationship between a probandum and a probans that move across different spaces and times, because it functions by means of a clear ascertainment directed toward an object present [to the senses]. Nor can that determination be derived from verbal testimony (*śabda*).
Because it would follow that there is no inference for one's own sake (*svārthānumāna*) since it consists of instruction by another;
because there is no instruction by another in that case;
and because, in the absence of that, the [logical] connection (*sambandha*) cannot be established.

"Because if that [perception] were unestablished, inference would not arise. For if the relationship were grasped through inference, an infinite regress without end would follow, since even the inference that grasps the relationship would itself depend upon the grasping of another relationship. To this it is replied: This fault applies only to those who hold the false dogma that there are only two means of valid cognition, namely perception and inference; it does not apply to us.

This is because another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), designated as *ūha* (presumptive reasoning), which arises subsequent to perception and non-perception that grasp positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), and which has for its object an unerring [relation] pervading the three times, is accepted as the grasper of the relationship; for if this were not accepted, there would follow the consequence of the collapse of all empirical practice (*dṛṣṭa-vyavahāra*), and if that were to collapse, inquiry (*vicāra*) would become purposeless. In this present context, however, *ūha* is not presented separately from inference (*anumāna*).
Because this [treatise] is intended to benefit beings who prefer concise presentations,
verbal [inference] has been established separately;
since that [verbal inference] is useful for inference for others (parārthānumāna) precisely here, let us leave it at that for now.

[NAV_19.0] Now, demonstrating the example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), he says: "That example is known as one by way of dissimilarity where, when the probandum (*sādhya*) is absent, the impossibility of the probans (*sādhana*) is also demonstrated. (NA_19)
A phenomenon (*dharma*) that is dissimilar to this is "heterogeneous" (*vidharmā*); the state of being such is "heterogeneity" (*vaidharmya*).
By means of that heterogeneity, there is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). To the question "Of what kind? he says:
When the probandum (*sādhya*)—that which is to be understood—is absent, the word "but" (*tu*), which has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), is impossible;
however, it should be seen here that this [impossibility] applies to the means of proof (*sādhana*)—the indicator—as well, meaning that its impossibility is exactly the same.

It is explained (*khyāpyate*) or demonstrated in some instance through a dissimilar example (*vaidharmyeṇa*), because of the recollection of the connection [between the terms] by means of the word "iti."

This also applies here: since there is no application of the formal argument (prayoga) even when the relationship is being recollected, for what purpose is an example employed against an opponent who has forgotten that very relationship, and not otherwise?
Anticipating this opportunity for an objection from another, he says:
Since the probandum is established by internal pervasion alone, an external example would be useless;
the experts in logic know that this remains so even in the absence of such an example.

[NAV_20.1] Furthermore, would the reason be employed when its relationship is being remembered, or when it has not yet been apprehended? If the first alternative is held, that is untenable. When the person to be convinced remembers the reason as being invariably concomitant with the probandum in all cases, then, having understood it in the subject (*pakṣa*) as well, how could they fail to comprehend the probandum?

Therefore, internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*)—which is the state of the probans being pervaded by the probandum within the interior [of the subject] during the middle of the debate—is sufficient for the establishment and cognition of the probandum to be inferred; consequently, the citation of an example in another locus, such as a corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*), outside the intended subject for the purpose of demonstrating pervasion, is useless and purposeless, because there is no object to be communicated by it. Rejecting the faultlessness of the second position as well, he says:

Even in the absence of that [external example], because the relationship is not grasped in this way, there is likewise an absence of internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*); thus, an external illustration is indeed useless. For it is not the case that because something is observed together with another in one instance, it possesses that same nature everywhere, since deviation is observed. Therefore, when the relationship is not yet grasped and is to be communicated, the necessary connection must be established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Once that is established, the probandum is established from that very source; hence, the citation of an example is of no consequence—so say the experts in logic, the knowers of the system.

It is said that they "understand. And in this context, although the definition has not been explicitly stated— because this [treatise] is intended for the benefit of beings who delight in brevity, and thus omits the remaining members characterized by the fivefold purification of the introduction and conclusion—
Nevertheless, from this very [text] alone, the three members [of the syllogism] have been established and should be inferred by the wise;

for, in relation to the members [of the syllogism], there are three types of discourse: inferior, middling, and superior. Among these, the inferior consists merely in the presentation of the reason (*hetu*); the middling consists in the communication of two or more members; and the superior consists in the statement of all ten members in their entirety. Of these, here—
By explicitly stating the middling [alternative], he implies the inferior and superior ones by implication, because their existence is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Having thus explained the definitions of the thesis and so forth, one should now, when there is knowledge of what is to be abandoned, [recognize] that which is to be adopted as more clearly distinguished.

Since it is that which is to be known, the fallacious thesis (*pakṣābhāsa*), reason (*hetvābhāsa*), and example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*) excluded by it must be stated. Among these, first he states the fallacious theses excluded by the definition of a thesis:

"A fallacious thesis is that which is already established for the person to be convinced (*pratipādya*) through perception (*akṣa*) or inference (*liṅga*), and that which is sublated in various ways by the world (*loka*) or by one's own words (*svavacana*). (NA 21)

Because it is presented in the position of the thesis (*pakṣasthāna*) and because it does not perform its function, it appears like a thesis; thus, it is a "pseudo-thesis" (*pakṣābhāsa*). This is understood to be of many kinds and manifold types—this is the connection [of the sentence]. How so?
He says:
whatever is already established for the opponent (*prativādin*), having indeed ascended into their cognition, that is a pseudo-thesis.

Because only that which is yet to be proven (sādhya) constitutes the subject (pakṣa), for that which is already established is unfit to be proven, and because it would lead to over-extension (atiprasakti). Thus, that which is sublated or set aside by perception, by inference, by the two types of causes [direct and indirect], or by common consensus and one's own words, is a pseudo-subject (pakṣābhāsa). Among these, an example of that which is already established for the person to be convinced (pratipādya) is as follows:
A pot belongs to the person (paudgalika), or for a follower of the Buddha (saugata):
"everything is momentary," and so forth. An example of what is sublated by perception (pratyakṣabādhita) is as follows:
Partless particulars, or the universal and the particular as mutually distinct—these are [examples of] what is sublated by inference, such as:
"There is no omniscient being. An example of what is sublated by worldly consensus is:
"One's mother is to be approached as a sexual partner. This is sublated by one's own words, just like the statement:
"All things do not exist.
Now, reminding us of the definition of a valid reason (*hetu*), he states the fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) that have been set aside:
The definition of a logical reason (hetu) is stated to be its being otherwise impossible (anyathānupapannatva).
Its fallacious appearance consists in the non-cognition, doubt, or error regarding that [definition].

The definition of the logical reason (*hetu*) that has been stated, understood, or established—due to its having multiple meanings—in the context of inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*), namely "the impossibility otherwise" (*anyathānupapannatva*):
the non-cognition of that is non-ascertainment (*anadhyavasāya*);
doubt (*sandeha*) is the state of oscillation.
*Mithyājñāna* (false cognition) is the determination of error (*vaiparītyanirṇaya*).
"Non-cognition," "doubt," and "error" form a *dvandva* compound; subsequently, that [compound] forms a *tatpuruṣa* with the word *saha*.
By those [cognitions] characterized by non-apprehension, doubt, and error regarding that [object];
"having the appearance of that" (*tadābhā*) means the manifestation as if it were that; "appearing like that" (*tadābha*) means appearing as if it were a correct cause (*samyag-hetu*);
its state is "that-ness" (*tattā*).
The meaning is that it becomes a fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*).
Now, he demonstrates by which definition each named fallacy of the reason occurs:
"But the unestablished (*asiddha*) is that which is not cognized, or that which is established otherwise."
That which is contradictory is that which is applicable here in another way as well; however, that is the inconclusive [reason].
Whatever is unperceived—that is, not made the object of cognition and not ascertained—is the fallacious reason known as "unestablished" (*asiddha*).

The word "but" (*tu*) indicates the distinction among all three types. That which occurs otherwise—meaning it exists only in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) and not in the probandum (*sādhya*) at all—is designated as "contradictory" (*viruddha*). Furthermore, that which is compatible even otherwise—that is, which is possible even in the opposite of the probandum—is...
By the word "also" (api), it is implied that [the reason] is also [inconclusive] with respect to the probandum;

thus, in this context of confusion, it should be known as being designated "inconclusive" (anaikāntika). In that regard, all reasons whatsoever put forward by the disciples of Kaṇabhakṣa, Akṣapāda, Buddha, and others—whose intellects are opposed to non-absolutism (anekānta) which is established by means of knowledge well-known to every living being—are [inconclusive].
For example: sound is exclusively impermanent, or else it is permanent, because of its existence,
or because of its having an origin.

It should be understood that [reasons] such as "because of being produced" (*kṛtakatvāt*) and "because of being recognized through re-cognition" (*pratyabhijñāyamānatvāt*), according to the speaker's intention, admit of being unestablished (*asiddha*), contradictory (*viruddha*), or inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
For instance, first of all, in the case of the absolute position that [sound] is impermanent (*anityaikānte*), all reasons whatsoever are unestablished.
Because they do not exist in sound— just as visibility does not exist in it—

and because they are conceptually constructed as false conventionalities through the exclusion of [the categories] such as "non-existent," and because if they were ultimately real, it would entail the fallacy of non-absolutism (anekāntavāda) due to a single entity assuming multiple forms.

Furthermore, because those things whose existence is constructed by conceptualization lack all causal capacity and are thus devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), even if they were to serve as means of proof (*sādhana*), the probandum (*sādhya*) would likewise be devoid of intrinsic nature; consequently, it would follow that a donkey's horn is the means of proving a rabbit's horn.
Thus, this practice of establishing a probandum and a means of proof is quite "excellent" [in its absurdity]. Indeed, this entire conventional operation of inference and the object of inference...
If it is argued that this is not a fault because the principle of the property and the property-bearer, as mounted upon the intellect, does not depend on external existence or non-existence,
then in that case, even "visibility" (cākṣuṣatva), when superimposed upon sound by the intellect and stated as a reason, should not be raised as being unestablished (asiddha).
Because there is no distinction [between them]. One can superimpose visibility upon [the object] by means of the exclusion of non-visibility, but not in an arbitrary manner;
and that [exclusion] does not exist in the case of sound.
If it is argued that this is not a fault because it is not graspable by the eye,
then what is this so-called "exclusion of non-visibility"?
Is it mere exclusion, which is formless;
or the excluded particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*);
or the excluding cognition, which, though immersed in its own part, floats as if grasping an external object?

If you argue that there is no other property of the entity (*vastudharma*) upon which you could base your desire to offer refutations by means of the two conceptual alternatives of difference and non-difference, then what kind of statement is this, that it does not exist in the word?

For if that were so, it would follow as an absurd consequence (*prasajyeta*) that one could not even conceive of properties such as existence (*sattva*) and so forth, on the grounds that "the sky-lotus does not exist therein. Furthermore, [what would happen]...?

Even though those properties of the probans exist in the subject (*dharmin*), they do not attain the status of being cognized according to your view; for perception, being devoid of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), is empty of any determination of properties, and because the conceptual cognition arising subsequently— which is produced by the awakening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)— has a nature that terminates in the apprehension of its own internal aspect, it lacks entry into the external particular (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Consequently, because they are not perceived, all [such properties] are unestablished (*asiddha*).

Even in the case of the absolute monism of permanence (*nitya-ekānta*), one should see that the properties of the subject (*dharmin*)—whether they are entirely distinct from it or merely non-ultimate—are unestablished, since they are not perceived by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
This is because it is impossible to deny all ultimate properties whose nature is inseparable from the subject, as they are established by perception and other means of valid cognition.

Likewise, contradiction (*viruddhatā*) is also to be inferred for all probative properties (*sādhanadharma*) in both positions (*pakṣa*), because they are inclined toward proving that [opposite], since their nature is not invariably connected [to the intended conclusion]. And this will be shown later [in NAV 23.5]:

"Thus, all reasons (*hetu*) being presented in both positions incur the state of being inconclusive (*anaikāntikatā*), because they are non-deviating [with respect to] mutually contradictory [conclusions]."
Because it is possible to demonstrate [the fallacy] even in the opposing case by adducing an identical reasoning.
For instance: the proponent of impermanence provides a proof against the proponent of permanence: "Everything is momentary, because of its existence (*sattvāt*)."

Because causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is incompatible with both succession and simultaneity in that which is non-momentary, and because the capacity for causal efficiency is the defining characteristic of an entity, it follows that when causal efficiency is excluded from a non-momentary thing, it must exclude existence itself, which is embraced by it; thus, momentariness is established. For a permanent entity is not capable of engaging in causal efficiency successively.
Because it proceeds toward a subsequent action by way of subverting the nature of performing the previous purposeful activity—
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of not ceasing from that previous performance—
and because its permanence would be lost upon the departure of that nature.

Because non-remaining in that same state is the definition of impermanence. If it is argued that even an eternal entity remains for a while waiting for auxiliary causes that function sequentially, and only after obtaining them performs the effect sequentially, we say no;
because auxiliary causes can contribute nothing whatsoever to an eternal entity.

Furthermore, even if it were to perform no function, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress in its waiting. Nor does a permanent entity perform causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) simultaneously, because that contradicts direct perception (*adhyakṣa*). For no one is observed to begin all actions at once;

or, even if it did, since the entirety of its actions would be completed in the very first moment, the fact that it performs nothing in the second and subsequent moments would inevitably entail its impermanence.
"Because performing and not performing [an action] are contradictory in a single [entity].

[NAV_23.7] Furthermore, the proponent of eternalism establishes his proof as follows: "Everything is eternal, because of its existence. For in that which is momentary, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is contradictory at the times of both existence and non-existence."
A being characterized by such [permanence] is not bound by states;
therefore, turning away from those [states], it establishes its own permanence due to having no other refuge. For instance:
a momentary object would either produce an effect while existing, or...
Or it would be non-existent,
because there is no other possible state. First of all, the initial position is not tenable, because an operation upon that which exists at the same time [as the agent] is impossible.

Furthermore, because all entities would result in the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of being mutually related as cause and effect, the second position also cannot withstand scrutiny; for that which is non-existent lacks the capacity to produce an effect. Otherwise, even things such as a rabbit’s horn would be capable of producing effects, since there is no distinction [between them and other non-existent things].

[NAV_23.8] Thus, in both of these one-sided positions (*ekānta*), whichever reasons (*hetu*) are adduced, because they are equal in their logical consistency (*yukti*), they do not deviate from their contradictory counterparts; rather, by being pleasing only so long as they are unexamined, they produce the blindness of deluded people. Therefore, they are "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*) reasons that do not deviate from their contradiction, because all things (*vastu*) are in reality bound to non-one-sidedness (*anekānta*). Consequently, since all these reasons, insofar as they are valid, are not possible without non-one-sidedness, it is precisely that which must be established.

Furthermore, it is established that when these [reasons] are presented by those of deluded intellect for the sake of proving the opposite side, they assume the states of being unestablished (*asiddha*), contradictory (*viruddha*), or inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) according to the speaker's intention.
Having thus explained the fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), he now states the fallacious examples (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*), which are excluded by the definition of a valid example:
"In this context, the faults of the example according to the method of similarity (*sādharmya*) have been proclaimed by the experts in logic."
Those [fallacies] such as the "deficient in the probandum" (sādhyavikala) and so forth arise from causes characterized by the absence of the [proper] characteristics.

That in which the similarity (sādharmya) intended to demonstrate the means of proof (sādhana) as being pervaded by the probandum (sādhya) exists—by that [similarity]. In this context, "defects" (doṣāḥ) refers to those things which are to be refuted (dūṣyante). Thus, "example-defects" (dṛṣṭāntadoṣāḥ) means the fallacious examples (dṛṣṭāntābhāsāḥ). They are "proclaimed by those who know the system" (nyāyavidīritāḥ), that is, spoken by the learned.
The "probandum" (sādhya) is that which is to be understood;

by the word "etc. (ādi), the inclusion of the probans (sādhana) and both [the probandum and probans] is intended. "Devoid of those" means empty of them. By the word "etc.," cases where the properties of the probandum, the probans, or both are doubtful are included. To the question "Of what nature are these?", he says:
Those from which the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) has departed are "devoid of characteristics" (*apagatalakṣaṇa*);
they are also the causes (*hetu*).
Those whose arising (*utthāna*) originates from them are "arising from causes devoid of characteristics" (*apalakṣaṇahetūttha*).

And this qualification is generally applicable, because even in the case of a correct reason (*samyag-hetu*), the status of being a fallacious example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsatā*) can arise due to defects in the speaker;
for example: "Sound is both eternal and non-eternal."
"Because it is audible,
like a pot," and so forth. Among these, an example that lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*) is as follows:
Inference is erroneous,
because it is a means of valid cognition, just like perception.
Because perception is free from error;

for if it were erroneous, there would follow the consequence of the total cessation of all worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), and if that were to cease, since there would be an absence of both means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and objects of cognition (*prameya*), nothing could be established by anything—thus the proponent of error would be rendered mute. An example of [an argument] lacking a probans (*sādhana-vikala*) is as follows:
The cognition of the waking state is erroneous,
because it is a means of valid cognition,
like the cognition of a dream.

Because dream-cognition lacks the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it is sublated by the occurrence of its opposite, namely, waking cognition. An example of that which is deficient in both [validity and sublation] is as follows:
"There is no omniscient being, because he is not perceived through perception and other means."
Like a jar; because a jar exists and is perceived through direct perception and other means. An example where the property to be proven is doubtful is:
"This person is free from passion, because he is subject to death."
Like the man in the street;

because it is doubtful whether freedom from passion exists in the man in the street, because the specific qualities of the mind are only accessible through signs such as specific modes of speech and so forth, and because there is no determination of that [freedom from passion] even in the case of the man in the street. An example of one where the property to be proven is doubtful is as follows:
This person is subject to death because he possesses passion and other defilements,
like a man on the street.

Because the presence of passion and so forth in a man on the street is doubtful, since it is possible for even one who is free from passion to appear in that manner. An example of a reason where both properties are doubtful is: "This person is not omniscient..."
Because of possessing passion and so forth,
like a man in the street; for, according to the logic demonstrated regarding the man in the street, both [reasons] are equally doubtful.

[NAV_24.3] But surely others have also stated three other fallacies of the example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*), namely: lack of positive concomitance (*ananvaya*), unshown positive concomitance (*apradarśitānvaya*), and inverted positive concomitance (*viparītānvaya*). Among these, lack of positive concomitance is as follows:
"The person intended is possessed of passion and so forth..."

"Because he is a speaker, like an esteemed person. Even though it is claimed that in the case of an esteemed person, both the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*)—the possession of passion and so forth—and the proving property (*sādhanadharma*)—the state of being a speaker—are observed, nevertheless, this example lacks positive concomitance (*ananvaya*), because the pervasion (*vyāpti*)—"whatever is a speaker is possessed of passion and so forth"—is not established. An example where the positive concomitance is not thus demonstrated is as follows: "Sound is impermanent..."

"Because it is produced, like a jar. Here, although there is indeed a real positive concomitance (*anvaya*), it has not been revealed by the proponent's statement; thus, the example is one where the positive concomitance is unshown (*apradarśitānvaya*). An example of reversed positive concomitance (*viparītānvaya*) is: "Sound is impermanent..."
Having stated the reason "because of being produced," one says, "whatever is impermanent is produced, like a jar";
because this demonstrates a reversed pervasion, it is a reversed positive concomitance (*viparītānvaya*).
For in a formulation based on similarity (*sādharmyaprayoga*), the means of proof must be shown as being encompassed by the probandum.

"But here, because of the perception of a perversion, there is a state of being contrary. Why has this not been stated by you? [NAV 24.4] To this it is replied: This formulation of the three fallacious examples was not well-considered by others; it is for the purpose of making this known. For instance: first of all, a lack of positive concomitance (*ananvaya*) cannot constitute a fallacious example. If the pervasion between the probandum and the probans were to be established by the force of an example, [then a lack of concomitance would indeed be a fault].
Consequently, there would be the fallacy of an example (dṛṣṭāntābhāsa) due to its failure to perform its own function; however,

it is established that the citation of an example is for the purpose of producing a recollection of the object within the scope of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that previously apprehended the relationship [between the probans and the probandum].
In that case, the fault of the example— characterized by a lack of positive concomitance (anvaya)— does not belong to the example itself, but rather to the reason (hetu),
because the necessary connection (pratibandha) has not yet been established by valid cognition (pramāṇa).

Furthermore, because positive concomitance (*anvaya*) cannot be established in the absence of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*), nor should a defect in the reason (*hetu-doṣa*) be alleged regarding the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Likewise, cases where the positive concomitance is not demonstrated or where it is demonstrated in a reversed manner do not constitute "fallacious examples" (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*),
for the failure to demonstrate the concomitance and the demonstration of a reversed concomitance are defects of the speaker.

Even by means of that fault of the speaker, the enumeration of fallacious examples would be undermined, because the faults of speakers are infinite. If it is argued that, although they are faults of the speaker, skill in them is required in inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), and therefore, when presented in this manner, these two do not establish the intended object and are thus "fallacious examples" (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*): [we reply as follows].
If that is the case, then deficiencies such as lack of proficiency in the instruments [of speech] should also be cited as fallacious examples (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*). For instance:
even in the absence of proficiency in the instruments, there is no communication of another;
because when phonemes (*varṇa*) are not clearly perceived, their meaning cannot be understood with clarity. Let this matter rest for now.
[NAV_25.0] Having thus established the fallacies of the example by way of similarity (*sādharmya*), he states them by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*):
"In this context, the defects of the example according to dissimilarity have been proclaimed by those who know the logic (*nyāya*):
because of the non-exclusion and because of doubt regarding the pair consisting of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*). [NA_25]

The *vaidharmya* (dissimilar instance) is that in which the absence of the probandum is intended to be shown as being pervaded by the absence of the probans; by this, the fallacies of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadoṣa*) as proclaimed by those who know the *nyāya* have been explained. Because there is no cessation—that is, no exclusion—of the pair consisting of the probandum and the probans, nor of both the object to be understood and the means of understanding, and because of the word "ca" (and), which is used in a displaced position, the meaning is: "and because of doubt regarding their cessation. By this, the six types of fallacious examples (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*) are indicated.
Namely: that which is non-different from the probandum, that which is non-different from the probans,
and that which is non-different from both the probandum and the probans.

Likewise, there are the cases of doubtful exclusion of the probandum (*sandigdhasādhyavyatireka*), doubtful exclusion of the probans (*sandigdhasādhanavyatireka*), and doubtful exclusion of both the probandum and the probans (*sandigdhasādhyasādhanavyatireka*).
[NAV 25.2] In this regard, an example of that which lacks exclusion from the probandum (*sādhyāvyatirekin*) is as follows:
"Inference is erroneous, because it is a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇatvāt*). Here, the example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta*) is:

Furthermore, that which is not erroneous is not a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), just like dream-cognition; since the absence of error is excluded from dream-cognition, there is a lack of dissimilarity with the probandum (*sādhyavyatireka*). An example of a reason that lacks dissimilarity with the probans (*sādhanāvyatirekin*) is as follows:
"Non-conceptual perception is a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) because it possesses the nature of being a means of valid cognition. Here, the dissimilar example (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta) is:
"That which is conceptual, however, is not a means of valid cognition."
For example, inference;
because validity is excluded from inference, it is non-different from the means of proof. An example of that which is non-different from both:
sound is both eternal and non-eternal.
"Because of existence. Here, the example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is as follows:
that which is neither eternal nor non-eternal does not exist, just like a jar.

Because neither [of the two properties] is excluded from a jar, there is a lack of exclusion from both. Likewise, there is that where the exclusion of the probandum is doubtful, as for example: "Kapila and others are not omniscient or are non-authoritative, because they do not teach the four noble truths. Here, the dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is:
"On the other hand, whoever is omniscient or authoritative, he taught the four noble truths."

For example: "Śauddhodani [is not omniscient]. This [reason] is one whose exclusion from the probandum is non-existent (*sādhyāvyatirekī*), because the four noble truths—characterized as suffering, origin, path, and cessation—are sublated by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); thus, it is established that the speaker of those [truths] lacks omniscience and authority. It is merely presented in such a way because it appears to those who lack the power of reflection upon the means of valid cognition that refute it as having a doubtful exclusion from the probandum (*sandigdhasādhyavyatireka*). To explain:
Even though the son of Śuddhodana taught the four noble truths,
nevertheless his attainment of omniscience is not established;
for it is not proven that the teaching of the four noble truths could not have occurred otherwise than in conjunction with those two [qualities].

Because even by a person who is not omniscient, who is not an authority (*āpta*), yet who possesses a clever intellect and acts with the intention of deceiving others, such a demonstration could be performed. Therefore, since the exclusion of the probandum—characterized by non-omniscience and non-authoritativeness—from the case of Śauddhodana is doubtful, this constitutes the fallacy of "doubtful exclusion of the probandum" (*sandigdhasādhyavyatireka*). An example of "doubtful exclusion of the probans" (*sandigdhasādhanavyatireka*) is as follows:
"No person intended [as a speaker] has acceptable speech, because he possesses passion and so forth. Here, the example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is:
"On the other hand, whoever has acceptable speech does not possess passion and so forth."

For example: "the Sugata. Although for those whose internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) are colored by the vision of him, the Sugata’s status as one whose words are authoritative has ascended to the pinnacle of proof;
nevertheless, because there is a lack of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish his freedom from passion and the like, that [freedom] remains within the range of doubt.

Therefore, due to the doubt regarding the Sugata’s exclusion from possessing passion and the like, there is the state of having a doubtful negative concomitance (*sandigdha-sādhanavyatirekitva*) of the probans. An example of a doubtful negative concomitance of both the probandum and the probans is as follows:

Kapila and others were not free from passion, because their minds were not permeated by compassion even toward objects of pity, as evidenced by their having given away pieces of their own flesh. Herein lies the example by contrast (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*):
those who, however, are free from passion give away pieces of their own flesh because their minds are permeated by compassion toward objects of pity.
For example: "Bodhisattvas. In this case, the exclusion of both the property to be proven (*sādhya*) and the proving property (*sādhana*) from the bodhisattvas is doubtful.
Because of the lack of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish that, it is not known whether they possess passion and so forth, or whether they are free from passion;

likewise, it is not known whether they gave pieces of their own flesh to those worthy of compassion, or not. Therefore, there is the fallacy of having a doubtful negative concomitance (*sandigdhasādhyasādhanavyatireka*).

[NAV 25.3] Others have also shown three fallacious examples (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*) due to speaking without due reflection; namely: the non-exclusive (*avyatireka*), the unshown-exclusive (*apradarśitavyatireka*), and the inverted-exclusive (*viparītavyatireka*). These need not be demonstrated by us because they are illogical. For instance:

Non-exclusion [of the probans from the dissimilar instance] has been shown by them as follows: "A certain person intended to be spoken of is not free from passion, because he is a speaker. Herein, the example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta*) is:
Furthermore, one who is free from passion is not a speaker,
just like a fragment of stone. Although, it is said, both [properties] are excluded from the fragment of stone, [it does not follow that it is a speaker].

"Nevertheless, because the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not established through pervasion (*vyāpti*), there is no negative concomitance. This is improper to say, because the absence of negative concomitance is a fault of the reason (*hetudoṣa*). For if the negative concomitance were established solely by the force of an example, then it would be appropriate for that which lacks such capacity to be a fallacy (*tadābhāsa*).
And this is not the case,

because the citation of an example is for the purpose of producing a recollection of an object within the scope of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that was previously inclined toward grasping the relationship [between the two terms]. For it is not established— apart from the means of valid cognition that grasps the necessary connection— that whatever is not observed in the absence of one thing does not exist in its absence.

Because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, this fault belongs only to the reason (*hetu*) whose negative concomitance (*pratibandha*) is unestablished, not to the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Likewise, it is improper to speak of "unshown negative concomitance" (*apradarśitavyatireka*) or "inverted negative concomitance" (*viparītavyatireka*), because those two are faults of the speaker. For instance:
They have stated one in which the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is not demonstrated,
such as: "Sound is impermanent because it is produced."

"Like space. Here, although the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) exists, it is faulty because it has not been brought forward by the proponent through speech. Furthermore, a reversed negative concomitance is stated, as for example:
"Sound is impermanent, because it is produced. In this case, the dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is: [text missing].

"That which is unconditioned is eternal, like space. Here, because the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is presented in a reversed manner, there is the fallacy of "reversed negative concomitance" (*viparītavyatirekitva*). For in a formulation based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) must be shown as being pervaded by the absence of the probans (*sādhanābhāvākrānta*);
yet this is not the case here.
Because it is stated that the absence of the probans is pervaded by the absence of the probandum.

(NAV_25.4) The failure to demonstrate the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) and the demonstration of a reversed negative concomitance are not defects of the thing itself; rather, they are the fault of the speaker who lacks skill in expression. Furthermore,

For those who hold this view— that namely, at the time of one's own inference, the realization of the probandum occurs from the mere perception of the reason itself, and therefore even on the occasion of inference for others,
only the presentation of the reason should be performed, according to the statement: "For to the learned, only the reason alone needs to be stated"— for them:

By the mere presentation of the reason "because of being produced," the intended probandum is established; therefore, even the description of all fallacious examples merely reveals a cleverness in composing statements that are contradictory from beginning to end. Let these two [fallacies] rest for now.
Because the example is not admitted to be a constituent part of the proof (*sādhana*). Now, you might argue as follows:
"If the person to be instructed lacks full knowledge of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), these two cannot be demonstrated without an example;
therefore, the example must be stated for the purpose of demonstrating positive and negative concomitance."
And if it is argued that those things which do not perform that function merely appear as such,
this is a mere quibble against one who has been caught by the throat;
nevertheless, examples that fail to demonstrate the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) or exhibit a contrary negative concomitance are pseudo-examples (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*) and are not real.
Rather, they arise from defects in the speaker;
therefore, it is not proper to state them,
because a person who is gripped by dense insentience and lacks the capacity to illuminate an existing reality has no entitlement to engage in debate.
Because it is improper for a learned person to engage in debate merely on the basis of proficiency in the recitation of the *mātṛkā*s.

Thus, while explaining inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*), that which was stated— namely, "it consists of the statements of the thesis (*pakṣa*) and so forth"— is for the most part concluded by the presentation of the thesis, the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), along with their fallacies (*sābhāsa*).
"Since it possesses correctness only by virtue of refuting the criticisms leveled by others, with this introduction, wishing to state that [so-called] refutation which is fallacious, he says:
'In the case of a proof stated by the proponent, the pointing out of the faults already mentioned constitutes a refutation;
however, when [the proof] is faultless, it is called a 'semblance of a refutation' (dūṣaṇābhāsa). (NA 26)"
A "speaker" (*vādī*) is one whose nature is to speak, that is, one who causes conviction. By him it is "stated," meaning presented. In what?

In the "proof" (*sādhana*). That by which the object of inference (*anumeya*) is established—that is, brought to the cognition of the person to be convinced—is the proof. And it was previously explained that this proof has many forms.

For example: in some cases there is only the reason (*hetu*); in some cases both the subject (*pakṣa*) and the reason; and in some cases the subject, the reason, and the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

In some cases they consist of those [members] alone with the application (*upanaya*); in some cases with the conclusion (*nigamana*); and in some cases by the purification and addition of each one individually.
Because that which is to be established can, in some cases and in some way, be made known,
and because the means for making it known constitutes a proof (*sādhana*); and because, in this context, a valid proof cannot be refuted,
since it is only a fallacious proof (*sādhanābhāsa*) that can logically be countered by its capacity.

That which is merely a fallacious proof (*sādhanābhāsa*)— unrecognized as such prior to the onset of the refutation, but referred to by the general term "proof"— is what is refuted. This refutation consists in the pointing out (*udbhāvana*), before the audience, of the aforementioned defects characterized by the presentation of a thesis subverted by perception and other means of valid cognition, an unestablished reason (*hetu*), a deficient probandum (*sādhya*), or an inadequate example (*dṛṣṭānta*), which results in the failure to communicate the intended probandum.
It should be understood that *dūṣaṇa* (refutation) is that by which the means of proof (*sādhana*) is brought to a state of corruption (*vikṛti*). Now he states its semblance (*tadābhāsa*):

it is "faultless" (*niravadya*) because the fault (*avadya*), meaning the wickedness characterized by defects such as those of the thesis (*pakṣa*) and so forth, has departed from it due to being correctly employed.

The phrase "stated by the proponent" continues to apply to that proof (*sādhana*). Nevertheless, when one, out of malice, crushes their own belly and points out faults that do not exist, that is called a "pseudo-refutation" (*dūṣaṇābhāsa*); for it is presented as a locus of refutation but fails to perform its function, and because it merely resembles a refutation—being nothing more than idle chatter (*pralāpa*)—it is a pseudo-refutation consisting in the pointing out of faults against a correct proof.

That very thing which has that name and that designation is "so-called. Because it consists in the presentation of a capable means of proof, when the probandum has been established, even the pointing out of defects such as ungrammatical words (*apaśabda*), lack of ornament (*alaṅkāra*), and so forth, is called a "fallacious refutation" (*dūṣaṇābhāsa*). By the word *tu* (but), he indicates for the purpose of qualification that the debate proceeds for the sake of establishing the actual state of things (*vastu*).
Because that [point] has already been established;
because, since corrupt words (*apaśabda*) and the like are irrelevant to the context, exposing faults by means of them would constitute mere incoherent chatter;
otherwise, if the refutation of the opponent were accomplished by that much alone, the effort of seeking out potent arguments would be rendered futile.

"Because there is no purpose. Thus, having established the definition of conventional valid cognition (*vyāvahārika-pramāṇa*), which is divided into categories such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), indirect (*parokṣa*), self-referential (*svārtha*), and other-referential (*parārtha*), we shall now [discuss] that ultimate (*pāramārthika*) [cognition] which is attained through the destruction of all obscurations and has the entire range of objects as its domain.

Since omniscience (kevalajñāna) is not accepted [by some], he speaks, desiring to state its definition in order to refute that view: "That which shines forth as pure, being the self liberated from all veils, is omniscience."
Direct perception is the constant manifestation of the nature of all objects.
"Entire" means all-inclusive. "Obscuration" (*āvaraṇa*) refers to that by which one obscures or is obscured;
the meaning is that it is karma which conceals its own true nature.
"Sakalāvaraṇa" means all the obscurations; "mukta" means freed from them, that is, devoid of them.
That whose self (ātman) or essential nature (svarūpa) is thus is described accordingly. For this very reason, it is "kevala," meaning solitary or without companion.
Because consciousness proceeds in various forms precisely due to the diversity of the destruction and subsidence of obscurations (*āvaraṇa-kṣayopaśama*),

whereas when the obscurations are entirely crushed, it manifests in a single form because the causes that act as obstacles are absent. Therefore, that which shines forth and expands independently of other cognitions—
meaning it radiates without any limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*)— is [the object of this knowledge].

That is direct perception from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Having thus defined this [perception] by way of its essential nature—as that which shines forth as absolute (*kevala*) through the medium of the cause consisting of a self liberated from all obscurations—he now defines it by way of its function, saying: "The constant manifestation of all things and their natures" means the uninterrupted illumination of the essential forms of all entities.
"Manifestation" (*pratibhāsanam*) means that by which something is manifested;

it refers, in other words, to cognition intended as distinct from the self by virtue of being its attribute (*dharma*). And its ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*) is established because the meaning of the word is applicable in a non-figurative sense. For instance:
The word *akṣa* is a synonym for the living self (*jīva*);

therefore, that which occurs in relation to the self is *pratyakṣa* (perceptual), wherein the activity of the self is direct. However, conventional perception (*vyāvahārika-pratyakṣa*), because it is produced by the activity of the self mediated by the sense organs, is in reality nothing but indirect (*parokṣa*).
Like the cognition of fire from smoke, because there is no difference in their being concealed.
[NAV_27.2] But surely, in all cases, the well-known definiendum (*lakṣya*) is restated and the unknown definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is prescribed?

This is the logical principle (*nyāya*). Furthermore, if the subject (*lakṣya*) is not already established, a definition (*lakṣaṇa*) being stated for it would become as devoid of scope as the definition of a lotus in the sky. Therefore, what is the intention of one who states a definition without having first established the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the thing?
To this it is replied: those whose internal organs are inflated with false pride oppose this [reality], even though it is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Because their intellects have been rendered blind by delusion, he shows that [the subject] must be determined by this [means]. If it is asked, "What is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes this?", we reply:
There exists a clear perception whose scope encompasses the entire expanse of all things, because inference operates with respect to its scope.
In this world, whatever object inference operates upon, there arises some perception that apprehends it,
just as in the case of fire.
Furthermore, inference operates with respect to all objects;
therefore, one who relies upon it must also possess a clear vision. If it is asked, "What kind of inference operates with respect to all objects?", we say this in reply:
In this world, whatever exists, all that experiences persistence, arising, and cessation in conjunction,
because it is a real entity (*vastu*); whatever is a real entity is embraced by stability, birth, and dissolution,
just as a finger is [defined] in relation to its finger-ness, curvature, and straightness.

And whatever object exists must be understood as being encompassed by these three aforementioned aspects. This very inference of non-absolutism (anekānta), which has the entire range of objects as its domain,
becomes a clear vision when all obscurations are severed through the excellence of the practice of knowledge and action, due to the absence of any obstructing causes.

Nor should one object that there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) because, even when an inference has occurred, the cognizer might fail to act due to lack of interest or other reasons, thereby making perception of the object of inference impossible; for what is intended as the probandum (sādhya) is possibility itself. And there is no deviation with respect to mere possibility.
Because all inferable things are pervaded by the possibility of being perceived.
Alternatively, we may infer in another way:
the self possesses all possible purity.
Because the means for purification exist;
for whatever exists here as a means for purification, that is capable of bringing about complete purification,
just as a particular jewel possesses existing means for purification such as alkaline substances, clay, and firing in a crucible.

And thus, the self is the means for the purification through the practice of existing knowledge and so forth; therefore, it is capable of attaining complete purity. Furthermore, when the self is completely purified, it is designated as "isolated" (*kevala*) because of the partial non-difference between knowledge and the knower. If it is asked how the practice of knowledge and so forth is the cause of purification:

We say it is because it has the nature of an antidote to the stains of obscuration. If it is asked how its status as an antidote is determined, it is from your own observation. For instance, it is observed that through the practice of knowledge and so forth, there is a moment-by-moment dissolution of obscuration.

Because we experience the cognition of those effects as being progressively more distinguished and even more distinguished still, we maintain that if there were a further intensification of that [cognition], there would be a total cessation of [all other] things. By this, we refute what others have asserted—namely, that since the perception of all objects transcends the domain of the five means of knowledge such as direct perception, it must fall within the scope of the sixth means of knowledge called non-existence (*abhāva*); that is incorrect.
Because its existence is established through inference, the non-occurrence of the five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to it is unproven. Furthermore,
how do you determine that the five means of valid cognition do not operate within its domain?
Is it by pervading a restricted space and time, or by encompassing all space and time?
If the first position is held,
then just as the five means of valid cognition, when failing to produce a cognition directed toward an object such as a jar in a particular place, establish its non-existence;
In this way, even though that [non-apprehension] has as its object the cognition of all things, when it ceases, it would establish an absence delimited by a specific place and time, not everywhere;
and consequently, like a jar or other objects, that [absence] would be difficult to avoid. Now, as for the second position:
That is simply impossible;

for it would be appropriate for one who directly perceives the consciousness of all assemblies of persons existing in every place and time to say that there is nowhere any perception of all objects— but not for you.

This is because we do not accept the possibility of such a person existing. Otherwise, anyone who might assert this with certainty would himself possess the light of knowledge pervading the entire expanse of all things, and thus the existence of a consciousness whose object is the totality of all entities would be established; let that matter rest for now.

Having thus refuted the disagreements regarding the definition and number of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) within its domain, we shall now address the disagreement concerning its objective sphere (*gocara*), which follows in due order, though we shall not yet refute it here as there is much to be said.
Desiring to refute misconceptions regarding the result [of valid cognition], he says:

"The result of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is, directly, the removal of ignorance; for the [cognition] that is purely [pleasurable], it is pleasure and equanimity; for the remainder, it is the cognition of what is to be acquired and what is to be abandoned. (NA 28)

For the fruit of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is twofold: direct and indirect; that is to say, immediate and mediated. Among these, the direct fruit is the cessation—meaning the specific bringing about of the dissolution—of ignorance, which consists of non-determination and the non-apprehension of the object of cognition (*prameya*).
This is the fruit of the means of valid cognition.

Since it functions by means of uprooting ignorance, and since that [ignorance] is the root of all misfortune and thus detrimental to the knower, its removal is indeed rightly considered the purpose [of the treatise].
This immediate purpose has been stated generally, because all forms of knowledge share a single nature. However, he states the remote purpose by way of distinction:
The meaning is as follows: "bliss" (*sukha*) is the experience of supreme joy that transcends sensual pleasure, belonging to the solitary knowledge of the omniscient one;
"equanimity" (*upekṣā*) is the state of neutrality arising from the absence of any desire for rejection or acquisition even while directly experiencing all objects.

These two—bliss and equanimity—are the fruit. "Of the remainder"—that is, of the ordinary worldly means of knowledge other than that [omniscience]—"taking" (*ādāna*) means grasping, and "rejection" (*hāna*) means abandonment.
The intellect (*dhī*) regarding those two—acceptance and rejection—is "the intellect of acceptance and rejection" (*ādānahānadhī*);
that is to say, it is the result. Consequently, the desire to acquire (*yāditsā*) things to be accepted, such as right vision (*samyagdarśana*) and so forth, or jasmine and sandalwood;

and likewise, the desire to abandon (*jihāsā*) things to be rejected, such as false vision (*mithyādarśana*) and so forth, or poison and thorns—all this is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it cannot be established through what is not valid cognition.
Thus, it has been stated that for those who act with prior reflection, activity [toward such an object] is untenable.
Now, he refutes the misconception regarding the object-domain (*gocara*):
"The object-domain of all cognitions is a reality (*vastu*) whose nature is manifold (*anekāntātmaka*)."
An object qualified by a single aspect is considered the domain of a *naya*.
That which possesses many, numerous ends (*anta*), parts (*aṃśa*), properties (*dharma*), or natures (*ātman*)—that is, its own forms (*svarūpa*)—is "multifaceted" (*anekāntātmaka*). What is that?
It is the entity (*vastu*), both external and internal, the domain (*gocara*) or object (*viṣaya*).

"Of all cognitions" means of all consciousnesses. By this, he shows the exclusion of the expansion of cognition without non-absolutism (*anekānta*); for even erroneous cognitions function by virtue of being highly proficient in illuminating non-absolutism.
They are merely designated as invalid because they are non-concordant with respect to certain parts. This is the intended meaning:

When even consciousness in its general form does not dare to function in the absence of manifoldness (anekānta), then the claim that a specific instance of it—namely, valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—will function in a single mode (ekānta) is a report whose opportunity has been cast far away. Nevertheless, because many people have their inner faculties perfumed by beginningless false attachment and their intellects deceived by flawed views, they disagree on this point; therefore, [the following] establishes that all means of valid cognition have manifoldness as their object:
The means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is defined as follows:

here, whatever is a means of valid cognition is the apprehender of an object endowed with multiple properties that are not mutually separated, because it is precisely that [object] which appears therein.
In this context, whatever appears in a particular place must be accepted as having that very thing as its object;
for example, a hibiscus flower appearing as red in a vision produced by eyes free from defects is accepted as having that [redness] as its object in exactly that way.
Furthermore, an object—whether external or internal—is manifested in all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as having a form pervaded by multiple natures that are mutually inseparable;
therefore, that alone is their objective domain (*gocara*).

Consequently, those disciples of Kaṇabhakṣa (the Vaiśeṣikas) and Akṣapāda (the Naiyāyikas), who assert that the subject (*dharmin*) and its properties (*dharma*) are mutually disjointed, cannot possibly demonstrate defects such as the unestablished nature (*asiddhatā*) of this reason (*hetu*).
Because without accepting that [relation], there would be no existence of the entity intended by oneself. For instance:
how could many properties, whose bodies are distinct from it, reside in a single substratum (*dharmin*)?

Since their difference is no different [from one another], it would follow that they would reside everywhere. If it is argued that they do not reside elsewhere because of their inherence (*samavāya*) in that very [substratum] alone, [then...]
Now, if that inherence (samavāya) exists even without the relationship of benefactor and beneficiary,
then it would follow that it occurs everywhere without distinction,
since there is no difference in the absence of such a relationship. If it is argued that the relationship of benefactor and beneficiary does indeed exist [in those cases], then...
Alas, you are destroyed!
For [if it were one], it would follow that the single benefactor possesses multiple natures;

yet in the absence of such [multiple natures], there can be no status as a benefactor of many. Indeed, it is not the case that by the very same nature through which it benefits one, it benefits a second.
Because that [first cause] has already been utilized right there, and because the second auxiliary, by way of destroying that [first], arises;
otherwise, it would remain assisting only one [cause].
If it is argued that [the cause] assists by means of distinct powers (*śakti*) while possessing a single intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
rather than by means of distinct intrinsic natures, and therefore there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*):

In that case, it must be explained how those [powers] exist therein. If the answer is "through inherence" (*samavāya*), then the ancient objection follows upon this: "How is it that inherence does not occur everywhere, unless there is a relationship of beneficiary and benefactor (*upakāryopakārakabhāva*)? If one instead accepts the relationship of beneficiary and benefactor, then the same argument regarding the possession of multiple natures (*anekasvabhāvatā*) already demonstrated applies; and if one further postulates distinct powers for each power-benefactor, the very same circularity recurs.

Therefore, even if one imagines distinct properties, there is no liberation from uncertainty; thus, it is better to abandon narrow-mindedness from the very beginning and accept a reality endowed with multiple attributes. What is the use of this baseless conceptualization of difference that only brings distress upon oneself? Furthermore, there is this advantage in accepting non-absolutism (anekānta):

When one considers how conjunction, inherence, the substratum of inherence, the quality, the whole, the individual, the universal, and so forth, exist within mutually distinct entities— such as the conjoined, the inherent, the quality-possessor, the whole, and the particular universal— a web of refutations arises.
That too has been refuted, because that [logical consequence] is possible only in the case of absolute difference;
for it cannot arise in the case of non-absolutism (anekānta). To explain:
Indeed, conjunctions and the like can be distinguished from the conjoined objects and so forth by considering how they exist within them:
do they exist by way of a single part, or rather in their entirety?
If it were by way of a single part, [then...]
That is incorrect, because it is admitted that they are partless. Even if they were possessed of parts, if [the whole] were non-different from those parts,
then the fallacy of inconclusiveness (anaikānta) would follow.

Because a single [entity] would consequently possess multiple parts. Now, if those [parts] are distinct, it must be explained how they subsist within it: either by way of occupying a single location (*ekadeśena*) or in their entirety (*sāmastyena*). In the case of occupying a single location, the same problem recurs, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If, on the other hand, they subsist in their entirety, that too is untenable.

Because if each were complete in itself, it would follow that there would be a multiplicity of conjunctions and so forth. Furthermore, conjunctions and the like, being non-different from those [entities], do not admit of such conceptual distinctions. If it is argued that even on the view of non-difference, there would be either merely the conjunction or merely the conjoined entity, we say no;
for that too is not accepted as being absolute.
Rather, all these [entities] are accepted as having mutually inseparable intrinsic natures, yet possessing distinctions that are to be demonstrated according to one's intention to speak;
for such [entities] possess the capacity to withstand the mass of refutations raised by fallacious reasoning and conceptual constructions,
and because they appear in that very way everywhere within uncontradicted appearances.
Otherwise, if one were to conceptualize things as being otherwise than they appear, one would fall into incoherence by way of abandoning what is observed and conceptualizing what is unobserved;
and in that case, doctrines such as the non-duality of Brahman or the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*) would achieve establishment,
since there would be no distinction [between them and your own position].
By this, even the followers of Kapila (the Sāṃkhyas), who wished to point out defects such as the unestablished nature (*asiddhatā*) of this reason, have been brought to silence. For indeed:
