internally, there is a single consciousness whose form is pervaded by the manifestation of an infinite variety of qualities, such as successive joy and despondency; and externally, there is an object such as a jar, whose body is occupied by many natures, such as being new or old, round, and earthen.
How could those who perceive [reality] directly proceed to speak in a manner contrary to it?

If you argue that only the substance (*dravya*) consisting of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* is the single, ultimate reality, whereas the illusory transformation (*vivarta*) that gives rise to the delusion of modes (*paryāya*) is non-ultimate, we say no.

Since both [the manifestation and the substrate] appear in all means of valid cognition, are uncontradicted, and serve as the basis for all worldly transactions, it is impossible to deny one of them without partiality. If that were the case, then one who favors the position of mere transformation (*vivarta*)—claiming that transformation alone is real while the substance (*dravya*) is false—would be difficult to refute. Now, you might say this:

It is incorrect to claim that substance (*dravya*) is real because its nature is non-deviating everywhere, whereas modes (*paryāya*) are unreal because they are deviating; for even if substance does indeed persist everywhere due to its undifferentiated nature, [the modes likewise do so].
Although the various modes (paryāyas) are distinguished because they consist of difference,
nevertheless, it cannot be said that "this alone is real and the others are false."

For it is not the case that something is unreal merely because blue does not possess the nature of yellow; for such an over-extension would result in the unreality of everything, since all things exist by way of excluding the nature of others. Now, if substances themselves are the modes (paryāyas),...
Because they are non-different from that [substance],
like its own essential nature,
or else there are no modes distinct from the substance.
If you establish [your point] by the argument that "because it lacks intrinsic nature, it is like a sky-flower," then in that case,
the modes themselves would be the substance.
Because it is non-different from that [the modes], it is like the nature of that [mode];
or else, substance does not exist as distinct from its modes,
because it would then be devoid of modes.

Who could prevent the other [opponent] from establishing [the same point] by saying, "It is like a flower in the sky"? Therefore, no distinction whatsoever is perceived between the two positions. Just as an object, which is superposed with infinite successively occurring modes (*paryāya*), appears in all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), so must it be accepted.
And since there is nothing else, it is established that that very object is the objective domain of those [cognitions].

[NAV_29.4] Likewise, even among those who follow the doctrine of the Sugata, the Sautrāntikas do not dare to manifest the unestablished nature (*asiddhatā*) of this reason, because their own philosophical system cannot be maintained apart from that very admission. For instance:
first of all, a single external cause is perceived to produce multiple effects by virtue of being included within various successive causal complexes (*sāmagrī*).

Just as a form (rūpa) simultaneously produces its own subsequent moment and the cognition that apprehends it; and if it is held that things existing in a single moment produce diverse effects in different locations precisely because they undergo differentiation through a difference in their causal complexes (sāmagrī), then the refutation raised against the position of permanence would fall upon one's own head, since even for that [permanent entity], there would follow the consequence of an absence of differentiation despite its producing effects at different times. Likewise, the acceptance of the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) of form and so forth—which is momentary and distinct—is based on a difference in appearance.

Furthermore, this [perception] would be without a basis, because even for a substance that maintains immutability (*kauṭasthya*), there would follow the contradiction of its producing effects characterized by the manifestation of qualities such as newness, oldness, color, taste, smell, and touch, due to its inclusion within various successive causal complexes. Moreover, this [perception], directly perceiving a single form that pervades its own parts and persists through different times, [cannot perceive] those things characterized as momentary atoms.

One should describe the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) [of things] and not otherwise, because that appearance does not persist even in a dream exactly as it was intended; and by demonstrating the identity [of the appearance] through the exclusion of what is uncharacterized from what is characterized, one supports—by one's own words—the appearance of non-exclusivity (*anekānta*). For instance:

Although its own nature (*svarūpa*) undergoes a transformation every moment, with the spherical dimension of atoms being imperceptible, it nevertheless manifests as something stable, gross, and so forth; otherwise, the world would be reduced to a state of deep sleep,

because if that [nature] were not revealed, other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)— which likewise reveal their own utterly distinct particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*)— would also fail to function.

Likewise, for one who accepts that internal cognition is a single entity appearing as external-facing, internal-facing, conceptual, non-conceptual, erroneous, non-erroneous, and so forth—relative to the nature of the object—how could the appearance of manifoldness (*anekānta*) be unestablished?

Similarly, [cognition] is colored by the forms imparted by a multitude of objects situated in various locations; otherwise, even if there were a difference in forms, the simultaneous manifestation of objects such as white and black would be untenable. Thus, it is a single [cognition].

How could one who accepts consciousness assert an absolute difference between it and the various transformations such as joy and sorrow occurring at different times, given that they share an identical state of being and security (*yogakṣema*)? There is no unity among joy and the like [themselves], but rather unity among the forms internalized within consciousness when they occur simultaneously.
If it is argued that this is due to the opposite of that [the object], we say no;
for it would follow that there is no difference between objects as established by the capacity of that [cognition].
Since they are one with that [cognition], cognition remains undifferentiated in its nature as awareness across white, yellow, and other colors. Thus, both externally and internally...

Since the fact that a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) possesses both a single and a manifold nature is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and since otherwise the systematic arrangement of one's own accepted philosophical views would be impossible, the proponent of external objects (*arthavādin*) ought not to reject the illumination of non-absolutism (*anekānta*). Likewise, even the Yogācāra position, once accepted, is forcibly entwined by the rope of the illumination of non-absolutism.

If it is argued that even a single cognition is one because it is established as manifesting in the form of multiple objects and subjects due to their sharing a single fate (*ekayogakṣema*), we say no;

for this would entail the absurd consequence that all mental continua, which possess simultaneous arising and cessation and are co-cognizers, would be one. If it is argued that since multiplicity is shown by conventional perception (*saṃvṛti*), it does not undermine the ultimate oneness directly realized through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), we say no.

Because there is the consequence that the doctrine of the proponents of Brahman would not be refuted—since, due to the power of beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*), even though Brahman is one, non-sequential, conscious, and directly realized through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-sākṣātkṛta*), it nevertheless appears as manifold, sequential, consisting of both the sentient and the insentient, and as both remote and immediate; this is no more difficult to establish than the cognition devoid of the forms of subject and object (*grāhya-grāhaka*) imagined by you. Or, let this appearance of manifoldness be erroneous.

Nevertheless, the non-duality of consciousness is not perceived; for if it were so perceived, all living beings would attain liberation this very moment. Yet, it is perceived in some way, otherwise there would follow the undesirable consequence of the cessation of all worldly activity, as in the state of deep sleep. Thus, even a single consciousness appears as manifold through its being both perceived and unperceived.
Since it is difficult to deny this, even the proponent of knowledge (jñānavādin) should remain silent regarding the demonstration of the unestablished nature (*asiddhatā*) of this reason.

If it is argued that for the proponent of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*), the manifestation of manifoldness (*anekāntaprakāśa*) is unestablished because of the total non-existence [of everything], we say no;
for even for him, in the absence of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and objects of cognition (*prameya*), there is no awareness of the non-existence of all things.

Otherwise, even for an opponent who asserts that "everything exists everywhere" without any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there would be no contradiction in their statement; yet, by accepting that [assertion], they would suffer a collapse of their own position. Furthermore, as has been shown, the non-exclusive nature (*anekānta*) of those two [existence and non-existence] is revealed; thus, the reason (*hetu*) is not unestablished (*asiddha*). For even when a cognition grasps the shimmering mass of mirages in the desert, there is no acceptance that water is its object.
Do not suspect that this [argument] is inconclusive, for it is erroneous;

indeed, non-erroneous manifestation is the reason for its acceptance. Now, if you should say that this too is erroneous because it is sublated by a cognition that perceives atoms as mutually distinct, momentary, and subject to destruction, [we reply:]...
That is incorrect;
for is that cognition merely a perception, or is it a definitive judgment?
If the first alternative holds, then inference would be undermined.
Because it is beyond the range [of conceptualization],
since even one belonging to the first eon, out of fear of contradiction, would have to admit the apprehension of an object in every respect through a non-conceptual vision of isolation;
and because, once an object has been determined by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), other means of knowledge would be redundant.

Because it would lead to an infinite regress. Now, if the second [alternative] were the case, then everything would become non-conceptual and thus fall into the state of being invalid. Furthermore, certainty does not subvert the manifestation of multiple aspects;
rather, it confirms it.

It is likewise both externally and internally due to its manifestation. Now, you might think that even when there is the apprehension of an object in every respect, non-conceptual [cognition] attains the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) only in that aspect where it subsequently generates a determinative judgment (*vyavasāya*) that brings about practical activity (*vyavahāra*), and not elsewhere.

If that were the case, then only that very determination (*nirṇaya*) following which a person proceeds with the desire for an object capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsamartha*) should be accepted as possessing validity.

It would follow that [the determinate cognition] is not indeterminate, even though it is produced by that [indeterminate cognition], just like sensory contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) and so forth. Indeterminate cognition is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it apprehends an object not previously apprehended;
it is not, however, a definitive determination (*vyavasiti*).
If it is argued that [inference is not valid] because it is conceptual (*vikalpa*), we say no;

for then inference would likewise entail a lack of validity. Nor is inference distinguished [from perception] by its skill in dispelling contrary aspects, since ascertainment (*nirṇīti*) is also capable of removing them.

Because it does not operate upon an object that is free from superimposition. If you argue that the distinction of being produced from a mark possessing the three characteristics (*trirūpaliṅga*) is what establishes inference as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then we perceive your childishness in asserting that arising directly from immediate experience (*anubhava*) is a great fault for a definitive cognition (*nirṇīti*).

Furthermore, just as non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka*), though uncharacterized and inclined toward grasping the specific particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) excluded from everything else, gives rise to a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) whose object consists of only certain aspects;

Likewise, the object itself, through its proximity to the sense organ, light, and so forth, may directly produce a clear conceptual cognition whose objects are certain of its own constituent parts; so what is the point of postulating a non-conceptual [perception] that is as useless as imagining the udder of a goat’s neck?
If it is argued that so many parts are contradictory in an external object, we reply:
why is this a royal decree that clarity, lack of clarity, and other such qualities cannot coexist even within a single visual perception?

Therefore, even you do not perceive at any time or place a perception that characterizes a particular (svalakṣaṇa) defined as a momentary atom; rather, solely because your internal organs are colored by your own philosophical views, you fail to realize its non-existence. A definitive ascertainment (nirṇaya) is that which, manifesting itself, illuminates an object and a cognition—both external and internal—as being unitary, pervading its own parts, and persisting through a succession of times.

Furthermore, he is not deluded because he is not subverted by rootless, fallacious conceptual constructions (*kuyukti-vikalpa*). Moreover, one who asserts his state of delusion uproots the entire systematic arrangement of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and their objects (*prameya*).

Thus, that very same [cognition] which is a means of valid cognition regarding the nature of existence, awareness, bliss, and so forth, is itself not a means of valid cognition regarding momentary destruction, the capacity to attain heaven, and so on;

likewise, that very same object which is an object of cognition in the form of blue, quadrangular, vertical, and so forth, is itself not an object of cognition in terms of its middle part, its momentary transformation, and so on.

Likewise, that which is conceptual or erroneous with respect to an external object—such as a dream-vision—is precisely that which is non-erroneous with respect to its own nature. Similarly, the determination is that even that which is false in its duality, such as two moons and so forth, is not false in its whiteness, its spatial restriction, its movement, and so on. However, if you, fearing contradiction, were to deny this [distinction], [the following would apply].
Our minds are curious to know what other exclusive means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and object of cognition (*prameya*) they might accept in order to establish their own position.

Now, if the proponent of knowledge (*jñānavādin*), having accepted the unperceived manifestation of non-duality (*advaitaprakāśa*), were to claim that cognition— which possesses manifoldness by means of that [manifestation]— is erroneous because it is sublated, that would be incorrect.

Because this would entail the abandonment of what is observed and the postulation of what is unobserved, and because non-conceptual perception that has not been characterized was already refuted earlier. Furthermore, if reasoning were to subvert the diversity of cognition, it is for this reason:
because it is impossible to effect a distinction between erroneous and non-erroneous awareness.
However, because pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*) is never absent anywhere,

non-dual awareness— manifesting through discerning reasoning— negates the various appearances such as white and black, which possess an existence displayed by conventional perception produced by latent impressions (*vāsanā*) accumulated since beginningless time.
Here we offer our rebuttal:
Does this manifold cognition differ from non-dual awareness because of its dual nature, or not? And what follows from this?
If it did differ, how could this [manifold cognition], whose effect is not observed [in non-dual awareness], lead one to infer that distinct non-dual awareness?

Furthermore, on the view that there is no difference [between consciousness and its objects], how could it not subvert non-duality (*advaita*), given that the manifold appears as identical with a single cognition?

If you argue that because this turbidity—consisting of external forms such as white, black, and so forth—is shown by conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) and is thus unreal, the conceptual alternatives of difference or non-difference between it and the ultimate cognition are untenable;
then, in that case, the opponent would maintain that cognition is not ultimately real (*apāramārthika*) because it is shown by ignorance (*avidyā*).

Furthermore, one who asserts that the reality of the existence of objects consists in their being the very nature of consciousness— because it never deviates from anything— would be difficult to refute. If it is argued that consciousness alone is real because an insentient object cannot be manifest, and not the object itself, [then...]

We maintain that non-duality is not real because there is no appearance of the one as many; therefore, plurality is true. If it is argued that even for that which is non-dual on the conventional level, a manifold appearance is not contradictory, then the deceitful rejoinder of the opponent would not be difficult to find: namely, that by the power of beginningless ignorance, the manifestation of even the insentient as sentient is not contradictory. Furthermore:

Since that [consciousness] is established by the force of the impossibility of its existence otherwise (*anyathānupapatti*)—given that the universal consciousness is defiled by various forms (*nānākāra*)—this [opponent] would be attempting to prove that non-dual cognition (*advaya-saṃvedana*) is unestablished;
for otherwise, the means of proof (*sādhana*) could not function due to a lack of basis.

And thus, by virtue of the objective parts characterized as stable, gross, and so forth, he who establishes the identity of discrete atoms and momentary perishing modes (*paryāya*) ought not to reject that proponent of non-absolutism (*anekāntavādin*).

Because the reasoning is equal in both cases. Furthermore, your intention is that this determination of various forms such as white and yellow is also non-dual in nature from the perspective of self-awareness;
and just as all cognition has been accepted as self-luminous out of fear of an infinite regress, [so too must it be here].
Likewise, every determination must be admitted to be self-determining;
otherwise, the fault of infinite regress would attach even there,
and determinations would have to determine their own nature in every respect.

Not by way of a single part, for it has been stated by [the opponent] themselves as a lamentation leading to their own destruction: "How can that form which is not determined by determinations be their object? And thus, if they were to apprehend the non-dual, momentary nature of the thing-in-itself, there would be an absence of superimposition of the contrary.
If there were no arising of saṃsāra from the very beginning, then the conceit of being unliberated would be devoid of reason;

yet this is not the case, because the state of existence is well-established for every living being. Therefore, this manifestation of substance and mode, which are inseparable from one another, is not erroneous.
It is established that there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish an object contrary to that [conclusion].
[NAV_29.8] But when the proponent of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*) asserts, "All cognitions are without an objective basis (*nirālambana*),"...
One might state its erroneous nature on the strength of an inference directed toward the opponent's own position, namely: "Because it is a cognition, like a dream-cognition."
Then, with respect to that [objection],
[the response is]: "All conditions possess an objective support, because they are conditions."

The counter-inference should be presented as follows: "It is like the cognition of the waking state. If he should raise the objection that the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatā*), then that same deficiency must be shown to exist in that example as well. Furthermore, if he does not cease his lamentation, saying, "You intend for the cognition of dreams to be without an objective basis (*nirālambanatva*)," [then the following response is required].
Then he should be questioned based on his conceptual construction: "Is our accepted position a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for you, or is it not a valid means of knowledge?
If it is a valid means of knowledge,"
Just as you provide support for the example by means of that [same] force, why do you not likewise provide support for the object within the scope of waking cognition?
What is this "half-old-woman" logic (*ardhajaratīyanyāya*)? Or, if it is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), [then why apply it selectively]?
This being the case, another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must be sought to establish that dream-cognition is without an objective basis;
what is the use of this grasping at straws like *kuśa* and *kāśa* grass? Regarding that other means of valid cognition as well, a pair of alternatives (*vikalpa-yugala*) unfailingly presents itself:
is it itself without an objective basis, or does it have an objective basis?
If it is without an object (*nirālambana*),
it is not capable of declaring another cognition to be without an object,
because it lacks a cognitive domain (*nirgocaratvāt*). Or, if it does have an object (*sālambana*), [then...]
"Alas, you are defeated!
Since all conditions are without support, your own thesis is undermined;

moreover, this very [example] constitutes a deviation [from your rule]. Thus, the rogue must be crushed by employing a counter-rogue tactic. Therefore, there is no inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva) in this."
Furthermore, any suspicion of contradiction has its scope cast far away,

because there is no disagreement among any proponents of philosophical systems regarding an object revealed by a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). By this, refutations such as doubt, contradiction, infinite regress, lack of common locus (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), and impossibility—
raised on the basis of rootless false conceptual constructions— are unable to survive, for their heads have been shattered by the falling mallet of direct manifestation (*pratibhāsa*).

[They] say, "They are capable. Therefore, this reason—characterized by such an appearance and free from defects such as being unestablished (*asiddha*)—compels others to accept that valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has a manifold range of objects. Enough with this elaboration. Consequently, [it is said]:
"Because that very [object] appears therein."
It is established that for all cognitions, the object of experience is a thing (*vastu*) whose nature is manifold (*anekāntātmaka*).

And this has been shown as the domain of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇagocara*) from the perspective of a cognizer who reflects upon the operation of the means of valid cognition as it actually exists. Now, in response to the question of what kind of object a *naya* considers that [thing] to be, he says:

"Eketyādi" and so forth. A *naya* is that which leads (*nayati*), brings about, or causes an object—upon which infinite properties (*anantadharma*) are superimposed—to be distinguished by one intended property, thereby causing it to be apprehended and ascended into consciousness;
the meaning is that it is a subsequent reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) following the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Its object, its domain, is held to be an entity characterized by a single part, such as the property of impermanence, which is distinct from other forms and constitutes the nature of the object of knowledge (*prameya*).
"Because it is established by its own nature that such a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) grasps an object of precisely this kind.

Alternatively, having refuted the fourfold misconception regarding the object of the means of valid cognition—consisting of its definition, number, scope, and result—he says "one," etc., while defining the scope of the method (*naya*) in this very context.
Now, one might object: was it not the case that with the opening statement, he merely promised the exposition of the means of valid cognition?
Is this then an irrelevant subject regarding the scope of the *naya* being presented here? True;
it is thought thus:
a *naya* does not depart far from a *pramāṇa*.
Rather, it is indeed a constituent part of that [pramāṇa],

because a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is produced by a collection of methods (*naya*); therefore, when there is a formal promise (*pratijñāna*) to explain that [pramāṇa], this [naya] is also included by the mention of it, as it falls within its midst.
By this principle, it is indeed accepted;
therefore, this is not irrelevant.
Here too, the meaning of the word is that very same one.

There is only a difference in the meaning of the sentences. For instance, the connection here is as follows: "The object qualified by a single aspect is held by those who know the principles of reasoning (*nītivid*) to be the domain of a *naya*. Now, one might object: "If, even though a *naya* is included within the scope of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), its distinct range is nevertheless set forth, then—just like valid cognition—a disagreement regarding its definition and so forth concerning its object must also be refuted. True.

However, the practice of formal reasoning (nayavyavahāra) is not established among others; therefore, due to the absence of a subject (dharmin), there is no disagreement regarding its object at all. Nor should they be led to realize the truth by means of that [reasoning], because the function of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) consists solely in the demonstration of reality.
Furthermore, because this system is restricted to only one part [of reality], it lacks the capacity to demonstrate that [reality];

for this very reason, the Teacher did not show great concern even in describing the essential nature of its definition and so forth. On the other hand, while casting the domain [of this system] into the category of what is to be rejected through the use of irony (*kāku*), he directly demonstrates [the truth]: "Let there be no [confusion] among those of dull intellect who fall within our own school, regarding the nature of non-absolutism (*anekāntātman*) which is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)."

"Dogmatic insistence (*kadāgraha*) is characterized by the stubborn adherence to establishing only one part of a reality. Alternatively, because this very description of its scope (*gocara*) serves as an illustration, it also indicates its definition (*lakṣaṇa*) and other attributes for those who fall within its own philosophical system. In that regard, the definition is: "A *naya* is the consideration of a single part of an object established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)," because it follows the specific distinctions of all *nayās* and possesses the capacity to exclude the nature of others. Furthermore, in terms of number, they are infinite.

Because an entity possesses infinite properties (*anantadharman*), and because a perspective that terminates in only one of those properties constitutes a *naya*, nevertheless, the ancient teachers have set forth seven *nayās* by means of postulating seven comprehensive perspectives. They are as follows:— [The text continues with the list of the seven *nayās*.]
"The *nayās* are the Naigama, Saṃgraha, Vyavahāra, Rjusūtra, Śabda, Samabhirūḍha, and Evambhūta.
Therefore, these very same ones are described by us as well.
If it is asked, "How do these encompass all intentions? [the answer follows].
It is said: An intention must proceed either by way of an object or by way of a word, since there is no other possible mode of operation;
and the object is either of the nature of a universal or of the nature of a particular.
A word [is understood] both through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) and through etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*);
and even etymological derivation may be prompted by a general cause or prompted by a cause existing at that particular time.
Among these, whatever intentions of the cognizer (*pramātṛ-abhiprāya*) are inclined toward the determination of meaning, they are all included within the first four *nayās*.
In that regard, the *naigama* [view] consists of the collection of those who maintain that the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*) are mutually distinct.

The *saṅgraha* [view], however, is produced by the synthesis of those who desire only the universal. Furthermore, the *vyavahāra* [view] is generated by the determination of those who intend objects such as a jar, which enter into worldly transaction (*lokavyavahāra*) without depending on the universals and particulars defined by technical treatises.

However, those who believe that the particularities characterized as atoms (*paramāṇu*), which perish moment by moment, are real, [for them] the "straight line" (*ṛjusūtra*) is that which is constructed from their collection. Likewise, for those who desire the application of words based on conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), the "word" (*śabda*) is that which is accomplished by the totality of such usage. But for those who desire the application of sounds based on etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) and not otherwise, the "thoroughly conforming" (*samabhirūḍha*) is that which is produced by means of those derivations.

Thus, those who maintain that words function only by taking as their basis the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti-nimitta*) pertaining to the present time and not otherwise—the *evambhūta* [naya] is indeed composed of such a collection. Therefore, it is established that there is no conceptual alternative within the domain of reality that is not included within these seven perspectives (*naya*); thus, these [seven] encompass all intended meanings.

[NAV_29.14] Now we shall describe the individual views of these very schools. In this context, *gama* means going; that is, discernment (*pariccheda*). A certain *gama* is *nigama*, which is the apprehension of a distinct object. That itself is *naigama*, because the suffix *-aṇ* is prescribed in its own sense (*svārthika*) since *prajñā* and so forth belong to the class of *ākṛtigaṇa* words. Alternatively, they are called *naigama* because things are definitively determined (*nigamyante*) [within them].

The *nigamas* are the objects that are being delimited; the intention residing within them, which consists of a fixed delimitation, is called *naigama*. For this [intention] takes into account the great generality (*mahāsāmānya*) characterized by existence (*sattā*), as well as the intermediate generalities such as substantiality (*dravyatva*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), and action-ness (*karmatva*), and likewise the ultimate particulars (*antyaviśeṣas*)—which are defined by their entirely unique forms—as well as the intermediate particulars, which are capable of excluding other forms through comparison.

He intends [a universal] whose own nature is utterly distinct from that of the particular. For it is said: the determination of entities is grounded in cognition, and there is no appearance of a particular within a cognition that apprehends a universal.
This is because that [universal] is grasped by means of a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of a single, recurring form;

otherwise, it would be impossible for cognition to grasp a universal. Nor does a universal appear within a consciousness capable of grasping particulars, because such [consciousness] functions by apprehending an object as delimited by a specific place and time.

Otherwise, it would be impossible for there to be cognition of a particular. Nor is it logical to somehow conflate these two—the universal and the particular—even though they appear as mutually distinct;
for this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), whereby all things, despite appearing as distinct, would attain identity. And thus he provides the proof:
The universal and the particular are mutually distinct,
because they are perceived separately;
for whatever is perceived here as separate is a substance that is mutually distinct.
For example—just as Devadatta and Yajñadatta are perceived as distinct entities—so too are the universal and the particular perceived separately;
therefore, they are mutually distinct. If it is argued that the particular is not perceived apart from the universal, [we reply:]...
How, then, is its apprehension to be explained? If it is argued that it is the apprehension of that which is pervaded by a universal,
then it is not the apprehension of a particular, because the universal is also grasped by it.

Furthermore, because that cognition lacks the apprehension of a distinct particular (*viśeṣa*), the cognizer would not employ the sound expressive of it nor the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) accomplished by it;

yet this is not the case, since we observe the employment of both the designation and the usage of particulars. Therefore, one who desires a particular and its corresponding linguistic usage [must acknowledge it].

While establishing that [universal], one must admit that the cognition grasping it is itself devoid [of the universal]. Likewise, if the universal were not manifested in the cognition grasping it by way of its own distinct form,

then— since even a particular would be apprehended by the very consciousness intended to have the universal as its object— the cessation of the application of the designation and conventional usage of "universal" would likewise have to be asserted.

Since those two [the universal and the particular] are rooted in a cognition that grasps the isolated universal and the isolated particular, if those [isolated forms] were not admitted, it would follow that the two themselves would also be non-existent. Nor is it appropriate to accept either the particular or the universal in isolation by setting aside the other, because there is no distinction between them, as both appear in the cognition that perceives each. Therefore, the *naigama* [view] holds that both of these are worthy of being accepted as mutually distinct.

[NAV_29.15] Now, the intention behind "subsumption" (saṅgraha) is described. In this context, it is called "subsumption" because it subsumes—that is, it takes up—the world by means of concealing all its particularities through the form of a universal.
For he thinks as follows:
either the particulars must be postulated as having forms distinct from the universal characterized as an entity (bhāva), or...
Or [they may be] of a nature that is not distinct [from the cause],
because there is no other possibility. In that case, if the first alternative is accepted, then they would have to admit their own lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).
Because they would be non-different from existence, like a sky-flower and so forth. Now, if the second alternative is taken, then they would result in being mere existence. For it is thus:
The particulars are merely the entity itself,
because they are not distinct from it;
for in this world, whatever is not distinct from something else becomes that very thing.

For example: the very nature of an entity itself, and its particularities which are non-distinct from it, are therefore of that very same nature. Now, if the reality is merely the entity itself, then because that [entity] is without distinction everywhere—

All those worldly transactions established for every living being—which are accomplished by specific objects such as pillars, the frontal globes of elephants, or lotuses—would consequently fall into dissolution;
therefore, particulars (*viśeṣas*) must also be admitted as the causes of distinct transactions. This is not so.
Because conventional practice is set in motion by the power of beginningless ignorance,
there is no obstruction to reality as established by ultimate valid cognition through it. Furthermore,
the failure to perceive distinctions must be specifically abandoned.
Because there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that establishes distinctions. For it is thus:
distinctions consist in difference, and yet no means of valid cognition apprehends difference.
For perception, which has its existence brought about by a positive entity (bhāva), is logically capable of directly apprehending that very entity alone,
and not non-existence (abhāva); because non-existence, being of the nature of the absence of all causal capacity, lacks any functional activity toward the production of that [perception].
Furthermore, if one were to directly realize that which is non-arising, it would follow that everything is realized;
and since there would thus be no distinction [between objects], every seer would be an all-seeing one. This is undesirable for you;

therefore, you must accept that [the cognition] apprehends only an existent entity (*bhāva*). And since that existent entity is undifferentiated everywhere, it must be apprehended by it exactly as it is.

Furthermore, the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that arises subsequently—having the form "this is a jar, it is not a cloth or the like"—and which constructs conventional usage, is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because its root is ignorance (*avidyā*).

Therefore, there is no apprehension of a specific property (*viśeṣa*) through perception. Nor is there such apprehension through inference and the rest, because the entire class of remaining means of knowledge is rooted in perception.
Therefore, the summary is that only the universal (*sāmānya*) is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), not the particulars (*viśeṣa*).

Now, the view of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is stated. In this context, "conventional usage" (*vyavahāra*) refers to the act of using or that by which worldly people act according to their intention. This [proponent], however, maintains the following:
Let the object simply be as it is grasped by the world;
what is the use of this painful grinding of flour—the conceptualization of objects that are neither seen nor conventionally expressed?
Furthermore, for whatever enters the path of worldly convention, a validating cognition (*pramāṇa*) is found to support it.
Not for the other [particular],
for a universal that is beginningless, endless, unitary, and intended as a unifier is not the ground of valid cognition,
because such an experience does not exist.

Furthermore, it would follow that everyone would be an all-seeing omniscient being. Nor are the particularities characterized as atoms—which perish moment by moment—the domain of valid cognition, because there is no such occurrence [of them being perceived]. Therefore, let this very nature of things—such as a jar, which is uncontradicted by the entire world, established by valid cognition, possessing a grossness lasting for some duration, and capable of accomplishing purposeful action such as carrying water—be the ultimate reality.
Furthermore, a detailed investigation into the sequence of those [moments] existing in prior and subsequent times is not superior,

because there is no scope for a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) therein, and because it is impossible to conduct an inquiry without a means of valid cognition. Moreover, this is because they lack substantial reality (*avastutva*).
What is the use of investigating their objective domain?
For instance, neither the transformations of substance occurring in prior and subsequent times, nor the particularities characterized by momentary perishing atoms, establish any worldly convention;
therefore, they do not possess the nature of real entities.

"Because only those things that are useful for worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) possess the nature of a real entity (*vastu*)," such is the conventional usage. Now, the intention of the *ṛjusūtra* is stated. In this context, it is "straight" (*ṛju*), meaning direct and non-crooked; because it abandons the crookedness of the past and future, it "threads" (*sūtrayati*)—that is, it delineates and demonstrates—the form of an entity existing in the present moment. Thus it is called *ṛjusūtra*. For instance:

His intention is as follows: because the past has perished and the future has not yet attained its own nature, they do not differ from things such as a donkey’s horn; since they are devoid of all causal capacities (*śakti*), they lack the fitness to accomplish purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
And a real entity (*vastu*) is that which is capable of purposeful action.

Due to the absence of that [capacity], those two [past and future] do not possess the status of real entities. Furthermore, the form of a real entity embraced by the present moment is engaged in all purposeful actions; therefore, that alone is ultimately real. That...
Moreover, it must be admitted as partless, because the pervasion by parts is devoid of logical justification;
for it is impossible for a single entity to pervade its own multiple constituent parts without possessing a multiple nature. If it is argued that "let it indeed possess a multiple nature," we say no.
Because it is beset by the tiger of contradiction. For instance:
if there is a single intrinsic nature, how can there be many?
And if there are many, how can there be one?

Because unity and plurality exist through mutual exclusion, therefore it is the atoms themselves—immersed in their own intrinsic nature—which, by means of approaching one another, somehow attain the state of an aggregate and participate in the activity of all effects. Thus, these alone are the *svalakṣaṇa* (particular), and not that which maintains grossness, for that is not ultimately real. Furthermore,
The determination of an object occurs through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), yet no means of valid cognition operates toward the apprehension of a pervasion across space and time,
because all means of valid cognition consist in the illumination of what is present. For instance:
To begin with, direct perception (pratyakṣa), having acquired its existence from the fourfold causes characterized by form, light, mental attention, and the eye, manifests only in the present moment;
for past and future moments are not present.

Consequently, it is capable of directly perceiving only that aspect of an object which is connected to that very time, and not its prior or subsequent aspects, precisely because of their non-presence. If, however, it were to perceive even a form existing in a past moment that has already perished, [it would follow that it perceives what is no longer there].
In that case, since there would be no distinction regarding their state of destruction, an infinite succession of moments would be perceived therein;

and this being so, it would follow that perception apprehends an entire series of births beginning from the very first moment. This same reasoning should be applied to the apprehension of future moments as well;
and this is an undesirable consequence.

Therefore, it must be admitted that [perception] is indeed capable of grasping only the present moment. Now, if perception were to observe the momentary destruction of the nature of objects, then that [destruction], appearing just like the color blue, would not fall within the scope of dispute; consequently, worldly linguistic practice regarding it would proceed.
But this is not the case.

"Because the engagement in conventional practice occurs by way of [perceiving] stability. To this, the following response is given: Even those who directly perceive momentary perishability engage in the conventional practice of a distorted stability because their intellects are deceived by the arising of successive similar moments, and due to the power of false conceptualization produced by the awakening of latencies (vāsanā) rooted in beginningless time; therefore, this is not the fault of direct perception.

Rather, it belongs only to the cognizers. Likewise, even the dense form is merely displayed by a false conceptual construction (*mithyāvikalpa*) arising after direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because its appearance is impossible in a vision of [the object] as it is in itself (*viviktadarśana*);
for the parts—hands, feet, head, neck, and so forth—appear there as mutually distinct.
There is no all-pervasive form, nor do even those [parts] appear as pervading their own portions,
because their parts also appear with mutually distinct forms, continuing in this way until only atoms manifest themselves.
It has already been stated that a pervasive form is incapable of withstanding analysis. Nor can a stable and gross object be established through inference;
for inference proceeds only by relying upon a relationship grasped through perception.

And since it has been demonstrated that perception possesses the skill of apprehending distinct parts characterized by momentary destruction, inference—which is rooted in that [perception]—also indirectly establishes its own object as being precisely of that nature.

Because its validity arises precisely through the establishment of that form which appears in consciousness, given that such a form is unreal (*alīka*). Now, one might object: "But recollection, recognition, and so forth, do not exist apart from a stable and gross entity, because they would be absent if such an entity had not been previously perceived;
for there is both recollection and recognition of wholes such as persons. This is not so.
Because these [cognitions] arise from the awakening of false latent impressions (*vāsanā*), they lack validity. Furthermore, even those [cognitions] manifest only in their own present moment;
however, due to a cognitive distortion (*viplava*), they determine their very own nature as having the form of past objects produced by latent impressions.
And they superimpose upon it a dense form that does not exist;

therefore, even from their perspective, a pervasive entity is not established. Consequently, since no means of valid cognition applies to a pervasive form, the *ṛjusūtra* [naya] maintains that, in ultimate reality, atoms alone are mutually distinct.
Thus has been described the opinion of the *nayās*, which are skilled in defining the essential nature of objects.
Now, for those skilled in the investigation of words, this is being described. In this regard, there is this common intention (*ākūta*) regarding all three—words and so forth:

namely, that the word alone is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), not the object, because the latter is non-different from the former. If it is asked, "How can there be non-difference, given that their status as distinct entities is established? [the response follows].
We say it is because of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For instance:
the object is not distinct from the word, because when that [word] is cognized, the [object] is also cognized.
In this world, when X is perceived, that which is perceived therein is non-different from X;
for example, when a word is being perceived, its own essential nature is perceived, and likewise, when a word is being perceived, its meaning is also perceived.

If it is argued that "this [form] is not distinct from that [taste]," because for one who has not grasped the linguistic convention, there is no cognition of the jar even upon hearing the word "jar," and therefore they must be distinct—
then, in that case, the fact that poison has the nature of killing would not appear to one ignorant of it; thus, it would follow that the quality is distinct from the substance,
which is not the case.
Otherwise, since there would be no distinction from that [non-difference], even poison would result in being non-lethal— just like jaggery or sugar-candy— and furthermore,
a relation with something distinct has already been refuted. Therefore,
the nature of a thing does not change due to the defects of an unawakened knower.

Otherwise, since "the blind person does not see form," its non-existence would also have to be admitted. If it is argued that those objects which exist without a designation are established as real entities (vastu) by virtue of their distinctness from words, we say no; for there are no such objects that lack a designation.

The only difference would be that some [entities] are denoted by specific terms, while others are denoted by general sounds. Alternatively, there is no evidence for the claim that there are no specific words capable of expressing all objects. Consequently, all objects, by virtue of being objects, [are denotable].

By the authority of the statement "like the object of a jar," it is established through the previously mentioned reasoning that all things are not distinct from the word, since they are their own designators. Therefore, in ultimate reality, there is no object existing apart from the word;

however, by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), it is so treated in worldly convention by those who have not scrutinized ultimate reality. Furthermore, this metaphorical object—which is essentially of the nature of the word—must be admitted to be momentary, because phonemes are perceived to perish in each instant.
And because of the collection of logical arguments set forth by the *ṛjusūtra* [naya].

Now, the specific intention of each of these is being stated. Among them, the *śabda* [naya] holds that as many linguistic expressions (*dhvani*) as there are that function toward a particular object according to conventional usage (*rūḍhi*);
Just as Indra, Śakra, Purandara, and so forth— all these refer to one and the same object according to the force of common cognition— so too,
just as the non-difference of the object from the word is established, its unity or plurality must likewise be demonstrated.

Furthermore, synonymous terms such as *indra*, *śakra*, and *purandara* are never perceived as denoting distinct objects, because from them there always arises a single, uniform conceptual reflection (*parāmarśa*), and because they are observed to function in that very way through unswerving usage. Therefore, the meaning of synonymous terms is one and the same; this is the [conclusion of the] word.

"By this intention, an object is signified (śabdyate) or summoned (āhūyate)," according to the *Nirukta*; thus, synonymous terms are employed solely with the intention of conveying a single meaning. Now, the view of the Samabhirūḍha is described. In that context, the "Samabhirūḍha" is that intention which, in the application of a word, ascends (*abhirohati*)—that is, it relies upon—the etymological ground (*vyutpatti-nimitta*) by way of unification (*sam-ekībhāvena*). For this [intention]...

One conceives of the meaning of synonymous terms as being strictly distinct; for example, Indra is so called because of his power (*indana*), and supreme sovereignty is, in the ultimate sense, what is denoted by the word "Indra."
Furthermore, [the word] functions through metaphorical application toward an object possessing that [quality], yet nothing at all possesses it;

for since all words function by conveying mutually distinct meanings, the relationship of substratum and superstratum (āśrayāśrayibhāva) is not established. Likewise, one is called Śakra because of his power (śakana).
By stating "Purandara because he shatters cities," and so forth, [the author] demonstrates that all words have distinct meanings;
and he provides the proof: "Synonymous words have distinct meanings."
Because they have distinct etymological bases for their derivation,
whatever words here have distinct etymological bases for their derivation, those all have different meanings;
just as the words "Indra," "jar," and "man" have distinct meanings.
Furthermore, synonymous words (*paryāya-śabda*) also have distinct etymological bases;

therefore, they do not have identical referents. As for the claim that they denote a single referent based on the force of unexamined common usage, that is incorrect, because it leads to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). To illustrate:

If perception alone, devoid of reasoning, is taken as the refuge, then in a very distant place and under extremely dim light, trees such as the nimba, kadamba, aśvattha, and kapittha— which, though distinct, appear with their bodies situated together as having the form of a single tree—
would have to be accepted as being one; yet this is not the case.

Because the prior cognition is sublated by the occurrence of a contrary cognition that grasps those [entities] as distinct in their own nature—and because one accepts that they are indeed distinct—there are no linguistic sounds (*dhvani*) that denote a single object;
rather, conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) belongs only to those who have not investigated their true meaning. This is the Samabhirūḍha [naya].
[NAV_29.21] Now, the intention regarding such a thing (evambhūta) is set forth. In this context, the word *evaṃ* expresses a manner (*prakāra*).

Consequently, a word that has become—that is, reached—such a manner as it has been explained is "evambhūta. The intention (*abhiprāya*) which primarily aims at establishing that [word] is likewise "evambhūta."
Because it has that as its object,

and because the word for the "object" (viṣaya) is used to denote the "subject" (viṣayin). For when a word is derived in relation to a certain meaning, that meaning which serves as the basis for its derivation is intended [by the speaker] whenever that very word is employed, even if that meaning has undergone a transformation.

Not by way of generality. For instance, at the time of fetching water and so forth, it is only a jar that possesses specific activity— such as one being carried on the head of a woman— that is denoted, and not any other, because the latter lacks the basis for the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti-nimitta*) of the word "jar."
Regarding the phrase "like a cloth, etc.": if it is argued that this is stated in general terms with reference to past or future activity, we say no;
for since those two have perished or not yet arisen, they are like the horns of a hare.
Even so, if a word were to be applied by means of them, it would have to be applied everywhere.
Because there is no distinction. Furthermore,
if the word "jar" were applied even to that which lacks activity on account of past or future activity,
then its application to potsherds, lumps of clay, and so forth, would be unavoidable.

Because there is no distinction [between them], therefore, in whichever moment the cause for linguistic convention (*vyutpatti-nimitta*) is complete, in that very moment that object is denotable by that word; such is the "evambhūta" [type of word].
Thus, the cognition that grasps an object enveloped by manifold properties (*aneka-dharma*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, the *naya* is a reflective judgment (*parāmarśa*) that, having arrived through those [doors], is intent upon establishing the meaning of one specific property; it functions by way of accepting, rejecting, or setting aside the remaining properties.
And because properties are infinite, it has infinite divisions;
nevertheless, by means of conceptualizing an intention that encompasses all [properties], it is shown here to have seven divisions. This very [system]—

Furthermore, because it functions by means of the exclusion of all phenomena through its nature of determining only those phenomena intended by oneself, such conceptualization (parāmarśa) receives the designation of "wrong method" (durnaya);
for indeed, these doctrines of other schools possess their very existence as brought about by the power of that [conceptualization]. To explain:

The Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas follow the Naigama-naya. All Advaita doctrines as well as the Sāṃkhya system proceed from the perspective of the Saṅgraha-naya. The Cārvāka system generally conforms to the Vyavahāra-naya. The Tāthāgatas (Buddhists) have their intellects inclined toward the Rjusūtra-naya. And the Grammarians and others rely upon the views of the Śabda-naya and so forth.
Thus [it is said]. Now, if you were to ask:

"In what way do these [views], while establishing their own respective objects through the door of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) and thereby negating the opposite, fall into the state of being a *durnaya* (a flawed perspective)?"—to this it is replied: because, when proceeding in such a manner, they lack a [proper] objective domain (*nirgocaratvāt*).

Because that which lacks a specific scope cannot function as a *naya*. For instance, a *naya* is an intention (*abhiprāya*) that leads—that is, it causes one to reach—an object qualified by a particular aspect.
However, that which proceeds by way of rejecting the remaining attributes other than its own intended attribute does not lead to anything at all.
Because it is impossible for an entity to be embraced by only a single property,
since that entity appears both externally and internally as having a nature encircled by manifold properties; therefore,
those evil intentions which seek to deny this [manifold nature] are false, being sublated by appearance itself.

For instance: first, that which was asserted by the Naigama-naya—that the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*) are mutually distinct—is incorrect, because they never appear in such a manner. Furthermore, as it has been said:
"Where the universal is apprehended through a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of a single recurring form, there the particular does not appear."
Furthermore, where a particularity (*viśeṣa*)—which is to be grasped by a cognition delimited by a specific place and state—is not apprehended, there is no comprehension of the universal (*sāmānya*);

that [assertion] is a mere word, because when all particulars such as the *dhava*, *khadira*, and *palāśa* trees are excluded, there is no appearance of the universal "treeness" (*vṛkṣatva*). If it is argued that even when the particulars are not perceived from a distance, that [universal] alone shines forth, we say no.
Even there, because a particularity that has become internalized appears [within the universal],
and because in its absence it would be like a hare's horn; likewise, particulars also do not appear as absolutely distinct from the universal,
since they are perceived only as submerged within it.

Otherwise, entities that exceed mere existence would themselves incur the state of being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*). Likewise, trees and so forth would not be distinct from universals such as "treeness," because the establishment of their own nature is dependent upon non-difference from those [universals]. Therefore, it is said that cognition itself grasps the universal when it makes its diversity subordinate and makes a single form primary; conversely, it grasps the particular when it suppresses equality and brings forth multiplicity.
Because identity and difference, which are in some way characterized by both distinction and non-distinction, exist mutually in all things;

for in their absence, such an appearance would be impossible. By this, it should be understood that the claim—"Even though these two, the universal and the particular, appear as distinct, it is not logical to mix them in any way"—is refuted.

Because there is no appearance [of the two] as distinct entities. Furthermore, every conventional usage is accomplished in some way through the primary and the subordinate, and thus necessarily involves a universal and a particular that are not mutually separated;
for a universal is not employed in actions such as milking or driving, since only particulars are employed therein.
Nor are the particulars alone the performers of that action,

because those devoid of "tree-ness" (gotva) are indistinguishable from things such as grass and wood, and thus lack the capacity to perform it. Furthermore, if there were absolute difference between the universal and the particular, why would one who is commanded, "Cut the tree," proceed to perform the cutting on a particular instance such as a *palāśa* tree?
If it is argued that [the relation exists] there because of its inherence (*samavāya*) in that [substratum], we say no; for there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends inherence,
and even if it existed, it would be incapable of producing the cognition of non-difference between two distinct things.

Furthermore, because it would be no different from other distinct entities due to its being separate [from them], and because it would follow that it must produce [its effects] everywhere by virtue of its eternality, unity, omnipresence, and so forth. As for what you further asserted, namely: "If the universal were perceived as residing in the particulars, or if the particular were perceived as pervaded by the universal," [that is not the case].

Consequently, because those two [the universal and the particular] are not perceived as distinct from one another anywhere, this entire worldly transaction—which is characterized by denotation and causal efficiency regarding universals and particulars that are [supposedly] distinct—would come to an end; for it would be impossible to effect their distinction due to their being merged together (*lolībhāva*).
But that too is incorrect.
For although both the universal and the particular are perceived everywhere as mutually inseparable,

nevertheless, wherever there is a cognizer’s purpose, it is precisely that [object]— whether it be the universal or the particulars— that is made primary, and it prompts the application of a verbal designation or a causal efficiency toward that object; for even the other [aspect] functions therein in a subordinate capacity.

For that which lacks those [particulars] would be like the horn of a hare, being of no use anywhere. Furthermore, if the universal were absolutely distinct from the particulars, the collection of refutations—falling like a thunderbolt upon its head by way of the dilemma regarding its subsistence and the necessity of a new relation with the particulars—would be unbearable. To explain:
How, then, would it exist in relation to those particulars—entirely or partially?

If the position of its being entirely present is taken, then because it would be fully complete in each individual particular, there would follow the undesirable consequence of a multiplicity of universals; and this is not accepted.
Because the admission of oneness would be undermined. Furthermore, if it were to exist in part, then as many particulars as there are, that many portions of the universal would follow;
yet this is not the case, because a universal is partless.

Furthermore, even if they possess parts, are those [parts] non-different or different [from one another]? If they are non-different, then why are the particulars not accepted as being themselves non-different, given the absence of any further particularity? In the case of their being different, however, how would that [universal] reside in them—by way of its entirety or by way of a single part?

That very objection remains unresolved and leads to this conclusion: the occurrence [of a single entity] in things that are absolutely distinct is not possible. Furthermore, if a single universal were to reside in all particular instances just as the particulars themselves do, [it would follow that it is itself particularized].
At that time, when there is the apprehension of a single particularity, is that [universal] apprehended or not?
If the first position is held, then because it is one, it would be apprehended everywhere.
Because the apprehension of the pervader is impossible in the absence of the apprehension of the pervaded,
it would follow that there must be the apprehension of every specific instance of that pervaded;
however, this is not the case.
Because one directly perceives only the particularity present before one,
while the remaining particulars are not in proximity;
that [perception] is apprehended as residing solely in the proximate particularity, since that alone is its manifestor.

If it is argued that this is because those other [particulars] are absent [in the others], we say no; for it is impossible for a single nature (*ekasvabhāva*) to be manifested in fragments. That [nature] is manifested precisely by the particulars present [at that time], since there is no other nature anywhere else. And since that form belongs to all the particulars, by what could its perception be prevented? Now, as for the second alternative:
That being the case, just as it is not perceived at the time of perceiving one particular feature,
so too it would not be perceived at the time of perceiving the remaining features, due to the absence of those features. Therefore, its non-existence alone would have been stated.

Because there is no perception of it in isolation; even if it were perceived, since it abides in its own nature, it would necessarily assume the form of a particularity (*viśeṣa*). Thus, how could that entity—which possesses an existence established by a long-standing particularity—experience a connection with that [new] particularity when a new particularity arises?
For it cannot possibly go from other particularities to the location of the particularity about to arise.
Because it is devoid of activity.

Nor did it exist in that very place, because prior to the production of the particularity, there was no perception of it in that location. Nor does it arise simultaneously with the particularity itself.
Because it is eternal,
and because production is incompatible with that which is eternal. Now, if— desiring to avoid this fault— it were asserted that it possesses activity,
even so, it would either abandon its previous manifestation or occupy a new location characterized by particularity.

Or [is it] by their absence? Not the first alternative, because it would follow that since ancient individuals lack the universal (*sāmānya*), there would be an absence of the cognition, verbal expression, and activity established through the connection with it; yet this is not the case.
Even though there is the production of successive particularities, [the universal] is observed in the preceding individuals. Now, if the second alternative is proposed, that too is incoherent;

for if it is partless, it cannot move toward the individual about to be produced while remaining deficient in its abandonment of the previous individual. Furthermore, the position that it possesses parts has already been refuted.
This rebuttal by way of acceptance is not the best solution. Furthermore:
if entities are identical because of their connection with a distinct universal, and not by virtue of their own intrinsic nature, [then...]
In that case, prior to the connection with existence (*sattā*), entities must be either existent or non-existent. If they are already existent, the connection with existence is redundant;

otherwise, an infinite regress would result, since there would be no way to prevent a further connection with another instance of existence. If, on the other hand, they are non-existent, then even things that are absolutely non-existent, such as a sky-lotus and the like, [would possess existence].

Through its connection with existence (*sattā*), it would attain the nature of a positive entity (*bhāva*). This same [argument] should be stated in full for the universals (*sāmānya*) such as substantiality (*dravyatva*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), action-ness (*karmatva*), and cowness (*gotva*),
because they share the same status of being and non-being (*ekayogakṣema*).

Therefore, the universal and the particular, which are mutually and absolutely distinct, can in no way coalesce. For this very reason, the intention that seeks to establish them while rejecting their identity is designated as the "naigama-durnaya" (the flawed naigama view), because it lacks a valid basis; for the naigama-naya consists precisely in asserting the distinction between the universal and the particular while disregarding their identity.
Even though those two [terms] are mutually exclusive, they nonetheless exist in some way within the entity;
otherwise, even by intention, it would be impossible to represent them as such,
because the relationship of primary and subordinate must reside in both.

For if there were absolute identity, it would follow that even the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*), which brings about that [identity], would be devoid of an object. Therefore, these two [the universal and the particular] are indeed non-different while being different in some respect;
furthermore, it is established that whichever of the two is supported by a one-sided view becomes a "bad method" (*durnaya*) because it lacks a basis.
Likewise, the *saṅgraha* (comprehensive) view is also a bad method, as it establishes a single universal by means of rejecting all particulars.
Because it is led [to its conclusion] precisely through the door of indifference toward that [particular], for a universal devoid of particulars is impossible. To explain:

as for what was stated—that is to say, "Are the particulars distinct from the universal or non-distinct? In the case of the position of distinction, they would lack intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatva),"...
"Because it lacks substantiality. In the case of non-difference, there would be mere existence,
because [the effect] is not distinct from that [existence],
just like its own nature"— this is incorrect.

This is because such a conceptual alternative is possible even for one who maintains the doctrine of particulars (*viśeṣavādin*). To explain: is the universal distinct from the particulars or non-distinct? If it is distinct, then it is not a universal.

Because it possesses a specific form by virtue of being established in its own essential nature. If [the universal] were non-different [from the particular], even so it would not be a universal, precisely because it is non-different from the particular, just like the nature of that particular itself. As for what was also said: "The conventional usage of particulars proceeds by the power of beginningless ignorance..."
"Real universality"— that too is mere words,
because it is devoid of logical justification;
universality itself is merely that which is displayed by beginningless ignorance.

Furthermore, since even the proponent of particulars (*viśeṣavādin*) does not suffer a collapse of his position when asserting that particulars are ultimately real, as to what was stated by one who seeks to establish the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for apprehending particulars—

namely, that "perception, having its existence produced by a positive entity (*bhāva*), directly perceives only that [entity] and not its absence, because it does not produce the latter," and so forth— [that argument is refuted].
That is even more improper,
because who among your very close friends has informed you:
"Only existence itself brings about direct perception"?
If you argue that "it is not even non-existence" by means of a collection of arguments intended to demonstrate the absence of the operation of non-existence, then you have been deceived by a fool,
because the absence of its operation is unestablished.

Because an entity that possesses both existent and non-existent forms is operative in all activities, there is no contradiction in the operation of a non-existence that is established as being identical in nature (*tādātmya*) with existence. If it is asked, "How can there be identity between existence and non-existence, given their contradiction?", we say no; for there is no contradiction in what is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). To explain:

An entity such as a jar exists by its own nature, but not by the nature of a cloth or other things; thus, it consists of both existence and non-existence. If, however, it were in some way not of the nature of non-existence, then, because it would exist even in the form of a cloth and so forth, it would follow that it possesses the nature of everything. This is logical.
If it is argued that for this very reason the dissolution of the manifold of difference is established,
this might indeed be so,
provided that even the proponents of emptiness (śūnyavādins) do not fulfill their own desires by means of the absolute non-existence of cloth and other such things. For instance:
A jar is experienced as distinct from a cloth and other such things; yet the non-existence of the cloth and so forth does not experience identity with an existing entity.
Therefore, this [jar] is indeed of the nature of non-existence.

In this way, even things such as cloth and so forth would fall into emptiness by virtue of being mutually dependent. Therefore, a real entity (*vastu*), while maintaining its own nature (*svarūpa*), is indeed differentiated from the natures of others; it is thus engaged in all causal operations.

This is because maintaining its own nature is a positive existence (*bhāva*), whereas the exclusion of other natures is a non-existence (*abhāva*). In this same manner, it is also engaged in the production of a perception whose object is itself.

Consequently, since it must directly realize that very form, perception operates only upon a real entity that is determined by its own nature and excluded from the natures of others, because it is produced by that [exclusion],
and not upon mere existence.

Because that [object] in its isolated state lacks a stable nature, it is incapable of being a producer. Furthermore, it has been stated that an object is not the apprehended because it is a producer, nor is cognition the apprehender because it is produced; for such [definitions] would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Rather, cognition—having acquired its existence through the removal of obstructions and so forth—apprehends [the object] by means of a transformation into the act of grasping.
The object, however, is apprehended through its proximity and other factors;

and since it is perceived as having both a persisting and an excluding form, it must be accepted as being of such a nature, and not merely of the nature of a universal (*sāmānya*). If it is asked how the positive and negative aspects can coexist in one place:

We say that [they exist] through identity (*tādātmya*). But surely, if there were identity, there would result either mere existence or mere non-existence, because they would not be distinct from one another, just like the essential nature of each; thus, the establishment of an entity possessing both forms would be impossible. This is not so.
Because identity is a relation,
and because a relation must reside in two things, in the absence of those two, what could have a relation with what?
Because they lack a [separate] objective domain?
Therefore, these two aspects— existence and non-existence— are non-different insofar as they take the form of the substratum (dharmī),
because the entity, which consists of both existence and non-existence, is a single unity.
Furthermore, when intended [as objects] by way of their nature as phenomena (*dharma*), they experience differentiation,

because they exist in their own form but do not exist in the form of another. Thus, in perception— which grasps distinct entities and stands at the forefront of all means of valid cognition— this is the case.

Once the particular has been established, the remaining means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), by following it, establish their own respective objects as being indeed distinct. Therefore, one who denies that [particular] while attempting to establish a mere universal adopts an evil intention that deserves the designation of the "wrong view of compendium" (*saṅgraha-durnaya*),
because the *saṅgraha-naya* is precisely that which establishes a universal in dependence upon particulars.

Likewise, conventional discourse (*vyavahāra*), while denying the true nature of things established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and instead justifying a worldly course of conduct that is devoid of reasoning and charming only when unexamined, incurs upon itself the state of being a "bad method" (*durnaya*). This is because even for one who establishes worldly convention, there can be no stable foundation if he does not accept the other [the ultimate]. For instance:
That which you intend to be real—namely, things such as pots that endure for a certain duration, possess grossness, and function within worldly convention—is not causeless;
rather, it is composed of eternal atoms (*paramāṇu*).
Otherwise, being without a cause, there would follow the consequence of their existence or non-existence at all times. If you say that those atoms do not appear as such [to perception], then:

For this very reason, their establishment cannot be achieved through inference. If, however, everything that does not manifest clearly in direct perception were to be denied, then alas, much would now have to be denied;
for since only the skin on the near side of an object such as a jar appears, it would follow that its middle, far side, and so forth must also be denied.
Furthermore, even the capacity for worldly transaction (*lokavyavahāra*) would collapse,
since that [transaction] is not established by that much alone. If, on the other hand, you establish a complete object capable of transaction here through the power of inference,
then let the establishment of past and future modes (*paryāya*) and atoms (*paramāṇu*) also be performed in the same way.
Because there is no distinction [between the two cases]. For instance:

just as when only the external surface of things appears, since there is no practical transaction (vyavahāra) with them based on that alone, those [objects] are established as complete and capable [of performing functions] by means of proving the existence of their middle parts and so forth;

in exactly the same way, even when only a dense form existing at a certain time is seen, let those [atoms] be established as having bodies constituted by a state of identity with beginningless and endless atoms.
For even in the absence of that [prior state], they cannot be established. To explain:

first, if one does not admit past modes for the initial mode—which enters into conventional usage and is capable of being perceived—then it would follow that it is causeless, and the fault in that has already been stated. Furthermore, if one seeks a subsequent mode as its producer, then the mode that produces that must also be admitted.

Thus, an infinite succession of modes would result.
