Furthermore, if a mode that reaches the limit of a thing engaged in conventional usage does not produce another mode, its status as a non-entity follows by necessity, because according to your own system, it lacks causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). If, on the other hand, it does produce [another mode], then this [mode] too must produce yet another mode.

Thus, it is established that [the whole] is impossible in an infinite series of parts. Likewise, even a solid form, when being directly perceived through clear vision, is not possible apart from constituent parts that extend to the limit of having no further spatial divisions;
for hands, feet, and other such members, being divisible into fragments, do not possess the nature of a whole (*avayavin*).

Because even those parts [of the object] are composed of further constituent parts, atoms alone are the ultimate constituent parts that serve as the cause for the appearance of a solid form in reality;
in their absence, moreover, such [solidity] would either be perceived everywhere by chance, or not perceived anywhere at all.
Because there is no distinction [between them]. By this, that which was asserted— namely,
that "for one who enters into worldly convention, there exists a validating cognition (pramāṇa) that favors a real entity, but not for anything else," and so forth—
should also be understood as refuted.

Because that [entity] is established precisely through the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the perceived object (*dṛśyamānārthānyathānupapatti*). Furthermore, as for what was said: "What is the use of investigating those past and future states, atoms, and so forth? Since they are not real entities because they are of no use for worldly convention (*lokavyavahāra*)," and so on—that is incorrect.

Alternatively, by means of indifference (*upekṣā*), a present object would lose its status as a real entity because it is of no utility; for everything is of no utility to every person. If something is a real entity due to its utility to someone, that [utility] certainly exists for those [present objects] as well, since they fall within the range of the knowledge of the Omniscient One and so forth—let this suffice for now. Thus, because it denies facts established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the doctrine of conventional reality (*vyavahāra*) is a flawed perspective (*durnaya*).
This is because, by disregarding that [conventional reality], the *vyavahāra-naya* (the conventional standpoint) is that which establishes the objects that conform to worldly transactional usage.

[NAV 29.26] Now, even the *ṛjusūtra* falls into the state of a "bad standpoint" (*durnaya*) if, by denying what is perceived, it regards as the ultimate reality only the nature of things characterized by momentary destruction and atomicity; for when the perceived stable and gross objects are denied, there is no arising of the reflective awareness that establishes its own intended object, as it would be entirely groundless. To explain:
Directly perceiving a form that pervades its own parts and persists through a succession of time, one might later analyze it through fallacious reasoning and conceptual construction, saying:

"Indeed, this visible form—stable and gross as it appears—cannot be established as real, because it cannot withstand analysis," and so forth. But this is not tenable, for such fallacious conceptualizations that misrepresent what has been seen would lead to a total lack of confidence in everything. Now, you might say:
"Just as the previous delusion of a venomous snake in a rope within a region of very dim light is sublated by a subsequent conceptual determination that establishes it as such,
so too is this perception of a stable and gross object sublated by the reflective awareness that establishes the momentary destruction of atoms;
what is unreasonable here?"
This is not so, because it is precisely the appearance of the rope that is capable of dispelling the previously arisen delusion of a venomous serpent;

and in its absence, it would be impossible to remove [the delusion] even by hundreds of conceptual constructions. Furthermore, in this case as well, the past and the future are not present, owing to their having perished and not yet arisen, respectively.

If it is argued that when gross components are analyzed through the lens of both difference and non-difference with respect to their own parts, they lack any stable existence and thus only momentary atoms appear; and consequently, this very appearance is what subverts the perception of stable and gross objects—
then, in that case, it would follow that appearance cannot be established through authoritative instruction (*upadeśa*).

In that very way, practical activity (*vyavahāra*) would proceed. If it is argued that it does not proceed because of the confusion caused by subsequent false conceptualizations (*mithyāvikalpa*), [we reply] no, because this same answer applies elsewhere as well, since it is the cause of confusion. For instance, even when a white lotus or similar object appears, one might think: "This blue object was perceived by direct perception (*adhyakṣa*)."

But who could prevent a rogue from asserting, according to the logic that "it appears white due to the confusion of a subsequent false conceptualization"? Therefore, the denial of what has been perceived cannot be made, because that [perception] itself is the seeing; whereas anything else, being established by means of that perception, is merely an object of inference.

If that [momentary nature] is not admitted, then that [capacity for causal efficiency] is also unestablished. By this, the demonstration that a stable and gross object lacks causal efficiency is also refuted;
for such an entity alone is observed to be operative in all actions, and because causal efficiency is denied to that which perishes moment by moment, as was stated previously:

"For the nature of an object is subject to momentary destruction; therefore, it would have to produce its effect either in its own prior moment or in a subsequent one," and so forth. Furthermore, because every entity is perceived as possessing both a persisting and a changing form—through such attributes as existence, personhood, and consciousness, as well as through states such as childhood, youth, old age, joy, and sorrow—it consists of both substance and modification (*dravya-paryāya*).
This is because non-difference constitutes substantiality.

"Because difference is of the nature of a mode (*paryāya*). Consequently, the demonstration that only the present moment possesses causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*)—by way of the non-presence of past and future moments—does not constitute a refutation for us; for since modes occur successively, it is only the substance (*dravya*) when embraced by the present mode that is capable of performing causal efficiency. Furthermore, that [substance] is not merely pervasive across the three times.

The perceiver, too, is likewise constituted as a substantial entity. Consequently, through the concealment of its momentary modalities and the synthesis of their forms, this [entity] appears to enter the path of cognition as something stable, engaged in all its activities;
for stability, too, is ultimately real.
Because even though momentary modes exist, they are not apprehended;

for the cognition of ordinary people has only a few parts as its object, depending as it does on the subsidence and destruction of obscurations (*āvaraṇakṣayopaśama*). If, however, the notion of a substance (*dravyabuddhi*) were unreal because it is derived from the power of not seeing the succession of modes, then one must state whether the preceding mode possesses continuity (*sānvayatva*) or lacks continuity (*niranvayatva*) in the production of the succeeding mode.

Because there is no other alternative state of being. If there were persistence (sānvayatva), the substance would be expressed by another mode (paryāya); if, however, there were no persistence (niranvayatva), then due to the absence of a cause, it would follow that subsequent modes could not arise. Therefore, the accomplishment of causal efficiency (arthakriyā) is not possible apart from an entity that possesses both forms [substance and mode]. Nor is causal efficiency the defining characteristic of a real entity (vastu), for the final moments of sound, lightning, a lamp, and so forth, would result in non-existence as entities because they do not initiate another moment.
Furthermore, if that [moment] were not a real entity (*vastu*), then even the penultimate moment would lack causal efficiency (*vyāpāra*) toward a real entity;

thus, by a chain of moments, all moments would lack the status of being real entities. Now, if it were postulated that causal efficiency consists merely in producing a cognition whose object is itself—even if no other subsequent moment is initiated—then a succession of past and future modes (*paryāya*) would also become the object of a yogi’s cognition and must therefore be accepted as real entities. Therefore, causal efficiency is not the defining characteristic of a real entity.
Rather, it is the state of being endowed with origination, destruction, and persistence,
because this is established by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). If it is argued that origination and destruction are contradictory to persistence,
from what source does this contradiction arise?
Is it from a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) or from an invalid one (*apramāṇa*)?

First, it cannot be the former position, because it has been established that all valid means of cognition are highly proficient at illuminating such an object both externally and internally. Nor can it be the second.

Because the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is incapable of producing any effect [in this regard]. By this, the refutation regarding grossness is also rejected, because it is struck down by [the fact of] manifestation;

for the raising of an objection based on contradiction through the denial of that [manifestation] is baseless and a mere prattle. Furthermore, since all means of valid cognition consist in the manifestation of the present, they possess the capacity to grasp objects connected with that [present time].
That is incorrect,
because it is not established that they are exclusively present,
since in some respect they are non-different from the self.
And because that [Self] pervades the three times,
those [cognitions] also exist in the form of it. Consequently, since the Self consists of the transformation of grasping objects,
the operation of all means of valid cognition occurs only with respect to an object that is subject to transformation.

It is not [the case] in the momentary [theory]. Nor does it follow that by grasping an object existing in a past or future moment, one would necessarily grasp an infinite succession of beginningless births; for that [grasping] depends upon the removal of obstructions, since only that [removal] is, in the ultimate sense, the cause for the manifestation of cognition.

Because the object of apprehension (*grāhya*) and so forth are external factors (*bahiraṅga*). Furthermore, when the veil of obscuration (*āvaraṇa*) is destroyed in its entirety, the consequence of grasping the entire expansion of all things—the succession of beginningless and endless moments—does not pose a contradiction for us, as it is indeed desired [by us]. However, when there is only a partial subsidence of that obscuration (*ekadeśakṣayopaśama*), the activity of cognition follows accordingly;
thus, the cognitions of ordinary people pertain to gross objects existing over a limited duration of time.
They proceed,
but not when [the object] is complete; nor are they false,
because the aspect grasped by them also exists within the real entity.
"Because worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is established by that much alone. And as it was said:
"Even though they perceive momentariness, the dull-witted do not ascertain it because they are deceived by the production of successive similar [moments];
and under the influence of false conceptual construction (*mithyāvikalpa*), they engage in the conventional usage of stability (*sthiratā*)."
That is incorrect, because there is no similarity with your intended meaning;

for in the absence of that [similarity], it is impossible for the error you intend to be produced by it to arise without a seed. Likewise, the superimposition of stability is only logical in some cases for one who has already apprehended stability, and not otherwise.

Just as there is the superimposition of a venomous snake upon seeing a rope in dim light when one has previously seen a venomous snake, [so too is this case]. Yet, for you, stability never at any time enters the range of cognition;

so how can there be such a superimposition, even though everything is observed by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as being associated with arising and passing away at every moment? Therefore, an object whose momentary transformations are concealed and whose distinctness from atoms is unperceived is [the object] of all conventional means of valid cognition (*saṃvyavahārika-pramāṇa*).

Because it is made an object of focus (*gocarīkriyate*), the intention that, by way of disregarding that [object], establishes unseen, momentary, and atomic [entities], receives the designation of the "straightforward" (*ṛjusūtra*) fallacious view (*durnaya*);
for only by disregarding that [object] does one who perceives it become a "viewpoint" (*naya*).

Likewise, those who argue that objects such as sound and so forth are in every respect non-different from the word itself are proponents of a fallacious view (*durnaya*), because the reason they adduce to prove this— namely, that the object is perceived whenever the word is perceived— is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
For it is not an absolute rule that whatever is perceived when something else is perceived must necessarily be non-different from it.

For even fire and the like, though distinct [from smoke], are perceived when smoke and such are cognized, by virtue of a relationship characterized by the impossibility of being otherwise (*anyathānupapannatva*). In the same way, a word also denotes an object that is distinct from it, because its denotative function (*vācakatva*) is contradicted by perception and other means of knowledge if there were no distinction; for the object is experienced precisely as distinct from the word. And while this reason remains inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), [it follows that] for all objects...

By means of proving that [words] denote their own [referents], the proof that words are non-different from them is also cast far away. Furthermore, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) here that grasps the necessary connection— that whatever object exists must be denoted by its own word—
since such a connection is not established merely by the example of jars and the like.

Furthermore, because momentary, imperceptible substances and their transformations cannot be expressed due to the absence of a means for grasping linguistic conventions, their ineffability is established.

Moreover, the claim regarding their momentary perishability must likewise be refuted, as it was for the *Ṛjusūtra* [Naya]. Thus, even when establishing their own intended position while disregarding the individual views [of other schools] and rejecting the word-meaning that contradicts it, they embrace the state of being a "bad logic" (*durnaya*).
For this much alone is established by valid cognition:
namely, that a word denotes an object by way of affirmation;
however, there is no such restriction that it is the denoter of this object alone and not of another.

Because all words are observed to convey various distinct meanings due to the diversity of place, time, persons, conventions, and so forth; because it is logically possible for them to denote various different objects through their possession of infinite attributes (*anantadharman*) and the resulting variation in their respective capacities;

because there is no contradiction in objects themselves being denotable by various different words precisely because they possess infinite attributes; and because we observe worldly linguistic practice (*vyavahāra*) occurring in such a manner without any disagreement.
For if that were not accepted, it would follow that those [sounds] would be lost. Therefore, all sounds are capable of denoting all objects by virtue of their inherent fitness (*yogyatā*);

however, depending on factors such as the subsidence and destruction of karmic veils (*kṣayopaśama*) in a particular place, they produce cognition in some way or another in certain instances. Consequently, in some cases they function through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) without requiring the etymological basis for their derivation, while in other cases they depend upon a general understanding of their etymology.

In some cases, this is due to dependence on the etymological basis as it existed at that particular time; therefore, an authoritative person should not insist on grasping a fixed meaning in such instances. Consequently, when these [doctrines] such as the *nayas* present their own intended word-meanings while disregarding the word-meanings accepted by others, they are called *nayas*.
Because that [other property] also exists therein. Furthermore, those [views] which function by mutual sublation take on the nature of *durnaya* (fallacious reasoning), because they lack a basis.
[NAV 29.28] Now, if it is the case that intentions which are intent upon establishing one single property while disregarding all other properties attain the status of *durnaya*, [then...]

At that time, even speech, when proceeding by way of teaching a single property, becomes false because it entails the exclusion of remaining properties due to its restrictive nature. Consequently, only speech that reveals an entity as being endowed with infinite properties is true, because it conveys the object exactly as it exists;
yet such is not the way speech functions.
Because we observe the use of words in linguistic practice directed toward the presentation of each individual property— such as "this jar is white" or "it is corporeal"—
and because it is impossible to express all properties simultaneously,
and because the words denoting them would likewise be infinite; furthermore, even though these utterances present only a single property at a time, they cannot be said to be false.

Because it would follow that all verbal usage (*śābdavyavahāra*) would be annihilated, and because if that [object] were unreal, purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*) based upon it could not be established. To this, it is replied: Here, first of all, there are two types of people who communicate about things—the worldly (*laukika*) and the seekers of reality (*tattvacintaka*). Among them, the worldly people, out of necessity and with an attitude of neutrality, designate at the time of practical transaction an object already established through perception and other means.
That is to say, [one perceives] "the blue lotus is fragrant and soft," yet one does not concern oneself with the apprehension or exclusion of other properties belonging to that substratum,
because of a lack of interest therein.
For by that much alone the intended conventional usage is completed. Nor is those statements false, because there is no exclusion of other remaining properties;

rather, it is only those [statements] that effect such an exclusion which are false. According to the principle that "every statement is restrictive," since it is established that even those [non-restrictive statements] perform the function of setting aside other remaining properties, they too would fall into falsity according to your own logic.
If this is argued, we say no;

for the function of the restriction is merely to exclude the impossibility of that [other alternative], just as when someone standing at the entrance of an assembly hall filled with many people wonders, "Is Devadatta here or not? and [the answer] serves only to exclude his absence.

Or, it may be stated by someone whose mind is wavering: "Devadatta exists. In this case, although the two words employed are understood to be restrictive—since otherwise their utterance would result in futility—
Nevertheless, that restriction excludes only the impossibility [of the cognition],
not other remaining persons,
nor non-existence in the form of another.

This is because the statement in question is employed with the intention of excluding that [other possibility], and because the capacity of a *dhvani* (suggestive word) to convey its own meaning depends precisely upon the speaker’s intention and other such factors. Nor is the relationship characterized as the signifier-signified (*vācya-vācaka-bhāva*) rendered useless;

for in its absence, it would be impossible to determine even the form [of the meaning] based on the speaker’s intention alone. Furthermore, we do not assert that a statement is true only if it conveys an object endowed with all its attributes.

If it were the case that the falsity of those [teachings] which demonstrate entities embraced by each individual property would follow, then what [would be true]? Rather, that which conveys a possible meaning is true;
and indeed, when there is no rejection of the remaining properties, those properties that have entered the domain of verbal expression are possible.

Therefore, that which establishes it is indeed true. However, when it is employed with an exclusive restriction (*sāvadhāraṇa*) by those of other schools whose intellects are obsessed with the views of fallacious reasoning (*durnaya*), with the intention of negating other properties belonging to that same subject (*dharmī*), such as "the object is exclusively impermanent" or "it is exclusively permanent," and so forth—
In that case, since it would lack a basis of support and thus fall into unreality, by whom could it be prevented?

Furthermore, those who contemplate reality, demonstrating that an object established through means of valid cognition such as perception is multiform (anekāntātmaka), would show it in two ways: namely, by way of partial predication (vikalādeśa) or by way of complete predication (sakalādeśa). Among these, partial predication is dependent upon a specific standpoint (naya).
The comprehensive statement (*sakalādeśa*) is dependent upon the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For instance:

when those who, out of a neutral disposition and by virtue of a specific purpose, desire to explain a certain attribute, employ speech with an intellect indifferent to the acceptance or rejection of remaining attributes, then even those who contemplate reality speak in a manner that appears indistinct, just like worldly people.

Namely: "The soul exists as the agent, the knower, the enjoyer," and so forth. Therefore, because it lacks the presentation of the complete reality, it is called a partial statement (*vikalādeśa*); the meaning is that it is merely a presentation of those attributes that are possible according to the standpoint (*naya*). However, when they intend to present [the reality] by reflecting upon the complete operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), they then demonstrate it through speech adorned with the word *syāt* (in some sense), which is accompanied by a restriction (*sāvadhāraṇā*) and indicates all attributes—including both the subordinate and the primary—whose status has been accepted.

It is by means of such statements as "the soul (jīva) certainly exists. Therefore, this [syādvāda] is the indicator of a reality whose infinite internal attributes are suggested by the word *syāt*, whose essential nature is emphasized by the direct presentation of the word "soul" and its verb, and whose impossibility [of being otherwise] is excluded by the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*).
It is called *sakalādeśa* (the complete predication), which means the statement of an object in its entirety as established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). As it has been said:
"In that regard, the comprehension of the specific characteristics of the object of knowledge consists of both the standpoint (*naya*) and the valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)."
It should be understood that the *māna* (measure) grasps the whole, whereas the *naya* (method) grasps a part.
This is what is meant:

the proponent of *syādvāda*, who is proficient in the methods (*naya*) and the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), speaks whatever he says with the desire to explain the true nature of a thing by means of both complete and partial descriptions; all that is true, because its domain consists of possible objects. On the other hand, whatever the proponents of one-sided views (*ekāntavādin*), who rely on the doctrines of false methods (*durnaya*), declare—all that is false.
"Because its object is an impossible thing.

Now, strengthening this very point, he says the following, demonstrating that even within the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), the sūtras composed according to the perspective of individual *nayās* do not express the complete meaning; rather, it is that which proceeds with the intention of their synthesis that reveals the undivided reality:
Because the various systems, each reaching its own singular conclusion, proceed along the path of scripture,
that which ascertains the complete meaning is called the teaching of *syādvāda*.

[NAV_30.1] Here, scripture (*śruta*) is threefold, namely: false scripture (*mithyāśruta*), scriptural perspective (*nayaśruta*), and the scripture of the doctrine of manifoldness (*syādvādaśruta*). In this context, "scripture" (*śruta*) refers to that which is heard; it is the traditional teaching (*āgama*). False scripture is false or unreal scripture; it is that which proceeds from the intention of a fallacious perspective (*durnaya*) and is associated with non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*).
Because it is beyond the scope [of other systems]. Likewise, "scriptural knowledge through methods" (*nayaśruta*) refers to that which is heard by means of the methods acting as causes;
this is contained within the Āgama of the Arhats and is bound to the intention of a single method (*ekana-ya*), such as:
"The present hell-being perishes," and so forth.

Because momentariness is also possible therein according to the intention of the *ṛjusūtra* perspective. Thus, "syādvāda" (the doctrine of manifoldness) is discourse joined with the term "syāt" (*may be*), which indicates all other remaining properties distinct from the property being pointed out; the teaching (*śruta*) that consists of the expression of the intended property is "syādvāda-śruta. To the question "Of what nature is that said to be?", he replies:

it is "complete" (*sampūrṇa*), meaning unimpaired; and it is "that very object" (*sa cāsāv arthaś ca*), so it is designated as such because it is the cause for the ascertainment (*viniścāyi*)—that is, the definitive determination—of that [object].

The meaning is that, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthataḥ*), it establishes the nature of all things because its essence is verbal, whereas certainty (*niścaya*) has the nature of cognition (*bodha*). [The opponent asks: "In that case, why does scriptural knowledge (*naya-śruta*) not become a determiner of the complete object? To this he says:

The underlying intention is this: because the *nayās*—such as the *naigama* and others—which have a single focus and culminate in the apprehension of a single property, proceed along the path of scripture (*śrutavartman*), that is, along the path of tradition, they do not depend on each individual intention, since it is the totality of them alone that determines the complete meaning.

Having thus explained the nature of *naya* and *pramāṇa*, he now says the following, desiring to describe the cognizer (*pramātṛ*), who pervades all *nayās* and *pramāṇas* because they abide therein through identity with him:
The living being (jīva) is the cognizer, that which manifests as other than itself, the agent, the enjoyer, and that which possesses transformation;
it is established through self-awareness and is not composed of the elements such as earth.
In this context, "jīva" (the living being) is so called because it lives throughout the three periods of time; the meaning is that it is the self (*ātman*) which sustains the vital breaths (*prāṇa*).
It is a "knower" (*pramātṛ*) because it cognizes, that is, it is the one who delimits the objects of knowledge (*prameya*). To the question of what its nature is, he says:
That which has the nature (*śīla*) of illuminating—that is, making manifest—both itself and others is "that which manifests itself and others" (*svānyanirbhāsī*);
that is to say, it is the illuminator of its own essential form and of objects. One who acts in such a way is the "agent" (*kartā*), and one who experiences is the "experiencer" (*bhoktā*).

*Vivartanam* is the turning toward successive states; *vivṛttiḥ* is transformation (*pariṇāmaḥ*). That which possesses this is *vivṛttimān*. That by which one's own self (*sva*) is cognized is *svasaṃvedanam*; that which is perfectly established (*samyak-siddhaḥ*), grounded, or realized through that is *svasaṃvedanasamsiddhaḥ*. Those of which earth (*kṣitiḥ*) and so forth are the first are "earth and the rest" (*kṣityādīni*).
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), water, fire, air, and space are included.
It is "without self" (anātmaka) because its own nature (svarūpa) does not exist as a self;
is this [absence of self] with respect to its own specific nature?
No; "non-selfhood of earth and so forth" (kṣityādyanātmaka) means that the self is not of the nature of earth and so forth—that is, it does not have the essential form of earth and so forth.
In this context, by the statement "the living being (jīva) is the knower" (pramātā), those who do not accept a transcendental (pāramārthika) knower are addressed.

However, those who maintain the doctrine of momentary dissolution consider that [self] to be non-ultimate, being constructed by false conceptualization and possessing an existence produced by beginningless, deeply rooted latencies awakened by the power of experiencing a succession of moments of consciousness;
he refutes them because the destruction of moments has already been rejected previously.
Because transformable things are established both externally and internally.
[NAV 31.3] Now, it may be objected that jars and the like are indeed seen to undergo destruction;
and their destruction must be produced either by a collection of causes such as a club or the like, or else for those things whose nature is indestructible.
Or [of things] whose nature is perishable. If the first alternative is held, that is incorrect,
because it is impossible to cause a nature to fall away,
since its form is fixed.

Otherwise, it would be impossible for it to possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Now, if you argue that its very nature—attained through the power of its own causes—is precisely such that it will perish upon encountering a cause of destruction, even so, is the proximity of that cause of destruction accidental, or is it produced by that very nature? If it is the first alternative, then [the nature] could be turned back even when present, through the intervention of a contrary condition.

Since the causes that bring those [factors] into proximity also depend upon their own complex of causes for bringing them into proximity, and since even those factors already in proximity can be removed by an opposing force,
and because of their accidental nature, their proximity is not necessarily certain to occur.
Consequently, some object such as a jar, for which the collection of causes for its own destruction is not present, would not perish;
yet this is undesirable, because there is no disagreement regarding the destruction of all produced things. Now, as for the second position:
If that were the case, then since those causes of destruction will also come into proximity later due to its power, let them come into proximity at the very first moment;

even so, the object remains momentary. If you argue that it was born with the specific nature of bringing about the cause of its own destruction after a fixed period determined by its own cause, even this does not escape momentariness. For instance:
It is said that by its own cause, this [entity] was produced with a nature capable of bringing about the conditions for its own destruction after a year.
Does that nature exist in the second moment following its moment of production, or not?
If it exists, then in that case, it must remain for another year.
In this way, even up until the final moment of the rainy season, if that entity possesses that very same nature, then it would follow that it remains for another rainy season;

and consequently, the entity would endure for infinite eons, because its nature as something remaining for the duration of the rainy season has not ceased. Now, if you say that in the second moment that nature no longer exists, [then...]
Alas, momentariness itself is established,
because remaining in that same state is the defining characteristic of it. Furthermore,
would the cause of destruction produce the destruction of an entity as something distinct from it or non-distinct?

If a distinct [effect] were produced, nothing would have been done [to the cause], and consequently, the entity would remain in its original state. If it is argued that "the relation with it is being produced," no;
for a relation distinct from identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*) has been refuted. Furthermore, neither of these two types of relations exists here.
Because identity with [the entity] is impossible for that which is distinct,

and because that which arises later from a different cause lacks the production of that [entity], it is not logical for destruction to be produced as something distinct. Furthermore, if it were produced as non-distinct, it would follow that the cause of destruction merely produces that very same entity itself.
Because non-exclusion is characterized by having that very nature. Nor is it something to be produced, since it is already established by its own causes;
for if it were produced, there would be only its persistence.
There is no dissolution. Therefore, for those things whose nature is non-perishable, destruction can never be produced at any later time;

however, for those whose nature is perishable, [destruction] occurs at every moment even prior [to any supposed cause], because it follows from the power of their own causes and does not depend on any other cause.
Because intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) has a fixed form;
therefore, it breathes even now, meaning it perishes at every moment.
To this, it is said: This is true.
However, just as you accept that destruction occurs at every moment because no cause for destruction is possible, why do you not likewise accept that subsistence and arising occur at every moment?
For the causes of those [latter two], when analyzed, are likewise impossible. To explain:
First, by means of a cause for stability, would entities be established as having an inherently unstable nature or an inherently stable nature?
The first position cannot withstand scrutiny,
because it is impossible to alter an inherent nature.
Because it possesses a specific, determinate nature— just like that which has the nature of being either conscious or unconscious—
otherwise its status as having a nature would be lost. Furthermore, in the second case, what need is there for a cause of persistence for things that are themselves stable by nature?
If it is argued that stability is indeed not accepted [by us], and therefore this is merely a criticism of what has not been admitted,
then alas, you are defeated!

For in this way, entities would not persist for even a single moment. If it is argued that they are indeed accepted as existing for only a moment, we reply that such non-persistence cannot be produced by even hundreds of causes for those things whose nature is inherently unstable; moreover, if that were their inherent nature, the operation of causes would be purposeless. Thus, being causeless, it would exist at all times.

A final oblation has been offered to the doctrine of momentary dissolution. Likewise, does the cause of origination bring about the production of that which possesses its own nature, or that which lacks it?
The first position is not fit to be accepted;
for a cause already occupied with producing what is itself productive merely grinds what has already been ground.
It whitens the conch;

for even in the absence of that [whiteness], it arises through its own inherent capacity. Nor is the second alternative worthy of acceptance, because that which is itself devoid of the nature of arising cannot be produced.
Otherwise, even things such as a rabbit’s horn would fall within the category of produced entities, since there is no distinction [between them and other things];
and consequently, there would be nothing that is an absolute non-entity (*atyantābhāva*). For example, because it is causeless, destruction occurs at every moment.

In the same way, since the reasoning has been demonstrated, one must accept that every entity that comes into being is pervaded by these three [characteristics]: persistence, origination, and cessation.

This being the case, the living soul (jīva) also—while maintaining its stability through its nature as a living being, consciousness, substance, and so forth—is characterized by arising and passing away through various transformations such as joy and sorrow, as well as through the grasping of successive objects; thus, it necessarily attains the status of a real, ultimate cognizer (pramātṛ).
[NAV_31.5] But surely, if you establish that arising, ceasing, and abiding exist at all times because they are causeless,

then how can this operation of the collection of causes— which is established by perception and other means of valid cognition through positive and negative concomitance— not be accepted? Nor is it possible to deny this.

For instance: jars and the like are perceived when there is the operation of a collection of causes such as the potter, and they are not perceived in its absence; thus they are said to be produced by those causes. Likewise, their persistence is due to that very power [of the causes] prior to the proximity of a cause of destruction.
Similarly, destruction—experiencing existence and non-existence depending on the proximity or non-proximity of a hammer and so forth—is understood to be caused by that [hammer].
"It is not without a cause. How is this so?

To this it is replied: "We do not deny the operation of causes in every respect; rather, when a substance undergoes transformation by way of its own arising, passing away, and persistence, causes exercise their function in producing its specific qualities."
Because we observe that their [the Vaiśeṣikas'] positive and negative concomitance follows that very [relation],
and because we do not engage in the denial of what is observed, for we adhere to the two criteria characterized by perception and logical reasoning.

We do not accept a reasoning that is devoid of experience, nor an experience that is bereft of reasoning, because such [an experience] would lack a cognitive object (*nirālambanatva*) by virtue of having an impossible thing as its domain; let this suffice for now.

By the phrase "manifesting itself and other things," he refutes the Mīmāṃsakas—who maintain that cognition is imperceptible—as well as the Yogācāras—who are proponents of cognition-only—just as he previously refuted them using the qualification of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as "illuminating both self and other."
Because there is no difference between knowledge and the knower in any way, the same logic applies to them.
By means of the two qualifiers "agent" and "experiencer," he refutes the Sāṃkhya doctrine;
for he introduces the statement "being an agent, one is also an experiencer" by way of a rhetorical question (*kāku*).

Because experience is impossible for one who is not an agent, since only one capable of accomplishing the act of experiencing can be an experiencer. Just as the designation of "redness" and so forth is applied to a crystal due to the proximity of a hibiscus flower or similar object, it is logical that even for one who is not an agent, there is the designation of experiencing pleasure, pain, and so forth, due to the influence of the limiting adjuncts of *prakṛti*. For instance:

If it is argued that the Puruṣa is designated as the "enjoyer" merely by its proximity to objects— consisting of pleasure, pain, and so forth— which have been reflected in the intellect (buddhi) that takes the form of a mirror for both primordial matter (prakṛti) and its transformations,
on the basis of the statement, "The Puruṣa perceives the object determined by the intellect," we say no;
because even when conditioned by primordial matter, no change of state is possible for the Puruṣa unless it undergoes some form of activity.
Because that which has not fallen away from its prior form is unfit for designation [as something else],
and because of the logical principle that upon such a falling away, activity would ensue through the abandonment of the former form and the superimposition of a subsequent form;

even in the example of the crystal, the redness appearing in a blind stone (andropala) due to the proximity of a hibiscus flower (*japākusuma*) and so forth, when it subsequently ceases to appear there, indicates a corresponding transformation (*pariṇāma*) of that [stone].
Otherwise, like a blind man or a stone, even in that case [of cognition], it would not manifest. Therefore, the status of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) is not possible for that which is inactive.
By the term "possessing transformation" (*vivṛttimān*), he rejects the knower (*pramātṛ*) postulated by the Naiyāyikas, Vaiśeṣikas, and others as being absolutely eternal and unchanging;

for it is impossible for one whose nature is entirely immovable to undergo the transformation of grasping an object. If it is argued that [the self] cognizes because of the inherence (*samavāya*) of distinct knowledge [in it], we say no.
Since inherence (*samavāya*) has already been refuted,
and since no other relation is possible with respect to a negative concomitance (*vyatirekin*),
because [the latter] is impossible otherwise; moreover, that [relation] does not exist in the case of a cognition characterized by negative concomitance.
Because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to apprehend it,
and because the experience of non-distinction (*avyatirekānubhava*) subverts that [notion]. Furthermore, if knowledge inheres in the self by virtue of the force of inherence (*samavāya*), [then...]
Since the selves (*ātman*) and their inherence (*samavāya*) are all-pervading and uniform in nature, why would [an object] not inhere in all selves, given the absence of any distinction?
And thus, by means of Devadatta’s cognition, Yajñadatta and others too would perceive the reality of the object. Furthermore, at the moment of the arising of cognition—

Furthermore, one who asserts that the subject remains exactly as it was in its prior state, such that it is a non-subject before and becomes a subject afterwards, indeed manifests madness within himself and nothing else; so let this matter rest for now.

Furthermore, with the second half [of the verse], by demonstrating that the living being (*jīva*) is distinct from the material elements and is apprehended through the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedanapratyakṣa*), he refutes the Cārvāka view;

for if it were not distinct from the material elements which are insentient by nature, there would follow the absurd consequence of the absence of the experience of transformations such as joy and sorrow, whose form is consciousness characterized by qualities different from those [elements]. [Objection: But surely it is the very material elements, transformed into the shape of the body, that project consciousness—which is distinct from the self—outward.
And that [consciousness] abides in those [elements] when they have been transformed by such a transformation; furthermore, in their absence, it dissolves back into those very same [elements].
Thus, even though there is an experience distinct from them, there is no proof of a transmigrating soul (*jīva*) who goes to another world.
This much alone suffices for the establishment of observed worldly transactions. This is not so;

for this pair is indeed perceived as experiencing conjunction—the body, which consists of the five elements, and consciousness. Even there, the body is experienced as insentient through a cognition that is outward-turned and takes the form of an object.
Furthermore, volition (*cetanā*) is directly realized through internal-reflexive perception (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*);

therefore, the position that [volition and its manifestation] are non-distinct has not even been raised, as it is refuted by their very appearance. Moreover, if you claim that when the two [the body and consciousness] appear as distinct, the elements themselves project volition, then it would follow that volition itself, having arrived from another existence as the place of birth, must produce the body which generates the delusion of the five elements.
Furthermore, if one desiring to go to another existence were to depart,
then that [body] presided over by it would perform activities such as moving,
whereas separated from it, it would remain like a piece of wood; thus, the body is indeed produced by the living soul (jīva).
Furthermore, we consider this conceptualization— that [the body] is produced by that [soul]— to be more logical,

because for the conscious soul (*jīva*), wandering through successive existences and producing successive bodies is possible due to its possession of karma. As the soul comes from another existence to the place of birth...

If it is argued that [consciousness] is not perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), then the same logic applies: the primary elements (*bhūta*) also do not manifest through direct perception as they project consciousness by means of assuming the form of the body. Alternatively, if it is postulated that consciousness is produced by those very elements transformed into the shape of the body and nothing else—on the grounds of "presumption from the impossibility otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*)—then [the following applies].
If that is so, then even though the bodily form is being assumed during the state of death, [the soul] is not perceived;

or rather, the transformation into the bodily form, being occasional, depends upon another cause. Therefore, by the force of the principle of "otherwise it would be impossible" (*anyathānupapatti*), we conclude that there must be a volition capable of producing that [body], which belongs to a living being who has come from another existence.
Furthermore, [it is said]:

It is indeed logical that the soul (jīva) proceeds toward the production of a body due to its connection with karma and consciousness; however, as for the elements (bhūta), what kind of elements would they proceed toward the production of consciousness—
would they be conscious or unconscious?
If the first alternative is accepted, then a pair of dilemmas arises:
is that consciousness distinct from them or non-distinct?

If it is different [from the elements], then, like the human body, even while existing together with the elements, it would lead one to infer a cause consisting of a self that is distinct from the elements; thus, the proof of the individual soul (jīva) remains exactly as before. But if it is non-different, then it follows that all elements would be one.

Because they are non-different from the single consciousness, like its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). If it is argued that there is no fault because the elements are non-different from their respective individual consciousnesses, we say no; for then it would follow that even in the human body produced by them, there would be five distinct consciousnesses generated by them. [The opponent might argue: "All five, acting together, produce the consciousness of the Great Person (*bṛhatpuruṣa*), just as many sesame seeds produce a jar of oil."
In that case, is this consciousness of the person (puruṣacaitanya) merely their conjunction, or is it produced by them, or is it something entirely different?
If the first alternative is held,
that is incorrect.
Because there is no mutual mixing among conscious entities, their conjunction is precluded;

otherwise, the consciousnesses of many persons would combine to produce another, even greater consciousness. Now, as for the second alternative, in that case too, do they possess any continuity or not?
If it exists, that is untenable, because— as before— it would entail the consequence of consciousness being produced as having five forms. If, on the other hand, it does not exist,
that too is incorrect.

Because production without a causal continuity (*niranvayotpāda*) is contradicted by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, the primary elements (*bhūta*), whether conscious or unconscious, cannot be capable of performing the activity of producing consciousness. Nor can they be unconscious, because being absolutely distinct [from consciousness], their production of consciousness would be contradictory;
otherwise, sand and the like would also be capable of performing the activity of producing oil and the like. Furthermore, [it is said]:

Consciousness must be produced either by the mere collection of those [elements] or by a specific transformation of them. The first hypothesis is not tenable, because consciousness is not perceived even when earth, water, fire, air, and space are combined. Regarding the second hypothesis, however, it must be stated what that "specificity" (vaiśiṣṭya) is. If you say it is the transformation into the shape of a body, then why does that not occur at all times?
If it is argued that [consciousness arises] due to dependence on some other cause,
then we infer that this other cause is the living consciousness brought over from another existence,
because that alone serves as the material cause corresponding to the consciousness produced by the transformation into the form of a body.
In its absence, even though there is the existence of a transformation into the form of a body during the state of death, consciousness is absent and activities such as walking are not observed;

therefore, we see it as logical that consciousness is not produced by the transformation into the form of a body, but rather that [the body] itself is produced by it. There is no means of valid cognition other than direct perception.

If it is argued that consciousness is not observed to undergo coming and going to other worlds by means of that [body], and therefore only those elements already perceived should be postulated as its cause— this is not so,
because we have already established that other means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) exist, having previously refuted the claim that perception alone is the only source of knowledge.

And thus, many inferences would proceed to establish the existence of a soul that follows to the next world. For example: the first desire for the breast shown by a newborn infant on that very day is preceded by a prior desire, because it is a desire, just like the desire for the breast on the second day or subsequent days.

Thus, this inference—by establishing that the desire for the first breast-feeding must be preceded by another desire—implies through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) the existence of a soul that migrates to the next world, because there is no other desire in that [present] birth. Other examples may be cited in the same way; let us leave it at that for now.
Therefore, this [soul] is the illuminator of itself and others, the agent, the enjoyer, consisting of both the eternal and the non-eternal, and distinct from the primary elements (*bhūta*).

It is established that the ultimate soul (*jīva*)— which is manifested through its own infinite modes (*paryāya*) occurring over beginningless and endless time, as inferred from the few of its own modes directly perceived, and which is grounded in valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)— is the knower (*pramātṛ*) that pervades all standpoints (*naya*) and means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Now, concluding the meaning of the treatise with the final verse, he says:

This systematic establishment of the means of valid cognition and so forth, though beginningless and endless in nature and well-known to all those engaged in worldly transaction, has nevertheless been proclaimed [here].
The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the categories of reasoning (*naya*) are included.
Their systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*) consists of their respective definitions and other characteristics, which constitute their established limits.
This very [sequence] is proclaimed as "conjunction" (*saṃsarga*) by virtue of the state just described. To the question "Of what nature is it?", he says:
"The beginning is the origin;
the end is the conclusion."
That whose nature (ātman) is such that it has neither beginning nor end is "anādinidhanātmikā";

although it is well-known— even conventionally established— for all worldly transactions (sarvasaṃvyavahārāṇām), which include the entirety of linguistic and practical dealings distinguished by various categories such as worldly people and non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthika), for if it were not so established, there would follow the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the total cessation of all worldly transactions.

And when that [investigation] is cut off and no further inquiry arises, there is no establishment of any reality whatsoever. This is understood to be proclaimed for the purpose of removing the delusion of those who are unlearned, those who hold contrary views, and those who are confused;

for even regarding an object established by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), some people still possess delusion in the form of non-determination or error due to powerful obscurations, false views, and latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), and it is with the aim of dispelling that [delusion] that compassionate persons apply themselves [to teaching], provided they have the capacity to do so.

Out of fear of the terrifying roar of the lion of the *syādvāda*, the deer-like heretics—who rely on fallacious reasoning and have no other refuge—flee in terror with their eyes rolling and trembling; leaving them behind, the Jina approaches that [refuge]; take refuge in him! NAV_32.1:1:1.
This devotion to the Blessed One has been manifested by me through the narration of a portion of His teachings, not from my own intelligence.
Therefore, whatever improper thing has occurred here due to delusion, may the virtuous, having shown compassion toward me, purify it.
By whatever accumulation of merit has been accomplished by me here through the desire to compose this various *Nyāyāvatāra-vivṛti*,
may my mind always be intent upon performing the welfare of others until the end of existence, and remain solely devoted to the doctrine of the Lord of Jinas.
Thus ends the Nyāyāvatāravivṛti.
This is the work of the teacher Siddhavyākhyānika, the author of the commentary on the *Tarkaprakaraṇa*.
